also_shown_in: discussed also in Supplement S5.6 (DM × ML) as the trace-only boundary
subgroup: trace and time-series anomaly models (no source access)
row_justification: Trained without labels on 9,480 hourly Olympus DAO points (12 features, April 2021 to April 2022), the model is judged only by case studies of the four highest-scoring periods it flagged; the paper reports no ground truth or detection metric ("data without accurate labels or ground truth", Section IV.B), and none of the four cases is confirmed as an attack (a rise in activity of unknown cause, one user's repeated unstake and restake of 79,844 OHM that "may be part of a more complicated attack" or "a simple mistake", the V2 announcement, and the end of bonding). With no labeled set, the stated target ("A malicious attack attempt and structural changes in DeFi protocols", abstract) → glossary line 3 (malicious attack attempts) → PM ‡.
column_justification: Presented as a deep learning model (title, abstract, contribution list) → ML; a TimeVAE encoder embeds each day of hourly features, a transformer built on the standard PyTorch transformer relates 28 daily embeddings, both trained from scratch without labels, and the averaged reconstruction error against a fixed threshold (32.3, the top 0.1 % of scores) issues the anomaly verdict; nothing is pretrained, and no text is generated.
type_evidence: title: "Anomaly VAE-Transformer: A deep learning approach for anomaly detection in decentralized finance"; abstract: "We propose a deep learning model, anomaly VAE-Transformer, which combines the variational autoencoder ... and the transformer"; contribution list: "the first study on anomaly detection in DeFi using deep learning technology" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML; the transformer is trained for the task, not a pretrained generative model (B.2 boundary)

first_release: cited version, 2016; preprint ePrint:2016/633 (2016-06) in the same year
row_justification: Oyente runs on 19,366 contracts from the first 1,459,999 Ethereum blocks and flags 8,833 of them (1,682 distinct bytecodes), counted in contracts per class in Fig. 12 (mishandled exceptions 5,411, transaction-ordering dependence 3,056, reentrancy 340, timestamp dependence 83), with correctness checked by hand on the 175 flagged contracts with source (10 false positives, Section 6.2.1); all four classes are statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES. Transaction-ordering dependence is coded ES as a contract-agnostic property (the final state depends on how miners order the transactions invoking the contract, Section 3.1); the sheet codes it ES wherever it occurs.
column_justification: Symbolic execution with hand-defined bug-pattern checks for the four classes; nothing is learned or generated
type_evidence: title: "Making smart contracts smarter" (no type named); abstract: "we build a symbolic execution tool called Oyente to find potential security bugs"; contribution 3 of four: "We provide Oyente, a symbolic execution tool which analyses Ethereum smart contracts to detect bugs" → one type named (symbolic execution with hand-defined checks) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

first_release: cited version, 2018; preprint arXiv:1806.01143 (2018-06) in the same year
row_justification: Securify checks the seven properties it defines over EVM semantics in Section 5.3 (Ether liquidity, no writes after calls, restricted writes, restricted transfer, handled exception, transaction ordering dependency in three variants, and validated arguments) on 24,594 bytecode contracts and 100 Solidity contracts, counted in relevant instructions (call or sstore instructions, and contracts for Ether liquidity); in the Solidity set every reported violation and compliance is confirmed by hand and each warning classified true or false (Fig. 12). Each property is contract-agnostic, restricted writes and restricted transfer being generic checks on the caller, so every case is ES without per-property counts → ES; transaction ordering dependency (an Ether transfer whose execution, receiver, or amount depends on storage or balance) is coded ES as a contract-agnostic property, as for Oyente.
column_justification: Hand-written compliance and violation patterns, in a domain-specific language over semantic facts that stratified Datalog derives from the decompiled contract, decide each property; nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Securify: Practical security analysis of smart contracts" (no type named); abstract: "we present Securify, a security analyzer for Ethereum smart contracts that is scalable, fully automated"; contribution 2 of four: "A set of compliance and violation security patterns that capture sufficient conditions to prove and disprove practical security properties" → one type named (hand-written patterns) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

first_release: cited version, 2019; preprint arXiv:1908.09878 (2019-08) in the same year
row_justification: Slither's quantitative evaluation runs only its reentrancy detector, on the 1,000 contracts with the most transactions and source on Etherscan (Section V-A), and flags 112 contracts with 10.9 % false positives, estimated by manual review of a random sample of at least 50 flagged contracts (Table I; true positives are not counted), and finds both the DAO and SpankChain reentrancies; one class needs no breakdown, and reentrancy is statable from EVM call semantics alone → ES. The other detectors the paper names (shadowing, uninitialized variables, suicidal contracts, locked ether, arbitrary sending of ether, and the closed-source race conditions, unprotected privileged functions, and incorrect token manipulations) are not evaluated, and none is defined as a standard-conformance check, so no secondary row is recorded.
column_justification: Anomaly is defined by hand-written detectors (over twenty, e.g. reentrancy, uninitialized variables, suicidal, locked ether) run as dataflow and taint queries over the SlithIR representation; nothing is learned or generated.
type_evidence: title: "Slither: A static analysis framework for smart contracts"; abstract: "This paper describes Slither, a static analysis framework designed to provide rich information about Ethereum smart contracts"; contribution 1 of three: "We present Slither, a framework for static analysis of Solidity contracts" → one type named (static analysis) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: ZEUS's results are reported on 1,524 unique contracts (by sha256 checksum, from 22,493 contracts at distinct addresses), each result validated by hand for false positives and false negatives (Section VI, Table 4); contracts flagged unsafe per class are integer overflow 1,095 (40 false positives), transaction order dependence 607 (16), failed send 447, unchecked send 324 (3), block state dependence 250, reentrancy 54, and transaction state dependence 8, with no false negatives, all statable from the code and EVM or Solidity semantics → ES; transaction order dependence is coded ES as a contract-agnostic property, as for Oyente. The fairness paragraph of Section VI-B checks user-written policies on representative DAO, game, token, and wallet contracts (blacklisted developers, a minimum investment, a cap on dice rolls per player, no transfer to oneself, a per-transaction limit), statable over contract state → PM secondary; its selfdestruct owner policy (284 of 1,524 contracts, about 5.6 % violating, no false alarms) is a generic owner check (ES).
column_justification: Built-in checks for each correctness bug class (LLVM passes) and user-written policies in an XACML-styled template are verified by abstract interpretation and symbolic model checking, with SeaHorn emitting constrained Horn clauses that SMT solvers discharge; nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "ZEUS: Analyzing safety of smart contracts" (no type named); abstract: "a framework to verify the correctness and validate the fairness of smart contracts"; contribution 3 of six: "a symbolic model checking framework for verification of correctness and fairness policies" → one type named (verification by symbolic model checking) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: The largest labeled set is the comparison with a manual audit of three projects (Genesis, Hive, and Populous; Section 4.2, Table 2), 51 true issues, of which SmartCheck reports 27 with 60 false positives and misses 24; it is reported per project with no per-type breakdown → glossary line 2 (audit findings) → ES ‡. The 4,600-contract scan (Section 4.3, Table 3, per-pattern counts) was "not manually verified" and is not a labeled set. SmartCheck's 21 target types (Table 1) are execution-semantics properties or development issues that reach no level. The Token API pattern encodes ERC-20's bool-returning approve, transfer, and transferFrom (reads_description yes, shared), but its advice not to throw in them is not a property ERC-20 states, so there is no DM secondary.
column_justification: XPath queries hand-written over an ANTLR-derived XML parse tree define every finding.
type_evidence: title: "SmartCheck: Static analysis of Ethereum smart contracts"; abstract: "an extensible static analysis tool that detects them"; no contribution list; Section 3.2: "We detected vulnerability patterns by using XPath [xpa] queries on the IR" → static analysis with hand-written patterns, B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: The governing set is the manual inspection of 13 flagged contracts with source code (Section 6.1, RQ1.B), 16 warnings of which 13 are confirmed vulnerabilities in 11 contracts (81% precision). Each warning belongs to one of MadMax's three classes (unbounded mass operations, wallet griefing, and overflow of loop induction variables), and the per-contract notes describe the confirmed cases as unbounded iteration, wallet griefing, and overflow or underflow, all gas or arithmetic properties statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES, no secondary. The run over the 91.8k unique contracts on the chain (4.1% flagged for unbounded iteration, 0.12% for wallet griefing, and 1.2% for loop-variable overflow, RQ1.A) was not manually verified and is not a labeled set.
column_justification: Datalog rules in Souffle over Vandal-decompiled bytecode (loops, data flow, memory structures) supply the vulnerability definitions
type_evidence: title: "MadMax: Surviving out-of-gas conditions in Ethereum smart contracts"; abstract: "a static program analysis technique to automatically detect gas-focused vulnerabilities with very high confidence"; contributions (Section 1): "A decompiler from EVM bytecode to structured low-level IR", "The identification of gas-focused vulnerabilities", "Abstractions for high-level data-structures and program constructs", and "We validate the approach"; no type named beyond static analysis → B.2 step 3, logic-based specifications in Datalog over Vandal output, nothing learned → Rule-based

row_justification: Osiris finds arithmetic (41,379), truncation (2,738) and signedness (405) integer bugs in 42,108 of 1.2M contracts, properties of EVM integer semantics alone
column_justification: Symbolic execution plus taint analysis with hand-defined out-of-bounds integer constraints per bug category
type_evidence: title: "Osiris: Hunting for integer bugs in Ethereum smart contracts"

first_release: cited version, 2018; preprint arXiv:1807.03932 (2018-07) in the same year
row_justification: ContractFuzzer fuzzes 6,991 Etherscan contracts with verified source and flags 459 contracts, counted once per class in Table 5 (timestamp dependency 152, gasless send 138, block number dependency 82, exception disorder 36, freezing ether 30, reentrancy 14, dangerous delegatecall 7), with a true-positive rate reported per class (100 % for five classes, 96.05 % for timestamp and 96.34 % for block number dependency) after manual checks (Section 5.4); every oracle is statable from EVM semantics → ES. The DAO contract and the contract behind the first Parity wallet attack are among the detections.
column_justification: Hand-defined test oracles over instrumented EVM execution logs decide; fuzz inputs come from ABI, not a learned model.
type_evidence: title: "ContractFuzzer: Fuzzing smart contracts for vulnerability detection"; abstract: "In this work, we present ContractFuzzer, a novel fuzzer to test Ethereum smart contracts for security vulnerabilities"; contribution 2 of three: "a set of new test oracles that can precisely detect real-world vulnerabilities within smart contracts" → one type named (fuzzing with hand-defined oracles) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: The four-page tool paper evaluates only reachability of inserted assert(false) targets, 459 placed after every statement of 12 clean VeriSmart contracts (44 discarded as reached in the constructor) and others inserted into TetherToken, with 40 randomly selected targets run from each (Section 4), and names no bug class; its oracle is user-written echidna_ properties and assertions, which state no named description. User-written properties with no evaluated bug class → glossary line 4 (B.1, user-supplied specifications) → ES ‡.
column_justification: The notion of a violation is supplied entirely by user-written Boolean echidna_ properties and Solidity assert statements, which the ABI-based fuzzer, with configurable coverage feedback, tries to falsify; no learned model or generative component enters the decision → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Echidna: Effective, usable, and fast fuzzing for smart contracts"; abstract: "This paper introduces an open-source smart contract fuzzer called Echidna that makes it easy to automatically generate tests to detect violations in assertions and custom properties"; no contribution list → one type named (fuzzing against user-written properties) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: Smartian's largest labeled set is B3, 500 Etherscan contracts, on which it raises 219 alarms, 211 of them confirmed by manual inspection (integer bug 170, block state dependency 20, transaction origin use 11, multiple send 5, ether leak 3, mishandled exception 2, Table V); its other sets are B2, 82 labeled bugs in 72 SmartBugs contracts (13 block state dependency, 50 mishandled exception, 19 reentrancy, Section V-A3), and B1, 58 integer-bug CVEs in 58 VeriSmart contracts (two found not to be real bugs). Every class is a contract-agnostic property statable from EVM semantics → ES.
column_justification: Fixed bug oracles in a data-flow-guided fuzzer; static and dynamic data-flow analysis only steer transaction-sequence generation
type_evidence: title: "Smartian: Enhancing smart contract fuzzing with static and dynamic data-flow analyses"; abstract: "We implement our ideas on a practical open-source fuzzer, named SMARTIAN"; contribution 3 of four: "We present SMARTIAN, a grey-box fuzzer for smart contracts" → one type named (fuzzing with fixed bug oracles, steered by data-flow analysis) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

first_release: cited version, 2023; preprint arXiv:2306.17135 (2023-06) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 42 previously exploited DeFi projects of Section 6.2, for 36 of which ItyFuzz finds a concrete exploit that executes on a fork; the 42 are not broken down by exploit type (Table 1 types six ablation targets, which the paper does not present as a breakdown of the set) → glossary line 3 ("previously exploited projects", exploits on DeFi protocols) → PM ‡. B1 (57 ERC20 contracts from VeriSmart), B2 (72 contracts), and B3 (500 contracts) measure instruction coverage only (Figs. 7 to 9) and carry no labels, so they are not labeled sets. The three reentrancy exploits in Table 1 give the ES secondary, and the two hacked projects of Section 6.4 (Nomad Bridge and Team Finance) are PM. Each exploit witnesses a finding of the work's own oracle in a paper that evaluates its findings, so the work is a detector, not offensive (B.3).
column_justification: Snapshot-based, coverage-guided fuzzing with dataflow and comparison waypoints (Sections 4 and 5) issues the verdict, a concrete exploit that runs on a fork; vulnerable states are decided by hand-written oracles (a custom oracle for Bacon Protocol and EGD Finance, Section 6.2), and nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "ItyFuzz: Snapshot-based fuzzer for smart contract"; abstract: "we introduce a novel snapshot-based fuzzer ITYFUZZ for testing smart contracts"; contributions (Section 1): "a novel snapshot-based fuzzing algorithm to reduce re-execution overhead" and "a fast and efficient smart contract fuzzer ITYFUZZ"; no type is named → B.2 step 3, the method's hand-written oracles over fuzzing, nothing learned → Rule-based

row_justification: The governing set is the 16 contracts, 52 before identical and alike code was grouped, that Sereum flagged when replaying 77,987,922 transactions up to block 4,500,000 and that were investigated by hand (Section VI, Fig. 10); two are confirmed re-entrancy exploits, the DAO (2,294 attack transactions) and DSEthToken (43), and the rest are classed by false-positive cause. Re-entrancy, the one class evaluated here and in the three attacks the authors craft (Section III), is statable from EVM call semantics alone, so no breakdown is needed → ES.
column_justification: A hand-written run-time policy issues the verdict, in which the hardened EVM taints storage variables that influence a conditional jump and write locks reject updates to them in a re-entrant call (Section IV) → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Sereum: Protecting existing smart contracts against re-entrancy attacks" (no type); abstract: "propose a novel smart contract security technology, dubbed Sereum (Secure Ethereum), which protects existing, deployed contracts against re-entrancy attacks in a backwards compatible way based on run-time monitoring and validation"; contributions (a prose paragraph in Section I): "a hardened EVM which leverages taint tracking" and write locks; no type is named, and the method is a hand-written run-time policy → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: VerX verifies 83 Past-LTL safety properties of 12 real-world projects (138 contracts; Section IX-A, Tables I and II), each property checked for violations; they are specifications formalized for the evaluation (the paper says only that properties are elicited by inspecting documentation and formalizing key requirements, and ties none to a named description), so they are placed by what they state (B.1 user-supplied specifications), 13 user-based access-control properties at ES and 70 at PM (44 state-based, 15 state-machine, 8 aggregate, and 3 multi-contract invariants over contract state) → PM; ES secondary from the access-control properties and from the 41 assertion and arithmetic tests of the engine comparison (Section IX-D, Table IV).
column_justification: VerX checks Past-LTL safety specifications written for each project by symbolic execution with delayed predicate abstraction, extracting most abstraction predicates automatically from the code and the property; the hand-written specification decides, nothing is learned, and no generative model is involved → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "VerX: Safety verification of smart contracts" (verification); abstract: "We present VERX, the first automated verifier able to prove functional properties of Ethereum smart contracts"; contributions 1 and 2 of three: a delayed predicate abstraction that combines symbolic execution with abstraction, and "The first end-to-end verification system, called VERX" → one type named (verification of specified properties) → B.2 step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: The governing set is the receiver contracts flagged over 9,661,593 transactions from block 7,000,000 and checked by hand from source code, decompiled bytecode, or traces (Sections 8.2 to 8.4, unit contracts), with re-entrancy confirmed in 17 of 30, UncheckedCall in 213 of the 216 open-source contracts among 1,430, and Suicidal in 18 of 18; re-entrancy, an unchecked call, and a selfdestruct with no caller check are each a VM-semantic property of the victim contract → ES.
column_justification: Hand-written Datalog detection rules, run in Soufflé over the control and data dependencies encoded from replayed EVM traces, issue the verdict → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "TXSPECTOR: Uncovering attacks in Ethereum from transactions" (no type); abstract: "we propose TXSPECTOR, a generic, logic-driven framework to investigate Ethereum transactions for attack detection"; contribution 1: "the first generic and logic-driven framework for inspecting the real-world attacks in Ethereum"; no type is named, and Section 7 reads "Detection Rules are written in Soufflé, which is a variant of the Datalog language" → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: Benchmark study, row n/a. Nine analysis tools are run on 69 annotated vulnerable contracts, whose 115 vulnerabilities the authors tagged by line and DASP category (Table 3), and on 47,518 unlabeled contracts with source code on Etherscan (428,337 analyses); together the tools detect 42% of the annotated vulnerabilities. By Table 3, 105 of the 115 are execution-semantics properties statable from the code (access control 19 in 17 contracts, arithmetic 22 in 14, bad randomness 31 in 8, denial of service 7 in 6, reentrancy 8 in 7, short addresses 1 in 1, time manipulation 5 in 4, and unchecked low-level calls 12 in 5); the other ten (front running 7 in 4, unknown unknowns 3 in 3) cannot change the majority → shown in the ES row.
column_justification: The benchmark scores nine analyzers (HoneyBadger, Maian, Manticore, Mythril, Osiris, Oyente, Securify, Slither, and SmartCheck), each applying hand-written patterns, rules, or oracles by static analysis, symbolic or concolic execution, or dynamic analysis → Rule-based, the column of the detectors it scores (B.3, benchmark)
type_evidence: title: "Empirical review of automated analysis tools on 47,587 Ethereum smart contracts" names no type; abstract: "we present an empirical evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art automated analysis tools"; contributions 1 and 3: "A dataset of annotated vulnerable Solidity smart contracts" and "An execution framework that includes 9 pre-configured smart contract analysis tools" → a benchmark of rule-based analyzers → Rule-based (B.3, benchmark)

row_justification: Every evaluated case is one class, a storage collision, in which contracts that share storage through DELEGATECALL disagree on the type of a slot (Section III), between a proxy and its logic contract or between two logic contracts. The largest labeled set is the 956 contracts for which Crush synthesized an end-to-end exploit replayed on a private fork, out of 39,895 collisions in 14,891 potentially vulnerable contracts (Section V); the ground truth of 5,335 proxies holds 102 true collisions, 98 of them found (Table VI, counted in collisions). A storage collision is statable from EVM storage and DELEGATECALL semantics alone (B.1 ES), and one class needs no breakdown → ES.
column_justification: Hand-written type inference by program slicing and symbolic execution over bytecode, and collision rules over the inferred slot types, decide each finding; exploit synthesis only witnesses findings, and no learned or generative component is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Not your type! Detecting storage collision vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "we propose CRUSH, a novel analysis system that discovers these flaws and synthesizes proof-of-concept exploits" (no type); contribution list, item 2: "a novel approach that leverages symbolic execution and program slicing to detect and exploit storage collisions"; one type named, symbolic analysis → step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: The governing set is the 23,327 contracts that six tools (Oyente, ZEUS, Maian, Securify, MadMax, and teEther) flagged in six classes, each checked for exploitation in traces up to block 10,200,000 (Figure 11, unit contracts), with re-entrancy 4,337 flagged and 116 exploited, unhandled exceptions 11,427 and 264, locked ether 7,285 and 0, transaction order dependency 1,881 and 54, integer overflow 2,492 and 62, and unrestricted action 5,163 and 42, or 463 exploited (1.98%) with each contract counted once. Every class is statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES.
column_justification: Exploitation is identified by hand-written Datalog queries, one per vulnerability class, over the EVM execution traces of 20,241,730 transactions (Section 4, Figure 11), with no learned or generated component → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Smart contract vulnerabilities: Vulnerable does not imply exploited" (no type); abstract: "We survey the 23,327 vulnerable contracts reported by six recent academic projects"; contribution 1: "We propose a Datalog-based formulation for performing analysis over Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) execution traces"; no type is named, and the method is hand-written Datalog queries over the encoded traces (Section 4) → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

identifier: IEEE Trans. Syst., Man, Cybern.: Syst. 2022
row_justification: Adjacent (account-level fraud on a smart-contract chain, B.3), row n/a. The labeled set is 1,259 phishing addresses reported by both EtherScamDB and Etherscan before March 10, 2019, against 1,259 randomly sampled unlabeled addresses, classified as nodes of Ethereum transaction subnetworks (about 60,442 nodes and 236,222 edges on average over 50 subnetworks, Table I). Phishing is a fraud against users, neither one of the B.1 scam mechanics nor a protocol-mechanism invariant; the entry is shown in the PM row, as account-level fraud is (Supplementary Appendix B.1).
column_justification: trans2vec, a random-walk network embedding biased by transaction amounts and timestamps and trained with a skip-gram model, learns address features, and a one-class SVM classifies each address as normal or phishing → ML
type_evidence: title: "Who are the phishers? Phishing scam detection on Ethereum via network embedding" names a learned method (network embedding); abstract: "we propose a novel network embedding algorithm called trans2vec to extract the features of the addresses" and "we adopt the one-class support vector machine (SVM) to classify the nodes into normal and phishing ones"; contribution 1: "the first investigation on phishing identification on Ethereum via network embedding" → one type named → ML (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: Chen et al. evaluate on 1,382 verified Etherscan contracts, 131 Ponzi and 1,251 non-Ponzi, inspected by hand by Bartoletti et al. and re-examined by the authors as ground truth (precision 0.94, recall 0.81, and F-score 0.86 with account and opcode features, Table 2); 45 of 54 hidden Ponzi contracts from Bartoletti et al. are also detected, and the estimate of more than 400 running schemes comes from applying the model to 280,704 unlabeled contracts. A Ponzi contract's payout mechanics breach holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams) → PM, and a detector of one scam class evaluated on that class alone needs no breakdown.
column_justification: Presented as an approach using data mining and machine learning (abstract) → ML; an XGBoost classifier over account-behavior features (known rate, balance, investment and payment counts, and others) and opcode frequencies from disassembled bytecode outputs a Ponzi probability, with 0.5 as the threshold (Section 3.4).
type_evidence: title: "Detecting Ponzi schemes on Ethereum: Towards healthier blockchain technology" (no type named); abstract: "this paper proposes an approach to detect Ponzi schemes on blockchain by using data mining and machine learning methods"; no contribution list, and the introduction says "a classification model based on XGBoost is proposed" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML

row_justification: The paper collects 184 Ponzi contracts, 138 whose Solidity code meets the four requirements of Figure 2 on manual inspection (Section 3.2) and 46 of 55 bytecode-similarity candidates (normalized Levenshtein distance below 0.35) confirmed by comparing their decompiled code with known schemes, and types them in Table 2 (151 chain-shaped, four tree-shaped, four waterfall, four handover, and 21 other); a set of one scam class needs no breakdown, and Ponzi payout mechanics are PM (B.1 scams). As a study it is shown in this cell and not counted.
column_justification: Ponzi contracts are identified by manual inspection against four hand-stated requirements R1-R4 plus a fixed normalized-Levenshtein bytecode-similarity threshold (NLD < 0.35), i.e. hand-stated criteria with no learned boundary → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Dissecting Ponzi schemes on Ethereum: Identification, analysis, and impact" names no type; abstract: "We present a comprehensive survey of Ponzi schemes on Ethereum"; contributions, first: "a set of criteria for determining when a smart contract implements a Ponzi scheme"; the criteria are requirements stated by hand (Figure 2), applied by manual inspection and a fixed bytecode-similarity threshold → one type (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

first_release: cited version, 2018; preprint arXiv:1803.00646 (2018-03) in the same year
row_justification: Classifies Bitcoin addresses as Ponzi-scheme related from transaction features; account-level scam detection on a non-contract chain
column_justification: Supervised classifiers (data mining over address transaction features) supply the Ponzi score
type_evidence: title: "Data mining for detecting Bitcoin Ponzi schemes"

first_release: cited version, 2020 (journal extension of the INFOCOM 2018 paper)
row_justification: Study shown; Algorithm 1 (Section 7.2) flags 48 of 48,298,522 accounts that created at least 10,000 rarely used contracts, 34 of them DoS attackers (created contracts with no jump-table structure) and 14 others, of which the authors examined six by hand (two tied to GasToken, four that collect once-per-account token promotion rewards, SiaCashCoin's among them, many times through created contracts); abnormal-account detection on the platform, not a DeFi-mechanism detector → adjacent also applies → row n/a (B.3); display_row PM, the row of the four reward-theft accounts and the sheet's display row for account-level abuse (Supplementary Appendix B.1); the DoS accounts exhaust platform resources and take no level, and no case lies at the trust boundary.
column_justification: No B.2 type is named in the title, the abstract's proposal sentence, or the contribution list, so the method decides (step 3); Algorithm 1 applies hand-set thresholds over the creation, invocation, and money-flow graphs (T1 = 10,000 contracts created, and T2 = T3 = 0.5 bounding the invocations and the Ether received per created contract), and a jump-table check marks the DoS accounts; nothing is learned (the paper leaves learned thresholds to future work) → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: 'Understanding Ethereum via graph analysis' (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: 'We conduct the first systematic study on Ethereum by leveraging graph analysis to characterize three major activities on Ethereum' (no type); contribution list: 'We propose new approaches based on the three graphs to handle three important security issues in Ethereum, including attack forensics, anomaly detection, and deanonymization' (no type) → step 3, the method decides.

row_justification: Two sets, each labeled per function as vulnerable or safe for one type at a time: ESC (40,932 Ethereum contracts, about 307,396 functions) for reentrancy and timestamp dependence, and VSC (4,170 VNT Chain contracts, about 13,761 functions) for infinite loop. The paper gives no positive counts, but each evaluation covers one class, and all three classes are execution-semantics properties statable from the code and the VM semantics (B.1, a set of one class needs no breakdown) → ES under any breakdown.
column_justification: Anomaly is a label learned by DR-GCN and the temporal message propagation network over normalized contract graphs built from syntactic and semantic code structure; no rules or generative model supply the boundary.
type_evidence: title: "Smart contract vulnerability detection using graph neural network" names ML; abstract: "we propose a degree-free graph convolutional neural network (DR-GCN) and a novel temporal message propagation network (TMP) to learn from the normalized graphs for vulnerability detection"; contribution 1: "We introduce a novel temporal message propagation network (TMP) and a degree-free GCN (DR-GCN)" → one type named → ML (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: Evaluated on ESC, 307,396 functions from 40,932 Ethereum contracts (reentrancy, 89.15% accuracy; timestamp dependence, 89.02%), and on VSC, 13,761 functions from 4,170 VNT Chain contracts (infinite loop, 83.21%), each labeled vulnerable or safe for one type. No positive counts are given, but every class is an execution-semantics property statable from the code (B.1, a set of one class needs no breakdown) → ES.
column_justification: A temporal message propagation GNN over a normalized contract graph, fused with expert-pattern features, is trained to output the vulnerability label
type_evidence: title: "Combining graph neural networks with expert knowledge for smart contract vulnerability detection"; abstract: "we explore using graph neural networks and expert knowledge for smart contract vulnerability detection" and "combine the graph feature with designed expert patterns to yield a final detection system"; contribution 1: "we are the first to investigate the idea of fusing conventional expert patterns and graph-neural-network extracted features", the two presented equally → tie-break (B.2 step 5), the newer type → ML (Rule-based secondary)

row_justification: The largest labeled set is 1,200 contracts drawn by keyword from the 47,587-contract Ethereum Open Dataset and labeled by hand by three graduate students, 300 per type (Table 3). Of these, 754 are vulnerable (reentrancy 203, block info dependency 184, nested call 187, and transaction state dependency 180), all statable from the code and EVM semantics (a call inside an unbounded loop is a gas denial of service, and tx.origin used for authorization is a generic signer check) → ES by evaluation. The wild set of 1,673 contracts (81 flagged, 120 labeled by hand) is smaller as a labeled set.
column_justification: A heterogeneous graph attention network with node-level and path-level attention, trained on contract semantic graphs built from a Slither-based intermediate representation, classifies each contract → ML. Hand-written core-node selection rules for each vulnerability type (Table 1) mark the nodes the network weighs and issue no verdict (Rule-based secondary).
type_evidence: title: "SCVHunter: Smart contract vulnerability detection based on heterogeneous graph attention network"; abstract: "we propose SCVHunter, an extensible framework for smart contract vulnerability detection. Specifically, SCVHunter designs a heterogeneous semantic graph construction phase based on intermediate representations and a vulnerability detection phase based on a heterogeneous graph attention network"; contributions: "an extensible new approach for smart contract vulnerability detection using CSG and GNN" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML

first_release: arXiv:2405.11035 (2024-05); same system, author list differs in part
row_justification: DeFiTail's largest labeled set is 14,301 data paths extracted from 3,216 hacked DeFi events gathered from the REKT database, with 61 access-control and 89 flash-loan positives (Section IV-A1, unit not stated) and, counted in data paths, 559 and 692 positives against 1,336 negatives (Section V-C). Access control, programs that "fail to effectively manage permission assignments", is a generic missing check (ES); flash-loan exploits, whose logic is meant to "influence market tokens and price fluctuations", violate price consistency (PM). Flash-loan positives outnumber access-control ones in both counts, so the majority is PM; the access-control class and the 15 CVEs of the access-control evaluation (Table VI) give the ES secondary.
column_justification: A BERT-structure encoder of four transformer layers over data-path sequences and a two-layer GCN over cross-contract CFGs, trained on labeled paths between attacker and victim contracts, give the verdict as a weighted sum of their outputs; an encoder that generates no text is ML (B.2 step 2), and a symbolic execution stack only removes infeasible paths (Rule-based secondary).
type_evidence: title: "Penetrating the hostile: Detecting DeFi protocol exploits through cross-contract analysis" (no type named); abstract: "In this paper, we propose DeFiTail, the first framework that utilizes deep learning technology for access control and flash loan exploit detection"; contribution 1: "we propose the first inspection framework DeFiTail, to detect DeFi attacks from the perspective of interaction between attacker and victim" (no type named); one type named, in the abstract → ML (B.2 step 3)

first_release: arXiv:2104.15068 (2021-04); same system, author list differs in part
row_justification: DeFiRanger detects direct and indirect price-manipulation attacks that violate DEX/lending price invariants: in a 26-day backtest over 92,325,423 Ethereum and BSC transactions, 129 of the 155 transactions it flags are attacks (precision 0.831), in 26 known and 15 previously unknown incidents, and a deployment found 14 zero-days (Sections I and VII-B, TDSC version)
column_justification: Hand-written attack patterns expressed over DeFi operations (trade, liquidity add/cancel) lifted from a cash-flow tree of the transaction
type_evidence: title: "DeFiRanger: Detecting DeFi price manipulation attacks"

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2406.11157 (2024-06) in the same year
row_justification: Evaluated on 208 confirmed price-manipulation attack transactions vs 2,080 benign; price manipulation violates the pool/oracle pricing invariant.
column_justification: GNNs trained on cash-flow graphs built from transaction token transfers learn the attack boundary; no LLM.
type_evidence: title: "DeFiGuard: A price manipulation detection service in DeFi using graph neural networks"

row_justification: The comparative set of Section 5.2 mixes on-chain attack transactions from Zhou et al. (2020), DeFiHackLabs, and BlockSec into randomly selected non-attack transactions at under 5 % attacks (unit: transaction), and its attacks fall in five stated categories only (reentrancy, honeypot, flash loan, integer overflow, and call injection), for which Table 1 reports precision and recall per category with no per-category counts. The 30-shot setting trains on 30 known attacks per category and tests on the rest, so each category holds more than 30 attacks and the set, at under 5 % attacks, more than 3,000 transactions, more than the 2,761 flags of the 31-day run in the wild (Section 5.4); it governs. Reentrancy, integer overflow (arithmetic), and call injection (an attacker-controlled external call) are execution-semantics, and honeypot (a trap mechanic, B.1 scams) and flash loan (flash-loan price manipulation, price consistency) are protocol-mechanism → ES by the plurality of its listed types (B.1, known-list rule), three of five, ‡ as no per-case breakdown exists; the honeypot and flash-loan categories give the PM secondary. The run in the wild, whose 1,707 attacks three non-author experts confirmed by majority vote (Table 3), adds the out secondary for its 1,692 address-poisoning attacks, in which the victim signs a transfer to a look-alike address, beside 13 rug pulls and two exploits.
column_justification: A transaction model pre-trained with web-scale function comments as supervision scores transactions by reconstruction, i.e. learned statistics over transaction data rather than rules or generated text.
type_evidence: title: "Hunting in the dark forest: A pre-trained model for on-chain attack transaction detection in Web3" (no type named); abstract: "In this paper, we propose a universal approach for detecting on-chain attacks even when there are few or even no new on-chain attack samples", and "we propose a new insight to train a generic attack transaction detecting model, i.e., transaction reconstruction"; contribution 2: "A pre-trained model. We develop a pre-trained model capable of identifying attack transactions in the absence of known samples"; no type named → B.2 step 3 reads the method, a graph transformer with MLP encoder and decoder trained to reconstruct transactions, comments embedded by a frozen CodeBERT, and an isolation forest or random forest on the result; nothing is generated → ML

row_justification: The governing set mixes 203 attack transactions into 40,000 normal ones (0.5 %), drawn from the 22 attacks against cross-chain business logic of Section 3.3, with no per-incident or per-class transaction counts (Table 4 reports precision and recall only, for the source-chain and target-chain classes). Coded by their named causes (Table 6), the six source-chain fake lock and fake deposit events and the seven target-chain unverified withdrawals each break the bridge's lock-before-release, one class as for Xscope → PM. The nine off-chain verification failures, which Section 2.3.2 describes as aimed at external authentication, lie at the trust boundary and give the out secondary; the unchecked signer of ChainSwap (Section 2.3.3) and the unvalidated initiator of pNetwork (Section 2.4), both generic checks, give the ES secondary.
column_justification: Graph2vec embeddings plus motif counts of cross-chain transaction graphs feed a KNN classifier (89.16% F1) that supplies the attack boundary
type_evidence: title: "Safeguarding blockchain ecosystem: Understanding and detecting attack transactions on cross-chain bridges" (no type named); abstract: "this paper aims to detect attacks against cross-chain business logic, and propose the BridgeGuard tool", which "employs a two-stage detection framework comprising global and local graph mining to identify attack patterns" (no type named); contribution 2: "we develop a tool named BridgeGuard for detecting cross-chain attack transactions" (no type named) → B.2 step 3 reads the method, Graph2vec embeddings and motif counts concatenated and fed to supervised classifiers, KNN selected → ML

row_justification: Skyeye's labeled set holds 174 adversarial contracts from 159 incidents (April 2020 to October 2023, about $1.36B, from Rekt, DeFiHackLabs, SlowMist, and CertiK) and 14,265 benign contracts (precision 0.9454 and recall 0.9286 on a 30 % test split); Table 6 types the 174 as flash loan 15, price manipulation 31, reentrancy 23, and access control 16 and puts 89 business logic bugs under "Others" with no class, so the typed part (85 of 174) is not most of the set and does not govern, and a detector of contracts built to attack DeFi protocols takes the row of those attacks → PM ‡ (attacker-contract rule, as for LookAhead; glossary line 3, incidents, gives the same). Reentrancy and access control (a generic missing check, as in the Uerii mint) are the ES secondary, and two attacks the paper attributes to "external factors like private key leakage or incorrect authorization" (Transit Swap and Wintermute) give the out secondary.
column_justification: The contribution list names one type (Skyeye "leverages LLM to analyze and classify vulnerabilities") → LLM (ML and Rule-based secondary); an encoder-only transformer over BERT-embedded bytecode segments and 12 deployment features flags adversarial contracts, a hand-written probabilistic matching score over the addresses and ABIs found by simulated execution localizes the victim, and GPT-4, given the inter-contract call sequences in a fixed few-shot prompt, returns the vulnerability type or "others"; the model calls no tool and its stage is terminal (flag no).
type_evidence: title: "Skyeye: Detecting imminent attacks via analyzing adversarial smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "we propose Skyeye, a novel technique that integrates adversarial and vulnerable contracts together to detect vulnerabilities and resulting imminent attacks" (no type), and later "Skyeye leverages Large Language Model (LLM) to decide the types of vulnerabilities exploited by adversarial contracts"; contribution list: "Skyeye constructs comprehensive attack behavior profiles, and then leverages LLM to analyze and classify vulnerabilities effectively" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → LLM; the deep-learning identifier and the matching score are components (step 7)

row_justification: The governing set is SmartBugs-curated, 142 contracts each labeled with its DASP vulnerability types (Section 3.1 and Table 1: reentrancy, access control, arithmetic issues, unchecked return values, denial of service, bad randomness, front running, time manipulation, and short address attack; Unknown Unknowns left out). The paper prints no per-type counts, but all nine types are execution-semantics, so every case is ES; front running, which Table 1 defines as "Two dependent transactions that invoke the same contract are included in one block", is transaction-order dependence, statable from the code and the ordering of transactions alone → ES. Five self-written price-oracle-manipulation contracts (Section 6.1, none detected by the plain prompt) give the PM secondary.
column_justification: gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4, prompted as "a vulnerability detector" with the nine DASP types, give a free-text answer that a second prompt converts to 0 or 1 labels per type, and that answer is the verdict → LLM; the models are queried through the API with prompts only, call no tool, and the model stage is terminal → flag no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "When ChatGPT meets smart contract vulnerability detection: How far are we?"; abstract: "we presented an empirical study to investigate the performance of ChatGPT in identifying smart contract vulnerabilities"; contributions: "We provided evidence that ChatGPT has different detection performance for different vulnerabilities" and "We compared ChatGPT with 14 smart contract vulnerability detection tools"; ChatGPT, a generative LLM, is the only type named → LLM (B.2 step 3)

subgroup: general auditors, row by glossary or by listed types
row_justification: GPTScan's largest labeled set is 48 Web3Bugs logic vulnerabilities in 72 Code4rena-audited projects (Table 2; unit: vulnerability), counting those already reported and those newly detected and confirmed by the community, reported per dataset without a per-type breakdown. The set holds only the 10 types of Table 1: a false negative is counted when GPTScan "fails to detect the ground-truth vulnerable function for the tested vulnerability type" (Section 5.1), and every false negative and every newly found vulnerability is of one of them (Sections 5.2 and 5.5). Nine types are protocol-mechanism properties (price manipulation by AMM and by buying tokens, price consistency; vote manipulation by flash loan, B.1 governance; slippage, B.1 missing checks; risky first deposit, wrong interest-rate order, and wrong checkpoint order, conservation of pooled value; approval not cleared and unauthorized transfer, holder-balance integrity), and front running turns on a missing sender check (ES) → PM by the plurality of its listed types (B.1, known-list rule), ‡ as no per-case breakdown exists, ES secondary. The DefiHacks set (14 vulnerabilities in 13 attacked projects, 12 of them price manipulation) is labeled by the same 10 types, so the larger Web3Bugs set governs. No type rests on a standard's specified semantics, so there is no DM secondary.
column_justification: GPT matches candidate functions to the scenario and property descriptions of Table 1 and names their key variables and statements, which the framework passes to static confirmation (data-flow, value-comparison, order, and call-argument checks); the static check issues the verdict and its result never returns to GPT, so the framework fixes the tool schedule → flag no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "... by combining GPT with program analysis"; abstract: "we propose GPTScan, the first tool combining GPT with static analysis"; no contribution list; the two presented equally → B.2 step 5 tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary)

subgroup: general auditors, row by glossary or by listed types
row_justification: The largest labeled set of cases is 24 attack incidents curated from SmartInv's benchmark (Table V, 17 detected). The paper lists them by project name only and types none of them (it sets aside SmartInv's 11 reentrancy and eight price-manipulation cases), so the set has no per-case breakdown → glossary line 3 ("attack incidents") → PM ‡; read with the abstract as one set of 37, the typed CVEs cover 13 of 37 cases, not most, and line 3 still applies. The 13 CVEs (Table IV; four access control, three overflow, four logic error, one delegatecall, and one bad randomness; nine detected) give the ES secondary. The 22 bounty findings (12 confirmed and fixed) carry no breakdown, and the 90 Certora ground-truth properties score property generation, not violations, so they are not cases.
column_justification: GPT-4-turbo (gpt-4-0125-preview) generates formal properties from reference properties retrieved by embedding similarity. The framework compiles and statically checks every candidate and returns the errors on a fixed schedule (at most nine revisions), a weighted score of embedding similarities with weights fitted by linear regression ranks the candidates, and the authors' Z3-based prover decides, so the work is an LLM detector with flag no; the prover and checks are the Rule-based secondary, and the embedding retrieval and fitted ranking the ML secondary.
type_evidence: title: "PropertyGPT: LLM-driven formal verification of smart contracts through retrieval-augmented property generation", the LLM named as driving the verification (B.2 step 4); abstract: "We have implemented these strategies into a novel LLM-based property generation tool called PropertyGPT"; contributions: the first item, "a novel LLM-based property generation tool, PropertyGPT, to drive comprehensive formal verification" → LLM

subgroup: agents converse or debate, no tool
row_justification: iAudit is evaluated on a labeled test set of 709 functions, split from 3,544 functions (2,268 training, 567 validation, and 709 test) that hold 1,734 vulnerable functions with reasons from 263 Solodit audit reports and 1,810 negatives (Section III-D; the abstract calls the source "263 real smart contract vulnerabilities"), with no class breakdown; audit-report findings with no class map to ES by glossary line 2, ‡. The paper names no target type above ES (its introduction speaks only of "logical flaws" and "logic vulnerabilities," with no class and no named description, and the reentrancy, overflow, and underflow instances its Limitations mention are ES), so no secondary row is recorded.
column_justification: Presented as combining fine-tuning and LLM-based agents (title, abstract), the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → Agentic (LLM secondary); the Detector, CodeLlama-13b fine-tuned with LoRA, issues the verdict by majority vote, and the Ranker and Critic agents (Mixtral 8x7B-Instruct, Section III-C) select and review the Reasoner's candidate causes by prompting alone, for at most five iterations (Section VI), with no tool call (flag no, method text only).
type_evidence: title: "Combining fine-tuning and LLM-based agents …"; abstract: "combines fine-tuning and LLM-based agents"; the fine-tuned Detector decides, the Ranker and Critic agents choose the cause

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2502.04347 (2025-02) in the same year; extended version: ACM Trans. Softw. Eng. Methodol. 35, 10, Article 329 (Oct. 2026), doi:10.1145/3795692 (placement and figures follow the cited version)
row_justification: SCALM's largest labeled evaluation set is 1,894 SmartBugs contracts in five SWC classes (Section 4.1, Table 1; results in Table 3), unit contracts: SWC-101 overflow, 104 unchecked call, 107 reentrancy, 112 delegatecall, and 116 timestamp, with "94 samples for positive examples of SWC-104 and 200 samples for both positive and negative examples of the remaining SWC categories" (Section 4.1), all execution-semantics classes → ES. DAppSCAN is the retrieval knowledge base, and the 35-category check on official SWC samples (Section 4.2, Table 2) records only detected or missed per category.
column_justification: An LLM with step-back prompting reads each target fragment with snippets retrieved from a vector store built before the run from DAppSCAN by static code analysis, and writes the JSON audit report that is the verdict → LLM, Rule-based secondary; retrieval precedes reasoning and the model calls no tool (flag no, method text only).
type_evidence: title: "SCALM: Detecting bad practices in smart contracts through LLMs"; abstract: "we propose a large language models (LLMs)-based framework, SCALM"; contribution 2: "We introduce SCALM, a novel framework based on LLMs for smart contract security audits", in which "static code analysis is used to extract code blocks containing bad practices" → LLM, the type the framework is based on (B.2 step 4), Rule-based secondary (step 7)

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2506.18245 (2025-06) in the same year
row_justification: The governing set is the evaluation set of 3,542 samples (Section 4.2), 1,230 of them vulnerable. Reentrancy (116 of 470), timestamp dependence (568 of 896), integer overflow or underflow (354 of 1,458), and delegatecall (76 of 340) give 1,114 vulnerable samples at the execution-semantics level → ES by majority. The 116 machine-unauditable vulnerable samples (of 378) span price oracle manipulation (25), inconsistent state updates (23), erroneous accounting (20), privilege escalation (15), ID uniqueness (13), atomicity (10), and contract-implementation specific bugs (10) and give the PM secondary; no case is tied to a named description, so there is no DM secondary.
column_justification: A CPT+SFT+DPO fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1-8B generates the vulnerability verdict together with its explanation; generative output is the decision, terminal, no tools.
type_evidence: title: "Smart-LLaMA-DPO: Reinforced large language model for explainable smart contract vulnerability detection"; abstract: "we propose Smart-LLaMA-DPO, an advanced detection method based on the LLaMA-3.1-8B"; contribution 1: "the first to introduce preference-based optimization in smart contract vulnerability detection and explanation"; one type named → B.2 step 3 → LLM

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2502.11521 (2025-02) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 153 transactions DeFiScope flags among 968 suspicious transactions from an industry partner (D2, Table II), each checked against attack reports, security alerts, or explorer evidence, of which 147 are price-manipulation attacks, 81 of them previously unknown (unit transactions, one class). The ground-truth set D1 holds 95 price-manipulation attacks on 90 DeFi applications ($381.16M; eight patterns, 49 cases in Pattern I; 76 detected, Table IV), and D3 holds 96,800 benign transactions. Price manipulation violates price consistency over DEX and lending state → PM, whichever set governs.
column_justification: A Foundry-data fine-tuned LLM reads Slither-extracted price-calculation code and balance changes and generates price-trend statements that, combined with rule-recovered DeFi operations, are matched to eight hand-written attack patterns; no tool output returns to the LLM.
type_evidence: title: "Detecting various DeFi price manipulations with LLM reasoning"; abstract: "we introduce the first LLM-based approach, DeFiScope, for detecting DeFi price manipulation attacks"; contributions: "We introduce the first LLM-based approach, DeFiScope" first, then "a graph-based method to recover high-level DeFi operations" (no type) → one type named, LLM (B.2 step 3); Slither extraction, graph-based operation recovery, and pattern matching give the Rule-based secondary (step 7)

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2502.03718 (2025-02) in the same year
row_justification: SMARTCAT detects price-manipulation attack contracts, and every evaluated set is that one class. The largest labeled set is the 214 in-the-wild attack contracts confirmed from their attack transactions and account labels (of 616 flagged among over 770K deployed contracts); the ground truth holds 84 price-manipulation attacks verified by two authors, 77 of them detected, and 8,000 benign contracts with two false positives (Table 1), and the 14 live alarms are of the same class. A detector built for one class of attacker contract takes that class's row (B.1 Attacker contracts), and a set of one class needs no breakdown, so direct and indirect price manipulation, a breach of price consistency, gives PM without ‡.
column_justification: Hand-written Datalog rules on Gigahorse-decompiled bytecode build a token-flow graph of the attack contract's calls, and four hand-written attack rules (two swaps on the same liquidity pool around a price move, with a flash loan for the direct case) decide each finding; no learned or generative component is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Following devils' footprint: Towards real-time detection of price manipulation attacks" (no type); abstract: "we propose SMARTCAT, a novel approach for identifying price manipulation attacks in the preattack stage proactively" (no type); contribution list, item 1: "We propose SMARTCAT for identifying price manipulation attack contracts through anomalous token flow" (no type); no type named → step 3, the method is hand-written rules over bytecode → Rule-based

row_justification: AdvSCanner is evaluated on 78 contracts that their source benchmarks (ERAP, ESC, SmartBugs-curated, RSD, ATR, and SSE) label as reentrancy-vulnerable and that static analysis detects (Table 1); its generated attack contracts succeed in 76.41 % of attempts, averaged over five trials on GPT-3.5, against 6.92 % and 18.97 % for its two LLM baselines. Reentrancy is statable from EVM call semantics, and one class needs no breakdown → ES.
column_justification: Presented as generating attack contracts "using LLM and static analysis" (title) by "combining LLM with static analysis" (contribution list), the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM, Rule-based secondary; Slither and the attack-flow matching run once before the model, and each contract GPT-3.5 generates is compiled and, when it compiles, deployed with its victim on py-evm, compiler errors and failure trajectories returning to the model for up to five rounds on the framework's schedule (Algorithm 2), so the flag is no (method text only; the prompts are not released).
type_evidence: title: "AdvSCanner: Generating adversarial smart contracts to exploit reentrancy vulnerabilities using LLM and static analysis"; abstract: "we introduce AdvSCanner, a novel method that leverages the Large Language Model (LLM) and static analysis to automatically generate adversarial smart contracts (ASCs)"; contribution list: "the first tool designed to automatically generate adversarial smart contracts (ASCs) by combining LLM with static analysis" → the two equally (B.2 step 5, tie-break, the newer type) → LLM, Rule-based secondary

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2407.06348 (2024-07) in the same year
row_justification: 34 DeFiHackLabs incidents classed as Token Burn (9), Pump & Dump (13), Price Discrepancy (5) and Swap Rate Manipulation (7), all violations of protocol pricing/supply invariants (27/34 synthesized)
column_justification: A hand-written DeFi DSL, token-flow-graph sketch enumeration and domain-specific symbolic compilation to SMT define profitable attack sketches
type_evidence: title: "FORAY: Towards effective attack synthesis against deep logical vulnerabilities in DeFi protocols"

first_release: cited version, 2023; preprint arXiv:2303.17877 (2023-03) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is APE's one-year replay of Ethereum and BSC (August 2021 to July 2022), 26,127 and 52,799 transactions that Table 3 counts as successfully attacked, each validated as profitable by local execution (Section 4.6). Only the top 100 most rewarding victims per chain are classified (Table 5: arbitrage and liquidation, known DeFi attacks, known vulnerabilities, and newly found vulnerabilities; Tables 8 and 9 name the protocols, and the 13 Ethereum and 22 BSC known attacks carry no type), which does not cover most of the set → glossary line 3 ("profitable transactions") → PM ‡. Four of the five undisclosed vulnerabilities it reports (a massDeposit anyone can call, unauthenticated minting, unauthenticated asset redemption, and faulty authentication) are generic missing access checks, recorded as the ES secondary; the fifth, a stake accepted without checking the staked asset's value, is PM.
column_justification: Dynamic taint analysis of pending transactions plus fixed program-synthesis rules and a profit oracle synthesize the adversarial contract
type_evidence: title names no type ("The blockchain imitation game"); abstract: "proposes a generalized imitation attack methodology called APE", "Leveraging dynamic program analysis techniques, APE supports the automatic synthesis of adversarial smart contracts"; contribution 1: "We design APE, a generalized imitation tool for EVM-based blockchains", "dynamic program analysis techniques can realize an imitation attack"; no type is named, and the method is dynamic taint analysis and synthesis by fixed bytecode amendments, with no learned or language model → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

first_release: cited version, 2026; preprint arXiv:2601.16681 (2026-01) in the same year
row_justification: Tracexp-ds holds 321 real-world attack incidents on Ethereum and BSC from January 2024 to July 2025 (176 from DeFiHackLabs with ground-truth PoCs, after two of 178 were filtered, and 145 deduplicated from CertiK, SlowMist, and TenArmor alerts), reported without a per-type breakdown (Figure 7 splits them only by PoC availability and failure reason) → glossary line 3 ("attacks", "incidents") → PM ‡. Section 6 evaluates across the attack patterns of Section 2.1 ("reentrancy, price manipulation, and flash loan attacks"), and reentrancy gives the ES secondary.
column_justification: GPT-5 fills the placeholders of a PoC sketch that the pipeline builds from trace-driven decompiled pseudocode, and the fund-flow oracle checks the PoC it writes; Foundry compiler errors and the oracle and trace-alignment results return on the framework's schedule (up to five syntax repairs and up to three semantic rounds, each stateless), and the model requests no tool → LLM, Rule-based secondary (decompiler and oracle), flag no (method text only; no code released).
type_evidence: title (ASE 2026): "Trace-driven automated PoC synthesis for on-chain attacks", and arXiv title "From transactions to exploits: Automated PoC synthesis for real-world DeFi attacks", name no type; abstract: proposal sentence "we propose TracExp, which localizes attack-relevant execution contexts from noisy, multi-contract traces and introduces a novel dual-decompiler", preceded by the key insight that attacker logic is recovered "via trace-driven reverse engineering, and then translated into executable exploits by leveraging the code-generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs)"; contribution list: a "dual decompiler" that recovers pseudocode "deterministically" and a refinement mechanism that "leverages fund-flow oracles", no LLM named → reverse engineering and LLMs presented equally in the key insight → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (B.2 step 5), Rule-based secondary

row_justification: Penetration testing of 13 HackTheBox and VulnHub machines (182 sub-tasks in 26 categories covering 18 CWE items, with no per-CWE counts), ten live HackTheBox machines, and 21 picoMini CTF challenges; no smart-contract or DeFi target → non-DeFi, row n/a (B.3). It is shown in the execution-semantics row by glossary line 4 ("vulnerabilities" with no class), its cases being generic software vulnerabilities with no class breakdown. Offensive is the marking shown (B.3 precedence), since PentestGPT attacks identified targets and is scored on the sub-tasks and machines it completes.
column_justification: Presented as "an LLM-empowered automated penetration testing framework" with "three self-interacting modules" (abstract), each an LLM session (Section 5.1) → LLM, Rule-based secondary (the security testing tools, such as nmap and nikto, whose output the Parsing Module reads, Section 5.5); no agent word in the title, the abstract, or the contribution list. The Reasoning Module picks the next sub-task from its task tree, the Generation Module turns it into a concrete command and chooses the tool (nmap, nikto), the tester runs the command and returns the output, and the Parsing Module condenses it for the Reasoning Module, which updates the tree and chooses the next step (Sections 5.4 and 5.5, Fig. 4) → flag yes, since the tester only executes and the model chooses each tool call; evidence basis trace or log (Fig. 4, a run on HTB-Carrier).
type_evidence: title: "PentestGPT: Evaluating and harnessing large language models for automated penetration testing"; abstract: "we introduce PentestGPT, an LLM-empowered automated penetration testing framework"; contribution list, third item: "Development of an Innovative LLM-powered Penetration Testing System" → one type named → LLM

row_justification: HPTSA is evaluated on 14 real-world web vulnerabilities published in 2024 (Tables 1 and 2: four XSS, three SQLi, two CSRF, one of them leading to privilege escalation, improper authorization, HTTP parameter tampering, a privilege escalation from improper input sanitization, arbitrary code execution, and information leakage), none with a blockchain or smart-contract target → non-DeFi, which sets row n/a while offensive is the marking shown (B.3 precedence); each case is a generic code-level vulnerability, so Supplementary Table 7 shows it in the ES row.
column_justification: Presented as teams of LLM agents (title) → Agentic: a hierarchical planner explores the target and instructs a team manager, which "determines which specific agents to use" and "retrieves the information from previous agent runs", and task-specific expert agents act through Playwright, a terminal, file tools, sqlmap, and ZAP, the last two scanners whose output the agents read (Rule-based secondary, B.2 step 7); in the case study of Section 6.1 the manager reads the SQL agent's traces and "determines that the CSRF agent should focus on the /admin.php endpoint" → flag yes (trace or log; code and prompts not released).
type_evidence: title: "Teams of LLM agents can exploit zero-day vulnerabilities"; abstract: "we introduce HPTSA, a system of agents with a planning agent that can launch subagents"; no contribution list (the introduction states "we develop a novel multi-agent framework for cybersecurity exploits") → Agentic (B.2 step 3, one type named)

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2503.17332 (2025-03) in the same year
row_justification: CVE-Bench (Zhu et al., ICML 2025) is a benchmark of critical-severity CVEs in sandboxed web applications on which LLM agents attempt real exploits; the best agent framework exploits up to 13 %; non-DeFi benchmark, row n/a.
column_justification: A benchmark is displayed in the column of the systems it scores: LLM agent frameworks (Cy-Agent, T-Agent, AutoGPT) that choose their tools, such as sqlmap, and observe the results in a sandbox before the next step → Agentic, Rule-based secondary (the tools whose output the agents read, B.2 step 7), flag yes.
type_evidence: title: "CVE-Bench: A benchmark for AI agents' ability to exploit real-world web application vulnerabilities"

row_justification: The proposal checker flags description-code inconsistencies: on 1,500 manually labeled functions (3,122 parameters) it reaches 0.81 precision and 0.87 recall for incomplete functions and 0.83 and 0.88 for parameters (Table VII), and it detected all 13 real governance-attack proposals (recall only: about 91 % of the analyzed proposals fail its check); the proposal text is the description (project-specific). The measurement in the TSE paper covers 3,348 DAOs and 65,436 proposals, 35,518 analyzed; governance-contract independence and CREATE2 code mutability (Tornado Cash) are the PM secondaries.
column_justification: Proposal inconsistency uses a fine-tuned BERT classifier to select code-describing sentences, dependency-parse rules to extract the stated intention, and a Sentence-BERT cosine threshold of 0.75 against decoded calldata; contract checks are opcode heuristics, and documentation compliance uses ChatGPT chain-of-thought
type_evidence: title: no type word; abstract: "we developed automated methods to detect such vulnerabilities" (no type); contributions (public dataset, comprehensive study, insightful findings): no type word → the method decides (B.2 step 3), and the proposal checker behind the row and the 13 detected attack proposals is a fine-tuned BERT sentence classifier, dependency-parse rules, and a Sentence-BERT similarity threshold, none a large generative model → ML; the opcode heuristics of the contract checks (Rule-based) and the ChatGPT documentation check (LLM) are secondary types

first_release: cited version, 2021; preprint arXiv:2103.02228 (2021-03) in the same year
row_justification: Over 150 days (blocks 9,100,000 to 10,050,000; 96 actions on Uniswap, Bancor, and MakerDAO; 25 assets), DeFiPoser-ARB finds 2,709 profitable strategies and DeFiPoser-SMT 13,317 (Section VI-C; the Fig. 7 caption gives 1,556), checked by concrete execution on a forked chain (Section VI-B) and given no breakdown by type, and DeFiPoser-SMT rediscovers the bZx attack of February 2020 → glossary line 3 ("profitable transactions") → PM ‡; the deliverable is executable profitable transactions whose revenue the paper measures → offensive.
column_justification: DeFiPoser-ARB finds negative cycles in a directed DeFi market graph with the Bellman-Ford-Moore algorithm and then searches the input amount (Algorithm 1), and DeFiPoser-SMT encodes hand-written state-transition models of DeFi actions for the Z3 theorem prover with seven pruning heuristics (Section V-B); profit is checked by concrete execution on a forked chain, and nothing is learned → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "On the just-in-time discovery of profit-generating transactions in DeFi protocols" names no type; abstract: "In this paper, we investigate two methods that allow us to automatically create profitable DeFi trades" and "We first adopt the Bellman-Ford-Moore algorithm with DEFIPOSER-ARB and then create logical DeFi protocol models for a theorem prover in DEFIPOSER-SMT"; contributions: "We build a directed DeFi market graph and identify negative cycles with the Bellman-Ford-Moore algorithm" and "we translate to a logical representation in the Z3 theorem prover"; the words name only a graph algorithm and a theorem prover, rule-based methods → one type (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

subgroup: scam and rug-pull tokens by market behavior
first_release: cited version, 2021; preprint arXiv:2109.00229 (2021-09) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 10,920 scam tokens the paper confirms (Section 4.6), 50.14 % of the 21,778 tokens on Uniswap V2, made up of 4,048 ground-truth scam tokens (4,017 copying an official token's name or symbol and 31 tagged on Etherscan; Section 4.3), 3,122 added by guilt-by-association expansion, and 3,750 classifier detections verified by heuristics and manual labeling; the Random Forest classifier, cross-validated (10-fold) on the seed and expansion tokens against 2,397 manually verified official tokens, reaches 96.45 % precision and 96.79 % recall; the set is one class, tokens whose pools 'are created for the "rug pull" scams' (Section 5.2), so no breakdown is needed → PM (B.1 scams, liquidity-removal rugs).
column_justification: The abstract's proposal sentence presents 'a guilt-by-association heuristic and a machine-learning powered technique' together, neither driving the other → tie-break (step 5), the newer type → ML, Rule-based secondary; the heuristic extends the scam labels to other tokens of known scam creators (Section 4.4), and a Random Forest classifier, the best of four learned models, flags candidate scam tokens (Section 4.5.1).
type_evidence: title: 'Trade or trick? Detecting and characterizing scam tokens on Uniswap decentralized exchange' (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: 'we propose an accurate approach for flagging scam tokens on Uniswap based on a guilt-by-association heuristic and a machine-learning powered technique' (Rule-based and ML, presented equally); contribution list, first item: 'we propose a guilt-by-association based expansion method and a machine-learning based classifier to identify the most reliable scam tokens' → step 5, tie-break, the newer type → ML (Rule-based secondary).

subgroup: scam and rug-pull tokens by market behavior
first_release: cited version, 2024; extended version: IEEE Trans. Dependable Secure Comput. 23, 4 (July 2026), 7673–7690, doi:10.1109/TDSC.2026.3675905 (placement and figures follow the cited version)
row_justification: The governing set is the 214,084 ERC-20 tokens of Section 4 (unit tokens), each reviewed independently by three of four auditors, with 212,278 scam tokens (179,995 rug pulls, 22,800 honeypots, and 9,483 Ponzi tokens) and 1,806 trustworthy ones; rug pulls and the payout and trap mechanics of honeypot and Ponzi tokens are PM (B.1 scams). A deployment from March to May 2023 detected 706 of 732 rug pulls, 174 of 183 honeypots, and 92 of 92 Ponzi tokens (Table 4; the abstract gives 90), also PM; the paper reports false-negative and false-positive rates for it but does not say how the totals were confirmed.
column_justification: Presented as temporal graph learning (title) → ML; a temporal graph neural network with contrastive refinement over the dynamic token-transfer multigraph learns the risk boundary.
type_evidence: title: "TokenScout: Early detection of Ethereum scam tokens via temporal graph learning"

subgroup: privileged-function and rug-pull classifiers over code
row_justification: The governing set is 2,320 tokens, 645 rug-pull incidents (one token each) that three experts labeled by manual analysis of code and transactions and 1,675 benign tokens (Sections III-A and V-A); a set of one class needs no breakdown, and rug pulls are PM (B.1 scams). Its code-side risks, Sale Restrict (203 contracts), Variable Manipulation (144), and Balance Tamper (189, hidden mint or burn and hidden balance modification), are privileges over holder balances, and the 229 incidents with no obvious code risk (Section V-B) are rug pulls all the same; the token standard states none of these, and no other description is named.
column_justification: Contribution 2 presents RPHunter as "utilizing GNNs for graph feature learning to detect Rug Pull schemes" → ML; Datalog rules over Gigahorse output label the semantic risk code graph (Rule-based secondary), and a relational GCN over BERT-embedded basic blocks, a GCN-based network over the token-flow behavior graph built from transactions, and an attention fusion classifier issue the verdict; BERT is an encoder and generates no text.
type_evidence: title: "RPHunter: Unveiling rug pull schemes in crypto token via code-and-transaction fusion analysis" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we propose RPHunter, a novel technique that integrates code and transaction for Rug Pull detection" (no type); contribution 2: "utilizing GNNs for graph feature learning to detect Rug Pull schemes" → ML (B.2 step 3, one type named)

subgroup: scam and rug-pull tokens by market behavior
row_justification: Srifa et al. label 7,450 Uniswap V3 tokens by rule from their liquidity and price history (a maximum drawdown to zero with no recovery, the method of Mazorra et al.) and train classifiers on the 3,793 normal and rug-pull tokens, 3,212 normal and 581 rug pulls, reporting precision, recall, and F1 for eight timeframes after token creation (Figs. 4 and 5); a rug pull here is liquidity drained or tokens dumped, which B.1 (scams) keeps at PM, and a set of one class needs no breakdown, so the row follows the evaluation without the glossary. The 38 pump-and-dump tokens are labeled but not evaluated.
column_justification: Presented as machine learning over transaction time series (abstract) → ML; XGBoost classifiers, tuned by grid search with stratified cross-validation and SMOTE, issue the rug-pull verdict for each timeframe from holder, transaction, price, and volume features, while the drawdown rule only labels the data.
type_evidence: title: "Rug pull detection on decentralized exchange using transaction data" (no type named); abstract, with no proposal sentence, nearest: "machine learning algorithms can leverage the vast amount of transactional data stored on the blockchain, particularly time series data, to identify scam tokens"; contribution list: "Development of detection models that are effective for different time windows" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML

first_release: cited version, 2019; preprint arXiv:1902.06976 (2019-02) in the same year
row_justification: HoneyBadger reports 690 honeypot contracts and 240 victims among more than 2 million contracts, 87 % of reported contracts confirmed by manual validation; a honeypot is a trap mechanic → PM (B.1 scams).
column_justification: Symbolic execution and hand-written heuristics, one per honeypot technique → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "The art of the scam: Demystifying honeypots in Ethereum smart contracts"

row_justification: PoCo generates PoC exploits for the 23 audit findings of Proof-of-Patch (unit: finding), collected through Solodit, each validated by the audit judges and paired with a developer patch (§4.1); Table 1 lists each with a one-line description and no type column. Tallied by us from the descriptions, 13 are protocol-mechanism (deposit-limit bypass, yield-fee theft, share and utilization rounding against the pool, royalty and flash-loan fee miscalculation, prize-distribution interference, first-depositor share inflation, stuck strike amount, auction hijack, value extraction by a royalty recipient, rsETH minting shortfall, and reserve manipulation) and 10 execution-semantics (stale approvals after an ownership transfer, zero-transfer reverts and DoS, missing access control, unchecked return values, locked ether, pause bypass, reentrancy, and nonexistent-token balances) → PM, ES secondary; the tally of the paper's own list counts as its breakdown. The input is an auditor's annotation, a third-party text, so no description is read.
column_justification: Presented as agentic (title, abstract, contribution 1) → Agentic, Rule-based secondary (Foundry's compile and test, whose output the agent reads, B.2 step 7).
