A single LLM in a reason, act, and observe loop "possesses full autonomy in selecting, ordering, and configuring tool calls" (§3.2) among glob, grep, read, edit, and write, a Todo planner, and Foundry's smart-contract-compile and smart-contract-test, whose output returns to it to self-correct; Listing 2 shows a run (Basin, #091) in which forge test fails and the agent adjusts its assertion until the tests pass → flag yes on a reported trace (⊕); the prototype is provided only on request (p. 27).
type_evidence: title: "PoCo: Agentic proof-of-concept exploit generation for smart contracts"; abstract: "We introduce PoCo, an agentic framework that automatically generates executable PoC exploits from natural-language vulnerability descriptions written by auditors"; contribution 1: "PoCo, a blueprint of real-world proof-of-concept exploit generation for smart contracts based on agentic AI"; one type named in all three places → B.2 step 3 → Agentic

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2406.15999 (2024-06) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the scan of 129 bridge applications (1,703 contracts), in which experts confirmed 278 of 324 warnings by majority vote and report 232 new cross-chain vulnerabilities (CCVs) in 126 contracts, with no breakdown by type (Section 5.5); the smaller labeled set holds 88 CCV traces in 16 bridge applications (203 contracts), 59 of access-control incompleteness and 29 of semantic inconsistency (Table 4). Both named causes, missing security checks on deposit, routing, authorization, and release (Table 1) and an asset type or amount that differs between the chains, break the bridge's lock-before-release and are read as one class, as for Xscope → PM; the generic signature checks (P4) are recorded as the ES secondary.
column_justification: An expert-built security-check model of the top 100 bridges (Table 1) is matched against each contract's control flow, and hand-written consistency rules over cross-chain control-flow and data-flow graphs decide each finding (84.95% precision and 89.77% recall on the 88 labeled traces); a probabilistic step with fixed priors (Table 2) only links resources to checks, and nothing is learned from data → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "SmartAxe: Detecting cross-chain vulnerabilities in bridge smart contracts via fine-grained static analysis"; abstract: "we propose SmartAxe, a new framework to identify vulnerabilities in cross-chain bridge smart contracts via fine-grained static analysis"; contribution list, item 2: "We propose SmartAxe, the first static analysis framework to detect CCVs for cross-chain bridge smart contracts"; one type named, static analysis → step 3 → Rule-based

row_justification: HighGuard is evaluated on 54 exploits, each labeled by the flaw its authors injected: 52 pairs of vulnerable variants and exploits of five contracts they modeled (Table 2), reviewed to exclude traditional types such as reentrancy, and two exploits of flaws injected into a cross-chain DEX on Ethereum and Avalanche (Sec. 5). The exploits violate business-logic specifications that the user supplies as DCR graphs (roles, guards, deadlines, and milestones over the contract's process state), and the paper gives no breakdown by the property violated. A user-written specification is placed by what it states (B.1, user-supplied specifications), and these properties are statable over state → PM, marked ‡ because the set has no breakdown.
column_justification: Hand-written DCR models serve as a fixed monitor over transactions across chains, in a pre-deployment testing setup and on live chains
type_evidence: title: "HighGuard: Cross-chain business logic monitoring of smart contracts" names no type; abstract: "Our tool, HighGuard, detects transactions that violate business logic specifications of smart contracts" and "HighGuard employs dynamic condition response (DCR) graph models as formal specifications to verify contract execution against these models"; no contribution list → hand-written specifications applied by runtime monitoring → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2411.09217 (2024-11) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the refined set of 1,241 contracts from 60 hacked projects, with 1,231 bugs confirmed from audit reports (Table 8; unit bugs), broken down by project, not by type → glossary line 2 (audit findings) → ES ‡. The per-type counts of Table 6 (51,505 bugs reported on 89,621 contracts, most of them reentrancy, integer overflow, and arithmetic flaws) are "not necessarily true positive or exploitable", and Section 3.4 gives only an aggregate review (46,360 confirmed), which fixes the class of no case, so they are not a labeled set. Six of the seven named functional types (price manipulation, privilege escalation, atomicity violation, inconsistent state update, cross bridge, and ID uniqueness violation) are statable over state and give the PM secondary; no named type or evaluated case violates a property that only a comment or document states, so there is no DM secondary. SmartInv reads code with its comments and documentation (reads_description = yes).
column_justification: A fine-tuned LLaMA-7B under Tier of Thought prompting over code and comments generates invariants, which a VeriSol-based verifier (Boogie inductive check, CORRAL bounded model checking) then checks one-way. The released code runs this fixed sequence and the model calls no tool → LLM, flag no on released code; the verifier is the Rule-based secondary.
type_evidence: title: "SmartInv: Multimodal learning for smart contract invariant inference"; abstract: "We propose a new prompting strategy to foundation models, Tier of Thought (ToT)"; contributions: "the first finetuning approach that can both infer invariants and detect bugs"; the title's "multimodal learning" and the abstract's "foundation models" both refer to the fine-tuned LLaMA-7B, a generative model, read as LLM by the boundaries of B.2 step 2 (step 3) → LLM; the VeriSol-based verifier is the Rule-based secondary

row_justification: InvCon mines invariants from the transaction histories of 246 ERC20-labeled contracts deployed after January 2021, whose conformance to its ERC-20 invariant specification the authors confirmed by hand, and finds 16 non-compliant contracts (Section 3), counted in contracts. Of these, 10 violate semantics EIP-20 states (one the approve invariant, the remaining nine the transfer and transferFrom invariants) → DM, shared; six violate the balance invariant (Inv#1, the sum of balances equals the total supply), which EIP-20 does not state → PM secondary.
column_justification: Likely invariants are instantiated from Daikon's fixed templates over decoded historical transaction state snapshots; presented as a dynamic invariant detector → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "InvCon: A dynamic invariant detector for Ethereum smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "we propose a dynamic invariant detection tool, InvCon, for Ethereum smart contracts" (no type); no contribution list → B.2 step 3, the method (Daikon's predefined invariant templates checked against state snapshots before and after each historical transaction) → Rule-based

row_justification: The governing set is the SECBIT buggy-ERC20 benchmark of RQ3 (Table VII), 1,332 vulnerabilities in 24 listed types (the text says 25), labeled by the benchmark, of which nine integer-overflow types (v1 to v9) account for 1,047 → ES. RQ1 recovers invariants on 361 ERC-20 and 10 ERC-721 contracts against a ground truth of standard properties (Tables II and III), an invariant-recovery task and not a case set; its targets are the source of the DM secondary (EIP-20 transfer, transferFrom, and approve post-conditions) and the PM secondary (c1, totalSupply equals the sum of balances).
column_justification: Templates instantiated by Daikon-style dynamic inference over each contract's transaction history, then filtered by static verification with VeriSol in a Houdini-inspired loop, yield verified invariants that decide whether a vulnerability is prevented; no learned or generative model is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Automated invariant generation for Solidity smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "In this paper, we propose a novel invariant generation framework, InvCon+, for Solidity smart contracts", which "extends the existing invariant detector, InvCon, to automatically produce verified contract invariants based on both dynamic inference and static verification"; contributions, second bullet: "We present a unified framework for generating verified invariants in Solidity smart contracts, combining dynamic invariant detection and static invariant verification" → no type named, B.2 step 3, template inference and verification → Rule-based.

row_justification: Evaluated on 54 DeFi applications that suffered price-manipulation attacks (52 detected) and 435 presumed benign, plus five live attacks while monitoring 441 projects; price manipulation violates DEX and lending price invariants → PM.
column_justification: A hand-built price-manipulation behaviour model with fixed price-fluctuation monitoring strategies and profit-calculation confirmation
type_evidence: title: "DeFort: Automatic detection and analysis of price manipulation attacks in DeFi applications"

row_justification: Of the 57,411 tokens it identifies, TokenScope flags 7,472 as inconsistent (Section 5.1); the governing set is the 2,353 flagged tokens with source code on Etherscan, all checked by hand with one false positive (Section 5.3), unit tokens. Every case is a mismatch between a token's balance changes, its standard method calls, and its Transfer events, the method and event semantics EIP-20 states. Among the 11 reasons Table 4 (Section 6) gives for the 2,352 inconsistent open-source tokens, it attributes 2,097 to the standard event not emitted or the balance map not modified, 654 to minting and 463 to burning without the standard events, 51 to fees charged inside a standard method or without the standard events, and 6 to transfer amounts that differ from the call (one inconsistency can have several reasons). The standard is the description (shared).
column_justification: Hand-written rules compare real balance-mapping updates with standard method calls and Transfer events in recorded traces.
type_evidence: title: "TokenScope: Automatically detecting inconsistent behaviors of cryptocurrency tokens in Ethereum" names no type; abstract: "We propose a novel approach to automatically detect such inconsistency by contrasting the behaviors derived from three" sources, no type; the contribution list names no type → B.2 step 3, the method (hand-written comparison of ERC-20 method semantics, Transfer events, and balance-map writes in replayed traces) → Rule-based

row_justification: Its largest labeled bug set is the permission-bug reports on SBwild (47,518 contracts; SPCon runs on those with at least 50 transactions) checked by hand, 384 across seven tools with all 44 of SPCon's among them (81.8% true, Table 4), beside the 17 access-control CVEs of Table 5 (SPCon detects 9) and 11 previously unknown bugs; the role-mining benchmark (50 of 228 labeled contracts) scores mined roles, not violations. Every case is a permission bug, code that contradicts the role policy mined from the contract's transactions; the smallest-context rule applies first, and the missing check refers only to the caller (B.1 missing checks → ES), while the recovered policy records practice, not a statement, and is no named description → ES, DM (recovered policy) secondary.
column_justification: Roles are mined from benign past transactions by a genetic algorithm that trades role similarity against role consistency, and the information-flow policies of a security lattice built from them (integrity, separation of duty) are checked over symbolic paths (Manticore); the policy check issues the verdict and no learned model or language model is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Finding permission bugs in smart contracts with role mining" (no type word); abstract: "We implement our role mining and security policy validation in tool SPCon", after "we mine past transactions of a contract to recover a likely access control model, which can then be checked against various information flow policies"; contributions: "We propose SPCon, a tool targeting permission bugs in smart contracts" → no type named; the method mines the policy with a genetic algorithm and checks it over symbolic paths → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: Pied-Piper confirms 189 backdoors in 13,484 token contracts — arbitrary transfer 2, generate token after ICO 34, destroy token 29, disable transferring 29, freeze account 95 — privileged balance manipulation, holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams); no description is named.
column_justification: Datalog identification rules over abstracted data structures followed by directed fuzzing that checks whether protections fire supply the backdoor decision
type_evidence: title: "Pied-Piper: Revealing the backdoor threats in Ethereum ERC token contracts"

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2403.01425 (2024-03) in the same year
row_justification: CRPWarner detects hidden mint, limiting sell order, and leaking token functions, checked by hand on a sample of 272 detections (92, 92, and 88; 231 true positives), and flags 4,168 of 13,484 tokens, all breaches of holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams); the token standard states none of these, and no other description is named.
column_justification: Datalog rules over Gigahorse-decompiled bytecode, which its authors call "a logic-based method that is heavily reliant on the patterns" (§V-D); Formula 1, for example, derives a Hidden Mint Function from "PublicFuncForOwner(f), ¬Burn(f), ¬ModifyBalancesNoCheck(f)" (as printed, §IV-C) → Rule-based, no secondary type. The standard functions of ERC-20 and ERC-721 are excluded only "to reduce false positives" (§IV-D), so the decision reads no description.
type_evidence: title: "CRPWarner: Warning the risk of contract-related rug pull in DeFi smart contracts", no type; abstract: "we propose CRPWarner (short for Contract-related Rug Pull Risk Warner) to identify malicious functions in smart contracts and issue warnings regarding potential rug pulls", no type; contribution 2: "CRPWarner, an analysis tool designed to assess the risk of Contract-related Rug Pull", no type; no type named → B.2 step 3, the method decides ("CRPWarner has established predefined datalog rules", §IV-C) → Rule-based

subgroup: business-logic specifications selected from UI text
row_justification: In 34 DApps (494 functions), Table 5 lists 19 violations, in 17 functions, of safety policies the authors write once per category (nine votes in an expired election, one double vote, four draws or purchases in an expired lottery, four auction-state violations, and one investment in an expired crowdsale; Section 5.2 calls them "19 unsafe functions"); each is a state invariant over the contract's deadline, phase, or voting record → PM (B.1 user-supplied specifications). Two further functions are UI-logic inconsistencies, #7 cryptokitties bid(), whose widget reads "buy" but runs an auction ("Ambiguity"), and #21 simple-vote vote(), whose voting logic is not implemented ("No Impl"); the front-end text is a project-specific description → DM secondary. The paper reports false positives in three of 38 safety-related functions.
column_justification: VetSC model-checks (NuSMV) safety specifications that the authors write once per business category (lottery, auction, voting, crowdsale) against a business-model graph built by static analysis of the contract's EVM bytecode (on Octopus), and a violated specification issues the verdict; UI text, cleaned with a POS tagger and matched through pretrained GloVe embeddings, selects the category, maps concepts to variables, and is checked for consistency with the logic. Program analysis and model checking are the only type named → Rule-based, ML secondary (the GloVe matching); no generative model.
type_evidence: title: "Towards automated safety vetting of smart contracts in decentralized applications" (no type); abstract: "We propose VetSC, a novel UI-driven, program analysis guided model checking technique"; contribution 1: "We develop a new technique that uniquely combines program analysis, model checking and UI interpretation" → program analysis and model checking, the one type named (UI interpretation is not a type) → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: FairCon checks four mechanism-design properties the authors supply (truthfulness, collusion-freeness, optimality, and efficiency) on 17 real-world contracts, 12 auctions and five voting contracts, and the authors confirmed every counterexample by hand. Every auction violates at least one property and eight violate all four (Table 2); every voting contract violates truthfulness, collusion-freeness, and efficiency when valuations are real-valued and satisfies them when valuations are zero or one (Table 4; optimality is not checked for voting). The properties are stated over the allocation and price model extracted from the annotated contract, so every case is PM (B.1 user-supplied specifications, as for VerX, Table 8, row 3).
column_justification: The four fairness properties are fixed formal definitions from mechanism design checked on a mechanism model extracted by symbolic execution from lightweight user annotations (@individual, @allocate, @price, @outcome); nothing is learned or generated.
type_evidence: title: "Towards automated verification of smart contract fairness" (verification); abstract: "we present a framework to perform (semi-)automated verification of smart contract fairness" and "We implement FairCon, which is able to check fairness properties including truthfulness, efficiency, optimality, and collusion-freeness for Ethereum smart contracts"; contribution 1: "We proposed a general fairness verification framework, FairCon, to check fairness properties of smart contracts" → verification, the one type named → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: The governing set is 30 DeFi apps attacked through Token Leaking, which lets someone "abnormally withdraw funds" far beyond their deposits, collected from the Slowmist and Rekt incident libraries (May 2020 to June 2022) and labeled by those incidents; DeFiWarder reveals 25 of them (Table I). Table I breaks the 30 down by root cause; price manipulation 10, improper token transfer 6 (the app mints LP tokens without checking that the deposit arrived, a check over mechanism state, B.1 missing checks), and other functional bugs 3 are PM, while arithmetic weakness 1 (an underflow), access control 2 (an unprotected initialize), and control-flow hijack 8 (reentrancy and parameter injection) are ES by the smallest-context rule → PM 19, ES 11, ES secondary. Role mining here only assigns user and app roles to reconstruct token flows; it is not an access-control policy, so no DM secondary is due.
column_justification: DeFiWarder replays the app's transactions, reconstructs token flows between users and the app from execution traces, assigns user and app roles by call-flow heuristics (role mining), links users by relation mining, and flags token leaking when a user's return rate exceeds a bar set at the mean plus five standard deviations of the observed return rates, or when a user withdraws without depositing; the rule is hand-written, its bar is computed from the data, and no model is trained → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "DeFiWarder: Protecting DeFi apps from token leaking vulnerabilities" (no type); abstract: "we propose DeFiWarder, a tool that traces on-chain transactions and protects DeFi apps from Token Leaking vulnerabilities" (no type); contribution 2: "We design DeFiWarder to trace fund flow and protect DeFi apps from Token Leaking vulnerability" (no type) → no type named; the method is token-flow reconstruction with a hand-written outlier rule → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: ScType is evaluated on 57 accounting bugs in 29 projects, the 72 accounting bugs among the 513 bugs from 113 projects collected by Zhang et al. (ICSE 2023), less 15 that Slither could not load or whose code was missing (Section 4.1). Of these, 33 are type errors (58 %), 10 in token units, 12 in scaling factors, and 11 in financial types (Section 4.4), and ScType catches 29 (87.9 %); mixing token units, scales, or financial types breaks the protocol's accounting invariants, statable over its balances and prices and not from VM semantics, so the 33 are PM and a majority on their own → PM. The other 24 ("pure math errors", coefficient errors, wrong formulas, and a wrong comparison) have no per-category counts and add no secondary row; the six zero-day bugs from a Code4rena audit are three financial-type and three token-unit errors.
column_justification: ScType, built on Slither, propagates abstract types (token unit, scaling factor, and financial type such as balance, fee, debt, or price) from a few user annotations and reports operations that break its fixed typing rules; nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Towards finding accounting errors in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "We hence develop a novel type propagation and checking system with the aim of identifying accounting bugs" (static checking, no learned or generative model); no contribution list → no type named; the method is static type inference and checking on Slither → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: The expected behavior comes from eight user intentions the authors predefine (Connect, Transfer, Swap, Approve, Deposit, Withdraw, Mint, and Claim; Table I), realized through author-written training cases; the front-end selects the intention by keyword (the action of clicking an Approve button) and supplies parameter values (a token name), and the paper frames the problem as transactions inconsistent with users' intentions (abstract). Of 92 DApps, 37 are flagged and confirmed by hand with no false negative (35 scams and two hacked front-ends, §V-C; Table IV counts them by DApp category only) → user-intent alignment → adjacent (B.3), row n/a. With no per-case breakdown by level, the display row follows glossary line 1 ("front-end vs. behavior", the front-end named) → shown in the description-mismatch row, where a transaction or contract behavior that differs from what the front-end presents would fall; basis stated, and no ‡ for an entry with row n/a; the front-end is the project's own (project-specific). The hidden-fee arbitrage scams (Tables V and VI) reach PM, and the two hacked front-ends, whose decisive step is an off-chain compromise, are out; both are recorded as secondaries.
column_justification: Rule-based by the method, in which author-written training cases are merged into an intention-action graph that guides keyword-located front-end actions (Algorithm 1); the transaction data are decoded through a method-id database and the transaction is simulated on a local node; fixed conditions over calldata and logs (Table II) map each source to a semantic behavior, and any mismatch among the front-end, wallet, and contract behaviors is reported. No model is trained (a training case is merged into the graph), so no secondary type.
type_evidence: title: "DAppHunter: Identifying inconsistent behaviors of blockchain-based decentralized applications", no type; abstract: "we proposed a novel approach to identify inconsistent behaviors of DApps on EVM-compatible blockchains by contrasting the behaviors of DApps that derived from the front-end, blockchain wallet, and smart contracts, respectively", no type; contributions: "a novel intention-driven approach to interact with the front-end of DApps for DApp testing", no type; no type named → B.2 step 3, the method decides → Rule-based

row_justification: SmartCoCo's largest labeled set is 439 unique comment-code inconsistencies selected from its 4,732 reports in 1,745 of 101,780 contracts and labeled by two domain experts (Table VI, 348 true positives, a precision of 79.3%), with per-type counts of 145 role permission, 116 parameter scope, and 87 event emission cases. In each case a code comment (NatSpec included) supplies the role, the parameter bound, or the event that the code does not implement as stated, so the comment is the named description (project-specific) → DM (303 of 348). The 45 role permission cases in which the code lacks a caller check altogether are generic missing access checks, statable from the code (smallest-context rule, B.1 missing checks), recorded as the ES secondary.
column_justification: Hand-written rules issue the verdict. SmartCoCo extracts role, parameter, and event constraints from comments with 20 hand-written keyword templates, using a Stanford CoreNLP part-of-speech tagger (a learned statistical tagger) to label the comment words the templates filter on, builds code facts from the abstract syntax tree, propagates them over a call graph by Datalog-style rules, and reports an inconsistency when a two-phase heuristic matching of types and entities finds no code fact for a comment constraint. The tagger only labels the input of the rule-based decision (B.2 step 7) → Rule-based, ML secondary.
type_evidence: title: "SmartCoCo: Checking Comment-code Inconsistency in Smart Contracts via Constraint Propagation and Binding" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "In this paper, we present SmartCoCo, a novel framework to detect comment-code inconsistencies in smart contracts" (no type); contribution list: "We propose SmartCoCo, a new framework to detect comment-code inconsistency for smart contracts" and "a set of constraint propagation and binding mechanisms for inconsistency detection" (no type) → B.2 step 3, the method: keyword templates with part-of-speech tagging and "a two-phase heuristic matching method", which the conclusion calls "a static analysis framework" → Rule-based; the CoreNLP tagger → ML secondary (step 7)

row_justification: The governing set, the paper's level-classified ground truth and so governing whatever its size, is 65 vulnerable contracts from real-world incidents in the Slowmist and Rekt libraries (January 2020 to June 2022, social-engineering incidents such as rug pulls excluded), classified by hand following SmartInv into Business Logic Flaw 30, Price Manipulation 17, Privilege Escalation 11, and Reentrancy 7 (Section 5.2.1 and the column heads of Table 5). Business Logic Flaw "strongly relies on the specific contract functionalities" (Section 6.1) and names no description; the paper's example, the THORChain fake deposit of Section 3.1, breaks a property statable over the contract's state (the deposited amount equals the change in the contract's token balance), so these cases are PM, as is price manipulation; privilege escalation, which "means the contract lacks a complete access control check", and reentrancy are ES → PM 47, ES 18. The 466 abnormal transactions (483 flagged, 17 false positives) related to the 31 detected contracts carry no type breakdown, and the ERC20 invariant evaluation (96 % precision) scores generated properties, not violations.
column_justification: Invariants instantiated from Comparison, Membership, and Arithmetic (linear and quadratic) pattern templates over historical transactions replayed in an instrumented EVM serve as the oracle, and a new transaction that violates one is flagged; the mining is deterministic, and nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "SmartOracle: Generating smart contract oracle via fine-grained invariant detection" (no type); abstract: "we introduce SmartOracle, a dynamic invariant detector that automatically generates fine-grained invariants as application-specific oracles for vulnerability detection", and "From historical transactions, SmartOracle uses pattern-based detection and advanced inference"; contribution 1: "We propose SmartOracle, a fine-grained dynamic invariant detector for smart contracts" → patterns and oracles, the one type named, mined from history as templates (as for InvCon, Table 8, row 4) → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: SafePay targets one class, unfair payments, violations of its Fair Value Exchange invariant, which pairs ether sent to an address with a transfer of data value (storage-held assets) for that address; the invariant is contract-agnostic and statable from the code and EVM value-transfer semantics, like ILF's leaking oracle (Table 6) → ES. The large-scale evaluation considers 46,237 deployed contracts and reports 11.9% of SafePay's reports as false positives (over 70% for Securify, Mythril, and Oyente) without a count of reports; the six cases of Table I are four reentrancy contracts (simple_dao, DAO, SpankChain_Payment, and modifier_reentrancy) and two fixed versions, also ES.
column_justification: A hand-defined invariant (Fair Value Exchange) is checked by symbolic execution over the control-flow graph, taint analysis, and Z3 path feasibility on transaction scenarios up to a bound k; no learned or generative model is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "SafePay on Ethereum: A framework for detecting unfair payments in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "To mitigate these limitations, we designed the SafePay analysis framework to find unfair payments in Ethereum smart contracts" (no type); contributions, second item: "We developed the analysis framework SafePay to automatically detect UP in Ethereum smart contracts" → no type named, B.2 step 3, an invariant checked by symbolic execution → Rule-based.

row_justification: CDRipper's largest labeled set is the hand-checked sample of Table VI, 559 detections drawn per defect type from the 82,446 of 244,424 contracts it flags (Table V counts flagged contracts per type), 524 of them true positives (single-signature mint 86, critical-variable manipulation 92, management without timelock 93, single proxy admin 85, single-signature self-destruct 90, individual contract output reliance 78). Mint privileges, owner control of critical variables such as fees and pausing, and changes to them without a timelock are privileges over holder balances (B.1 scams, holder-balance integrity), and reliance on one external contract's output, such as a DEX pool's price tick, is an on-chain-manipulable oracle, so 349 cases are PM; the proxy-admin and self-destruct cases lack only a multi-signature requirement, a generic signer condition (B.1 missing checks), so 175 are ES → PM, ES secondary. The six types come from 597 Ethereum Stack Exchange posts and 117 audit reports, and no description is named.
column_justification: CDRipper matches hand-defined defect patterns over a permission dependency graph extracted from source.
type_evidence: title: "Definition and detection of centralization defects in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "we introduce a tool named CDRipper (Centralization Defects Ripper) designed to identify the defined centralization defects", which "identifies centralization defects based on predefined patterns"; contribution 2: "We developed a tool called CDRipper for detecting the defined centralization defects" → patterns, the one type named → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: On its 234-contract labelled sample Tokeer finds 423 risk instances — BlackList 134, ModifyBalance 118, TimeLimit 54, AlienDepend 117 (Table 1) — balance and transfer control, holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams); the token standard states none of these, and no other description is named → PM.
column_justification: Datalog oracles for the four risks are written over a component-configurable model of the token transfer process, a hand-specified boundary.
type_evidence: title: "Stop pulling my rug: Exposing rug pull risks in crypto token to investors"

row_justification: SSR's largest labeled set is the hand-checked sample of Table VI (Section V-C), 456 detections drawn per defect type from the 3,557 of 15,992 staking contracts it flags, 414 of them true positives. The true positives of rewards without time delay (79), single liquidity pool reliance (29), omission in status update (79), and unsafe verification, a missing check on staking state such as an NFT already unstaked (80), break staking-mechanism invariants (PM, 267); those of staking logical variables manipulation (68) and unauthorized staking asset access (79) are functions that let any caller change a reward variable or move another user's stake, a generic missing access check (ES, 147) → PM, ES secondary. The 40-contract ground truth (21 positive; Table V, 28 defect instances) gives the same majority, 19 PM and nine ES.
column_justification: Presented as a static analysis tool (abstract) → Rule-based; an LLM extracts staking variables and functions into a staking model whose control- and data-flow features predefined logical rules then check (LLM secondary).
type_evidence: title: "SSR: Safeguarding staking rewards by defining and detecting logical defects in DeFi staking" names no type; abstract: "we developed SSR (Safeguarding Staking Reward), a static analysis tool designed to detect logical defects in DeFi staking contracts" and "SSR utilizes a large language model (LLM) to extract fundamental information about staking logic"; contributions, second: "We proposed SSR, a tool for detecting logical defects in DeFi staking. It extracts fundamental information about DeFi staking using an LLM and constructs a DeFi staking model for logical defect detection"; the static analysis tool is presented as the contribution and the LLM only extracts the input its rules check (B.2 steps 4 and 7, as for NumScout) → Rule-based, LLM secondary; read by step 6 instead (the two types named in different places, the contribution list naming only the LLM), the column would be LLM (Supplementary Appendix B.7)

row_justification: FairChecker's governing set is Web3Bugs, 462 developer-confirmed high-risk bugs in 113 Code4rena projects, among which two authors labeled 34 fairness bugs (the exploit leaks funds and the attacker pays nothing); it reports 32 of them among 69 warnings (94.1 % recall, 46.4 % precision) and all nine fairness bugs with source code among 155 recent DeFi hacks. Each bug violates one or both of the paper's fairness properties (12 both, 18 the first only, four the second only), that a caller's balance rises only when another of its balances falls and that another holder's balance falls only when one of its balances rises; both are invariants over the protocol's balance state → PM. The two arbitrary-external-call bugs among those detected (Table V), which the paper calls low-level, are recorded as the ES secondary.
column_justification: Presented as an inter-procedural and inter-contract static analysis technique that uses symbolic execution and an SMT solver (abstract, contribution list) → Rule-based; the two fairness properties are written by the authors, a Z3-based symbolic executor collects each external function's balance changes on Slither's IR, and a function is reported unfair when the solver finds a counterexample. Balance variables are annotated by ERC naming conventions, taint heuristics, keyword matching, and an NLTK sentiment package for asset and debt names, which only labels the input of the rule-based decision.
type_evidence: title: "FairChecker: Detecting fund-stealing bugs in DeFi protocols via fairness validation" (no type named); abstract: "We propose an inter-procedural and inter-contract static analysis technique that utilizes symbolic execution and an SMT solver to automatically detect fairness bugs in DeFi smart contracts"; contribution list: "combining an annotation mechanism, a symbolic execution engine, and an SMT solver-based validator that verifies the two defined fairness properties" → one type, hand-written properties applied by symbolic execution (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: JANUS's largest labeled set is a manual inspection of 1,000 of the 33,151 real-world contracts (500 flagged and 500 unflagged, reviewed by three researchers; 455 true positives, 91.0 % precision, and 91.37 % recall), with no per-type breakdown; its comparison set holds 540 contracts, 270 risky ones from the Pied-Piper dataset and security events and their 270 repaired versions (Table II). Every positive case is of one class, a privileged account that can arbitrarily transfer, destroy, or mint tokens, freeze an account, or disable transferring (Section II), and the two patterns found only in the wild are an owner-set transfer fee and a transfer whitelist, so neither set needs a breakdown; all are breaches of holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams) → PM. The token standard states none of these, and no other description is named.
column_justification: JANUS symbolically executes each function (on Slither and Z3) as a privileged and as an ordinary account and flags a contract when the resulting state differences include a financial variable, a fixed check that issues the verdict → Rule-based. A trained GNN (GCN and GAT layers) only labels which state variables are financial, the input of that rule-based decision, so the work stays Rule-based with ML as secondary type (B.2 step 7, NumScout).
type_evidence: title: "JANUS: A difference-oriented analyzer for financial centralized risks in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "In this paper, we propose JANUS, an automated analyzer for Solidity smart contracts that detects financial centralization risks independently of their specific behaviors" (no type); contributions: the first, "a framework for detecting financial centralized risks based on the differences in contract states reached by privileged and ordinary accounts", and the third, "a GNN-based method to automatically identify financial variables" (ML) → the work presents an analyzer, and the GNN only labels the input of its decision → Rule-based, ML secondary (B.2 step 7)

row_justification: AllocScope's governing set is the ground-truth set released with Devils' Footprint (SmartCat), the top 8,000 active contracts plus 84 contracts with confirmed exploitable attacks, which SmartCat labels as price-manipulation targets; AllocScope reports all 84 (86 findings, 84 true positives, no false negatives, and two false positives that the authors trace to snapshot-based accounting, Table 1). It governs as the larger labeled set; the second set, 200 audited DeFi contracts with a medium or high risk of allocation manipulation, recovers all labeled allocation risks but gives no per-case count and is the same class. The violated property, a reward share in an allocation episode disproportionate to the user's contribution, is statable over vault state → PM; both sets are one class at one level, so no breakdown is needed and no glossary applies.
column_justification: Presented as a static analysis framework (abstract, contribution list) → Rule-based; built on Slither's analysis engine, it summarizes each allocation episode in a funds allocation graph of stake, allocation, and payout edges, and hand-written pattern-specific predicates over that graph issue the finding (Section 4.3).
type_evidence: title: "AllocScope: Towards automated vetting of allocation manipulation in smart contracts" (no type named); abstract: "we present AllocScope, an auditor-centric static analysis framework that identifies allocation manipulation vulnerabilities"; contribution list: "We propose AllocScope, an auditor-centric static analysis framework that takes contract source code as input" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

subgroup: privileged-function and rug-pull classifiers over code
row_justification: The governing set is the 10,000-contract evaluation split (rows 20,000 to 29,999) of over 40,000 BSC contracts whose intent labels come from StaySafu with developer and auditor input (Section IV), each contract carrying any of ten risky intents (multi-label); Table I gives each intent's share of all intent labels (reflect 37.50 %, fee 26.86 %, maxTX 13.76 %, mint 8.53 %, disableTrading 5.34 %, blacklist 3.82 %, reward 3.37 %, rebase 0.53 %, honeypot 0.23 %, and maxSell 0.05 %). Every intent is a fee, freeze, blacklist, mint, sell-limit, supply, payout, or trap mechanic over holder balances, so every class sits at PM (B.1 scams) and the set needs no per-case breakdown; the token standard states none of these, and no other description is named.
column_justification: A universal-sentence-encoder embedding, K-means highlighting, and a BiLSTM multi-label classifier, which issues the verdict, learn the intent boundary → ML; the pretrained model is an encoder and generates no text.
type_evidence: title: "Deep smart contract intent detection" (deep learning); abstract, proposal sentence: "we propose SmartIntentNN (Smart Contract Intent Neural Network), a deep learning model designed to automatically detect development intent in smart contracts"; contribution 1: "the first study to propose an approach for detecting developer intents behind smart contracts using deep learning models" → ML (B.2 step 3, one type named)

first_release: cited version, 2026; preprint arXiv:2609.13601 (2026-09) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is 3,864 proposals collected from Tally, which indexes 154 Ethereum DAOs; two independent annotators labeled 893 of them mismatched and 2,971 matched, a third resolving their 58 disagreements (Section 6.2, Appendix D.1; unit proposals, one class). A proposal is mismatched when at least one action of its execution trace is neither stated in nor inferable from its description, a violation of the proposal text as the named description → DM. A scan of 10,190 executed proposals (Section 7) found 69 malicious proposals, nine of them confirmed by their projects, and Table 8 lists the Pepe Cash fund drain and the attempted proxy-admin takeover at the Fei DAO among the confirmed cases. Its criterion also counts a description that states nothing, which B.1 places at no level and leaves out of the count; the irresponsible proposals of its scan include such texts (Section 7.2), and whatever their number in the labeled set, for which the paper gives none, the cases counted are DM. No evaluated set or named target lies at another level, so there is no secondary row.
column_justification: An LLM (GPT-4o by default) maps each action of a simulation trace, computed beforehand by replaying the proposal on a Foundry fork, to a supporting span of the proposal description; the Robustness Guard is a specificity constraint appended to the same prompt (Section 4.5), and five passes are combined by majority vote. The model calls no tool, and the released checker likewise makes one chat call per proposal with no tools → LLM, flag no on released code; the simulation is the Rule-based secondary.
type_evidence: title: no type word; abstract: "we present the first systematic framework for DEMI detection in real DAO governance" (no type), then "an evidence-mapping paradigm that requires an LLM to locate explicit per-action textual justifications" → one type named, LLM (B.2 step 3); contributions: no type word; the Foundry simulation whose trace the model reads gives the Rule-based secondary (step 7)

subgroup: front-end descriptions against bytecode, row by the evaluation majority
row_justification: The governing set is the 291 reports sampled from the flags on 835 real-world DApps and labeled by hand by three authors (Table IV; unit: reported inconsistency), 268 of them true positives (UR 20, HF 38, AL 15, UTS 46, UFF 66, CDS 34, and VNA 49). UR, flagged when the description cites a fixed reward rate, is DM; UFF and CDS are flagged when the description does not mention an owner's withdrawal or pause (Table I, §IV-D), undisclosed capabilities that the B.1 scam rule puts at PM (arbitrary transfer, transfer freeze), since a property no description states is not DM; AL is flagged "irrespective of whether users are informed or not" (§IV-D), an owner-adjustable liquidity lock, PM. These four types cover 135 of the 268 cases, most of the set, and give PM 115 to DM 20 (PM 100 to DM 35 if AL is read as a claimed lock time) → PM; HF, UTS, and VNA (133) are flagged both on a stated fee, supply, or accessibility claim that the code contradicts and on silence about it (Table I), and the paper does not split them. UR and the stated cases of HF, UTS, and VNA give the DM secondary. The ground truth of 69 inconsistencies in 54 DApps (Table III) is smaller.
column_justification: Presented as using "LLM and dataflow-guided symbolic execution" (title), the two named equally → LLM by the tie-break, Rule-based secondary. HyperText, LLaMA2 instruction-tuned with LoRA, answers fixed prompts over segments of the front-end description; NLTK, not the model, turns its free-text answers into key-value attributes (§IV-B); HyperCode decompiles the bytecode with Elipmoc, runs Datalog data-flow analysis and IR symbolic execution with an SMT solver, and reads storage through public nodes (§IV-C, §IV-D); predefined detection rules then compare the two. The model calls no tool, and the framework fixes the schedule → flag no; the code and the fine-tuned model are released (§I), the paper prints no trace or ablation of a tool step, and the flag rests on the method text.
type_evidence: title: "Hyperion: Unveiling DApp inconsistencies using LLM and dataflow-guided symbolic execution"; abstract: "we introduce Hyperion, an approach designed to automatically identify inconsistencies between front-end descriptions and back-end code implementation in DApps. This method leverages a fine-tuned large language model LLaMA2 to analyze DApp descriptions and employs dataflow-guided symbolic execution for contract bytecode analysis"; contribution 2: "a tool that leverages LLM and dataflow-guided symbolic execution to automatically detect defined inconsistencies"; the two types named equally in all three places → B.2 step 5 tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary)

subgroup: business-logic invariants inferred without a description
row_justification: The governing set is the 40 accounting errors in 23 projects taken from the dataset of ScType (Zhang et al., ICSE 2024) (Section 4.2, Table 1); 19 fall in categories such as pure math errors (a '>' swapped with '<') and are out of scope, and 19 of the remaining 21 are found, plus four known and two new bugs in eight further projects. The 21 in-scope errors misuse the financial meaning of raw balances, net and interest rates, debt, prices, and reserves, which the tool infers rather than reads from a named description (description test), so they violate mechanism invariants → PM; they are most of the 40 cases, and the 19 out-of-scope errors, which carry no per-class counts, cannot outnumber them (as for ScType).
column_justification: Presented as "a hybrid system combining LLMs and rule-based reasoning", the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary). GPT-3.5-turbo annotates the financial meaning of variables, and rule-based reasoning, implemented inside Slither (whose APIs identify entry functions from the control-flow graph), propagates the annotations and flags inconsistent operations; for each flagged bug the framework returns the reasoning trace to the model for self-reflection and reruns the reasoning on any new annotations, keeping the bug only if it persists. The model calls no tool and the feedback follows a schedule the framework sets, so the flag is no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "Detecting bugs with substantial monetary consequences by LLM and rule-based reasoning"; abstract, proposal sentence: "This paper proposes a hybrid system combining LLMs and rule-based reasoning to detect accounting error vulnerabilities in smart contracts"; contribution 1: "identifying financial meanings of variables with LLM, and checking correctness of operations with rule-based reasoning" → the two presented equally, tie-break, the newer type → LLM (B.2 step 5)

subgroup: business-logic invariants inferred without a description
first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2503.23718 (2025-03) in the same year; extended version: PromFuzz++, ACM Trans. Softw. Eng. Methodol. (Sept. 2026), doi:10.1145/3849091 (placement and figures follow the cited version)
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 30 zero-day bugs PromFuzz found in real-world DeFi projects under public audit, all reported to their vendors and 24 assigned CVE IDs (Table 7). Section 4.5 splits them into 13 AMM and seven non-AMM price oracle manipulation, four wrong checkpoint order, four risky first deposit, and two wrong interest-rate order bugs, all protocol-mechanism invariants → PM. The 23 ground-truth bugs (seven exploited, ten developer-confirmed from Web3Bugs, and six injected; 20 detected, Table 6) are also PM, with price oracle manipulation (five), insecure calculating logic (five), incorrect control mechanism (five), and unauthorized behavior (eight), the last checked over the allowance state (Table 2); no case is ES, so there is no secondary row.
column_justification: The title presents the analysis as "LLM-driven", and the abstract's "novel Large Language Model (LLM)-driven analysis framework, which leverages a dual-agent prompt engineering strategy" places the two agents, auditor and attacker prompt roles of one GPT-4-turbo, inside that framework → LLM, the type named as driving (B.2 step 4), with Rule-based and Agentic secondary. A separate extraction prompt (Fig. 6) supplies the variables that fill six predefined invariant-checker templates, which a customized ItyFuzz executes; the checker issues the verdict and fuzzing results never return to the model → flag no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "PromFuzz: Leveraging LLM-driven and bug-oriented composite analysis for detecting functional bugs in smart contracts"; abstract: "a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-driven analysis framework, which leverages a dual-agent prompt engineering strategy"; contribution 1: "a novel dual-agent prompt engineering strategy that enables LLM to effectively extract hidden business logic"; LLM named as driving the framework → B.2 step 4 → LLM (Rule-based and Agentic secondary)

subgroup: documentation checks against generic standard text
row_justification: The largest labeled set is 119 tokens from CRPWarner's data, 92 malicious and 27 normal (Section 6.1, Table 1; GPT-4 precision 0.97 and recall 0.92). The 92 malicious tokens have "modified transfer functions to restrict selling" (Section 6.1), logic the paper says counterfeit tokens typically implement by blacklisting, transaction pauses, or high fees, and the paper judges them against the generic ERC20 documentation as code-only inconsistencies; ERC-20 states no sell restriction, blacklist, or fee rule, so each is a privilege over balances → PM (B.1 scams). The 20 arbitrage-bot scams (18 flagged, 90 % recall; Section 6.3) are payout mechanics and the Uranium Finance K-value check (Section 6.2) is a pool invariant, both PM; the DM secondary is the work's named target, mismatches with the project's own documentation such as a whitepaper or user guide. The description its evaluation reads is the generic ERC20 documentation, so description_scope records shared.
column_justification: The title names symbolic analysis and large language models equally ("Leveraging Symbolic Analysis and Large Language Models"), so the tie-break gives the newer type, LLM (Rule-based secondary). The LLM reads the documentation together with SEVM's symbolic summaries of balance changes and branch conditions, computed beforehand and supplied in one prompt, and its JSON output is the result; no tool is invoked, so the flag is no.
type_evidence: title: "DeFiAligner: Leveraging symbolic analysis and large language models for inconsistency detection in decentralized finance", the two named equally → B.2 step 5, tie-break → LLM (Rule-based secondary); abstract: "we developed DeFiAligner, an end-to-end system to identify inconsistencies between documentation and smart contracts" (no type); contributions: the first names no type, the second "We develop a symbolic generation tool named SEVM" (a Rule-based component)

row_justification: The governing set is the 25 % held-out split of a six-class set of 5,592 code slices, 1,000 for each of five classes and 592 for the sixth (§3.8; 1,398 slices under scikit-learn's default split, with no per-class test counts printed; unit: code slice), labeled where Slither or SmartCheck output agrees with regular expressions (§3.4), with per-class results (Table 5). All six classes (reentrancy, uninitialized local variables, recursive calls in loops, incorrect low-level calls, locked ether, and incorrect equality checks) are statable from the code and VM semantics → ES. The nine logic classes the paper defines from 614 hand-labeled code changes (§5.1), on which the detector is not evaluated, include incomplete standard function implementation ("fails to implement all the required functions of a standard", §5.1.3; DM, shared) and incorrect validation of oracle data and stale oracle data (§5.1.4, §5.1.5; PM), recorded as secondaries.
column_justification: The detector is CodeBERTa, a six-layer, 84M-parameter RoBERTa-like encoder whose final linear layer maps its 768-dimensional output to six classes (§3.7); an encoder that produces labels and no text is ML however the paper names it, and B.2 applies that boundary before reading the named types (step 3) → ML. LLM, named in the title, the abstract, and the contribution list, is the secondary type (step 7, as for MANDO-LLM); the generative models GPT-2 and T5-Base are compared baselines (Table 6).
type_evidence: title (arXiv v1): "Sóley: Identification and automated detection of logic vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts using large language models"; abstract: "introduce Sóley, an automated method for detecting logic vulnerabilities in smart contracts, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs)"; contributions: "We present Sóley, based on CodeBERTa, to detect logic-related vulnerabilities in smart contracts" and "We also explore the performance of well-known LLMs on the same task"; B.2 step 3 applies the step 2 boundary first, and CodeBERTa is an encoder → ML, LLM secondary (step 7)

row_justification: SmartComment's largest labeled set is the 254 inconsistencies it reports in 1,000 Etherscan contracts sampled at random, each labeled valid or not by two authors with a third resolving disagreements; 203 are valid (79.9 % precision, 127 contracts), and Table 2 divides them into conditions on parameters and variables (64), missing or wrong operations and operands (61), other function-specific logic (36), function interfaces (25), and access control (17). In every type the comment supplies the property the code violates (a bound's value, a visibility, a required event, an owner-only policy), so the comment is the description (project-specific) → DM; the annotated 200-contract set (43 inconsistencies) is the same class.
column_justification: Presented as combining LLMs with program analysis (title, abstract, contribution list), the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM, Rule-based secondary. Flag no on the released code (github.com/SmartComment-Tool/Artifact, the repository the paper's Data Availability section gives, read at commit d03e252, 5 September 2025, the later of its two commits, which differ only in the README), which agrees with the method text (§3.2 to §3.4, §4.1.3). For each contract the framework fetches the source, constructor arguments, and compiler version from Etherscan and builds the Slither instance before any model call (Code/main.py); deepseek-r1 then matches comments to code entities and propagates them to each function, five checker prompt versions (v1 to v5 in Code/checker.py, one call each at temperature 0) judge each function against its comments over a Slither code slice and return, for an inconsistency, the violated comment and a fix variant, and five confirmation prompt versions (Code/verifier.py) judge each candidate, which needs three of five checker votes and three of five confirmations (Code/match_comment.py). The framework then compiles the variant, returning the compiler error to the model for one function-level and one contract-level repair if compilation fails (Code/rewrite_smart_contracts.py), applies static difference rules, and runs Echidna differential testing when those find no difference (Code/differential_testing.py, §3.4.3); these results do not return to the model. Every model call is a plain chat completion with no tool or function interface, whose JSON or code reply the framework parses (Code/chat.py), so the model chooses no tool and the compile feedback returns on the framework's schedule (B.2 flag rules). The code takes the fix variant from the checker's reply and confirms candidates before compiling their variants, where the paper generates the variant in a separate step and compiles it before confirmation (§3.3.3, §3.4.2); neither difference touches the flag.
type_evidence: title: "Detecting code-comment inconsistencies in smart contracts by combining LLM and program analysis"; abstract: "this paper presents SmartComment, the first technique that combines LLMs with program analysis techniques for detecting code-comment inconsistencies in smart contracts"; contribution list: "We propose SmartComment, the first technique that combines LLMs with program analysis techniques" → the two equally (B.2 step 5, tie-break, the newer type) → LLM, Rule-based secondary; the abstract's next sentence, "SmartComment introduces an LLM-driven workflow", agrees

row_justification: The 60 ICO pairs are labeled by project (31 legitimate; 12 fraud-labeled, six of them by SEC or DOJ action; 17 borderline; Table 1), labels that classify projects and not violations, since two of the six regulatory frauds (CTR, PRG) involve "misrepresentation of team credentials and business partnerships, not contract-level deception" (§4.1); the 86 specification-implementation inconsistencies in 21 of 54 analyzed ICOs are reported without a precision or a breakdown by category (Table 3 counts claims); and the F1 of 0.72 on 19 ICOs scores claim extraction. The work therefore has no labeled set of findings, and its stated target, whitepaper claims against contract code, names the description → glossary line 1 ("documentation vs. behavior", the whitepaper named) → DM ‡, project-specific. One scored rule falls under the B.1 scam rule and gives the PM secondary, a fixed-supply claim against a mint() function (C1, §3.4), as does the owner-controlled freezeAccount() of the Bitconnect case (§4.1); the rule for "no admin privileges" (C8) tests only whether the code inherits Ownable or uses onlyOwner, a property only the whitepaper states (DM).
column_justification: No type in the title; the abstract and the first contribution name LLM-based claim extraction and Slither analysis, joined in "a hybrid rule-based and LLM-based consistency scorer" → LLM by the tie-break, Rule-based secondary. Every project passes through the same four steps (section parsing, claim extraction by Qwen3.5-122B, Slither features from each contract that compiles (57 of 60, §3.3), and consistency scoring), the scoring by deterministic rules for supply and access-control claims and by an LLM verdict, given the claim text and the relevant code snippet, for vesting and burn or mint claims (§3.4). The model calls no tool and its verdict ends the run → flag no (the framework fixes the schedule); no code is released, so the flag rests on the method text.
type_evidence: title: "Cross-referencing whitepaper claims and smart contract code for automated ICO auditing", no type; abstract: "We built ICOAudit, a pipeline that bridges this gap. ICOAudit extracts structured claims from ICO whitepapers using LLM-based information extraction ..., analyzes the corresponding Ethereum smart contracts via Slither static analysis, and checks each claim against code-level features using a hybrid rule-based and LLM-based consistency scorer"; contribution 1: "A claim-to-code verification pipeline that extracts structured claims from whitepapers using LLM-based information extraction and checks them against contract features from Slither static analysis"; the two types joined as equals ("a hybrid rule-based and LLM-based consistency scorer") → B.2 step 5 tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary)

row_justification: XploGen has GPT-4 inject business-logic flaws into five contracts the authors modeled as DCR graphs (Governance, Escrow, MultiStageAuction, PrizeDistribution, and ProductOrder) and write an exploit for each variant; of 104 variants, 91 compiled and 52 formed exploitable pairs, those whose exploit executed a transaction the HighGuard monitor found to breach a DCR property (Table 1, counted per contract with no breakdown by the property violated). The DCR models are the authors' process models, not a description (B.1 user-supplied specifications); their time windows, orderings, and vote thresholds are conditions over process state (the two flaws described, a time check removed from vote and proposals executed without enough votes, are of this kind), while their role constraints are generic access checks, so the set spans two levels without per-case counts → PM ‡ by rule, as for HighGuard, ES secondary; the deliverable is an exploit → offensive.
column_justification: The verdict is issued by the HighGuard monitor, which applies the authors' DCR model to each exploit's transactions on a simulated chain; GPT-4, prompted once with the DCR semantics, the contract, the summarized model, and an example exploit (Fig. 3), writes the vulnerable variant and its JavaScript exploit, and nothing returns to it (Fig. 1) → Rule-based, LLM secondary.
type_evidence: title: "Oracle-guided vulnerability diversity and exploit synthesis of smart contracts using LLMs"; abstract: "XploGen, which uses a model-based oracle specification of the business logic of the smart contracts to synthesize valid exploits using LLMs"; contribution (2): DCR graphs applied "statically (guiding an LLM in producing vulnerable mutants and diversifying exploits) and dynamically (as a runtime oracle to confirm whether an exploit is valid)" → the oracle is named as guiding the LLM → Rule-based (step 4), LLM secondary (step 7)

row_justification: Arbiter is evaluated on INTENT-TX-18K, 18,000 pairs of a user intent and a transaction built from 6,000 real CoW Protocol, Uniswap V2 and V3, and Compound V2 transactions (4,500 aligned and 13,500 violations, each a single minimal edit), in four violation categories the paper calls balanced without giving per-category counts (Section V): intent misalignment (token substitution, amount skimming, slippage loosening, deadline shifts), technical violations (format and decimal errors, missing or inconsistent fields), adversarial manipulation (MEV exposure, zero-amount CoW orders, manipulated Compound collateral ratios), and legal violations (sanctioned or illegitimate entries from lists such as OFAC, about 10 % of negatives). A user's intent is not a named description, and the misaligned and adversarial cases are statable over the transaction and protocol state, so this adjacent entry (row n/a) is shown in the protocol-mechanism row; the technical violations are the ES secondary, and the sanctions cases break a compliance rule, no property at any level and not the trust boundary, so they are left out.
column_justification: GPT-4o issues the verdict in the LLM nodes of a fixed Graph-of-Thoughts DAG, which read the natural-language intent and the transaction JSON after deterministic rule nodes (address format, decimal scaling, protocol structure); the Controller schedules the nodes by their dependencies and stops early on a critical failure, and each LLM node returns PASS, FAIL, or SKIP and calls no tool → LLM, Rule-based secondary, flag no (method text only; no code released).
type_evidence: title: "Auditable LLM Arbiter for DeFi security: A hybrid Graph-of-Thoughts approach to intent–transaction alignment" (LLM); abstract: "We introduce Arbiter, a hybrid Graph-of-Thoughts validation framework" composing "deterministic rule-based checks with LLM-based semantic reasoning"; contributions: "a modular hybrid validator that composes protocol-aware deterministic checks with LLM-based semantic reasoning" ("agentic DeFi systems" in the first contribution names the setting, not the validator) → the two presented equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (B.2 step 5), Rule-based secondary

row_justification: CFF's largest evaluation samples 1,000 random blocks per month with at least two AMM transactions from Uniswap V1, Uniswap V2, and SushiSwap data through May 16, 2021 (Section 6.3, Fig. 10), counted in blocks, with every extracted ordering validated by simulation on an archive node; the paper gives neither the number of months nor a count of blocks with MEV, only about 1.5 million USD of MEV in the 2021 sample. Its cases are of one class, value extracted by reordering AMM trades (large trades front- or back-run by a bot), a property of the AMM pricing mechanism statable over pool state → PM. The other experiments are PM as well, liquidations over the top 100 MakerDAO CDPs with Uniswap V2 as a hypothetical price oracle (542,827 USD over the top 20 liquidation blocks, Section 6.4), an on-chain-manipulable oracle, and the flash-loan ApeCoin airdrop exploit and a flash-loan governance model (Section 6.5).
column_justification: K-framework models of Uniswap V1, Uniswap V2, SushiSwap, and MakerDAO, written by hand, and an extractable-value property; the kprove deductive verifier (Z3 backend) explores transaction orderings and yields counterexample strategies, each validated by simulation on an archive node → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Clockwork Finance: Automated analysis of economic security in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "We introduce the Clockwork Finance Framework (CFF), a general purpose, formal verification framework for mechanized reasoning about the economic security properties of composed decentralized-finance (DeFi) smart contracts" (formal verification); contributions (introduction): "We instantiate our definitions in our CFF tool in order to find arbitrage strategies and prove bounds" (no type) → one type named → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: DEFIER's governing set is its ground truth (Section 4.4, Table 6), 57,855 attack transactions from the paper's measurement study, labeled by attack stage, and 39,124 benign transactions, unit transactions, evaluated by 10-fold cross validation (98.2% micro-precision, 98.1% micro-recall). The measurement study types every attack by the vulnerability exploited (Section 3.1, 42 incidents on 25 Dapps; Table 2, 58,555 attack transactions in the derived set, with 40,766 for bad randomness, 17,088 for denial of service, 591 for integer overflow or underflow, 575 for improper authentication, and 30 for reentrancy), and each type is an execution-semantics property (a weak PRNG, gas exhaustion or unchecked exceptional conditions, arithmetic, a missing ownership or access check, and reentrancy) → ES. The 476,342 transactions DEFIER labels among those of 104 popular Dapps (Section 4.5) are checked by hand only on a 4% sample (3,671 of 4,003 clusters confirmed), so they do not govern.
column_justification: A Bi-LSTM with attention over graph-embedded transaction sequences, followed by an MLP, classifies each sequence into an attack stage or as legitimate; it is trained on the labeled bad and good transaction sets (Sections 4.3 and 4.4) → ML.
type_evidence: title, abstract ("we proposed the first technique DEFIER to automatically investigate attack incidents on a large scale"), and contribution list (item 2, "our new understanding and CTI discovered can help mitigate the threat to Dapps") name no type; the method does (Introduction, "we run a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to classify each time series"; Section 4.3) → ML by B.2 step 3

row_justification: DeFiTainter's governing set is 23 DeFi protocols exploited in real price-manipulation attacks, selected from 1,125 web3rekt incidents by their labels and manual inspection; it detects 21 of the 23 (91.3 % recall) and, on 1,195 high-value DefiLlama protocols, flags four, three of them undisclosed exploitable vulnerabilities and one a false positive. In each case a transfer or reward amount depends on a balance or reserve that a flash loan can move, a pricing invariant over protocol state; one class at one level needs no breakdown → PM.
column_justification: Presented as an inter-contract taint analysis framework that detects the vulnerability "from a static analysis perspective" (abstract, contribution list) → Rule-based; several hundred hand-written Datalog rules over Gigahorse's decompiled bytecode take the return value of balanceOf as the taint source and the amount of a transfer or transferFrom whose recipient the caller controls as the sink, with call targets restored from contract storage and call parameters, and any tainted flow into a sink is reported.
type_evidence: title: "DeFiTainter: Detecting price manipulation vulnerabilities in DeFi protocols" (no type named); abstract: "we propose DeFiTainter, an inter-contract taint analysis framework for detecting price manipulation vulnerabilities"; contribution list: "a new approach for detecting price manipulation vulnerabilities via inter-contract taint analysis ... from a static analysis perspective" → one type, static analysis with hand-written rules (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

first_release: cited version, 2021; preprint arXiv:2103.02873 (2021-03) in the same year
row_justification: The governing set is Table I's eight DeFi projects (unit: project), labeled for an oracle-dependent state update, with bZx, DDEX, and Eminence vulnerable (TP) and Aave, dYdX, Compound, Nuo, and Oasis not (TN), all found "with no false positive or false negative alert" (§IV). The three positives are one class, a state update fed by an on-chain-manipulable price oracle, which needs no breakdown → PM. Table II's larger counts (about 7,138 bZx and 1,486 Eminence transactions, with 19 to 25 and 37 to 124 "suspicious" ones by slippage threshold) are detections the paper does not confirm, not a labeled set, so they do not govern.
column_justification: BLOCKEYE extends the Seraph analyzer to reason symbolically (§II-B), with Z3 as its solver (§III-A), about whether a value read from another project's oracle flows into a payment or storage update, then monitors the transactions of vulnerable projects for "violations on invariant as predefined heuristic rules", a profit above a configured threshold (§II-C) → Rule-based, no secondary type.
type_evidence: title: "BLOCKEYE: Hunting for DeFi attacks on blockchain", no type; abstract: "we proposed BLOCKEYE, a real-time attack detection system for DeFi projects on the Ethereum blockchain", no type; no contribution list (a four-page companion paper); no type named in the three places → B.2 step 3, the method decides (symbolic oracle analysis and "pattern-based runtime transaction validation", §VI) → Rule-based

row_justification: FlashSyn is evaluated on 18 benchmarks (Table 2), 16 real flash-loan attacks and two Damn Vulnerable DeFi challenges, and synthesizes an attack for 16 of them (Table 3). Table 2 types each benchmark; eight oracle manipulations, one pump and arbitrage, and one forced investment are price manipulations, and one asset mismatch and one deflationary token break the accounting of pooled value, all PM (12), while six are typed only "design flaw", which the table note defines as "The logic designs of one or more functions in the victim contracts is flawed" and which carries no level. The typed cases cover most of the set → PM by majority, tallied from the paper's per-benchmark list (even the nine oracle and pump-and-arbitrage cases alone would at least tie, and a tie goes to PM); no benchmark is described as a missing check, so no ES secondary is recorded.
column_justification: FlashSyn enumerates action sequences under fixed pruning heuristics, approximates each protocol function by polynomial regression or nearest-neighbor interpolation fitted to executions on a forked chain, maximizes profit over the approximations with SciPy's SHGO optimizer, and replays each candidate on the fork, adding counterexamples where estimate and execution differ; the approximations stand in for protocol functions and are neither a decision function nor a search policy learned from data (B.2, ML), and the verdict is a fixed check of positive profit on concrete execution → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "FlashSyn: Flash loan attack synthesis via counter example driven approximation" names no type; abstract: "In this paper, we introduce a new framework for automated synthesis of adversarial transactions that exploit DeFi protocols using flash loans", approximating protocol behavior "using numerical methods (polynomial linear regression and nearest-neighbor interpolation)"; contributions, first: "FlashSyn: The first automated end-to-end program synthesis tool for detecting flash loan attack vulnerabilities"; the numerical approximation is not a learned decision function or search policy (B.2 step 2), so no type is named → method (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: 37 hacked protocols, one hack type each (Table 2), tallied by level. 21 are PM (eight oracle manipulations; eight logic flaws, protocol logic with no named description and statable over state; the BeanstalkFarms DAO governance attack, a flash-loaned majority; and one each of fake tokens and fake market, assets the protocol's own state does not list, decimal difference, and price miscalculation), and 16 are ES (six reentrancies, one read-only reentrancy, four access-control cases, two with no input validation, and one each of uninitialized proxy, initialization bug, and arbitrary call) → PM, ES secondary.
column_justification: Four predefined control-flow whitelisting policies and two simplification heuristics, enforced on-chain by an instrumented guard that reverts any transaction whose control flow is not whitelisted; by default only simple invocations are allowed and administrators may add patterns, with no rule inferred from past transactions (0.26% average false-positive rate per protocol, Table 3)
type_evidence: title: "Enforcing control flow integrity on DeFi smart contracts" names no type; abstract: "we developed CrossGuard, a novel framework that enforces control flow integrity onchain" and, in the next sentence, "it enforces control flow whitelisting policies and applies simplification heuristics at runtime"; contribution 2: "the first control flow integrity technique for smart contracts with whitelisting policies and simplification heuristics" → hand-written whitelisting policies enforced at runtime → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2406.00921 (2024-06) in the same year; extended version: ACM Trans. Softw. Eng. Methodol. 34, 4, Article 106 (May 2025), doi:10.1145/3707458 (placement and figures follow the cited version)
row_justification: The governing set is the XBlock ground-truth dataset of 6,498 contracts, 314 of them labeled Ponzi by crawling Etherscan and manual cross-checking (Section 5.2.1; 96.9 % precision and 98.2 % recall, Table 3). The set holds one scam class, so no breakdown is needed, and a Ponzi contract's payout mechanics are a protocol-mechanism property (B.1 scams) → PM. The 805 Ponzi contracts found on Mainnet (50 of them sampled and checked by hand, Section 5.5.1) and the 15 Ponzi schemes found among about 10,000 contracts deployed in March 2024 (0-day detection, Section 5.5.2) are deployment detections, not the governing set.
column_justification: A two-layer graph attention network trained on labeled contract runtime behavior graphs classifies each contract and issues the verdict; the invoke-sequence generator and dynamic taint engine build the graphs it reads → ML, Rule-based secondary (the taint analysis whose output the model reads, B.2 step 7, as for SCVHunter).
type_evidence: title (ICSE): "PonziGuard: Detecting Ponzi schemes on Ethereum with contract runtime behavior graph (CRBG)", and title (extended version): "Towards effective detection of Ponzi schemes on Ethereum with contract runtime behavior graph", no type named; abstract: "In this paper, we propose PonziGuard, an efficient Ponzi scheme detection approach based on contract runtime behavior", and "it formulates the detection process as a graph classification task on CRBG"; contribution 1: "We propose PonziGuard, an efficient approach for detecting Ponzi schemes on Ethereum", contribution 2 frames detection as a graph classification task; no type named → B.2 step 3 reads the method, a graph attention network trained on labeled graphs → ML

row_justification: SPP-CNN is trained and tested on an open-source labeled set of 3,774 Ethereum contracts, 132 Ponzi and 3,642 normal, whose bytecodes the authors crawled from Etherscan, split 60 %, 20 %, and 20 % into training, validation, and test sets (on the test set precision 98.2 %, recall 93.8 %, and F-score 95.9 %, Table I); a Ponzi contract's payout mechanics are a protocol-mechanism property (B.1 scams), and a set of one scam class needs no breakdown → PM (row by evaluation, one-class set).
column_justification: Presented as an improved convolutional neural network (title, abstract) → ML; each contract's bytecode is converted to decimal values, standardized, and rendered as a single-channel image, and a CNN whose last hidden layer is a spatial pyramid pooling layer, so that bytecodes of any length yield a fixed-size vector, issues the Ponzi verdict through a sigmoid output.
type_evidence: title: "Ponzi contracts detection based on improved convolutional neural network"; abstract: "we propose an improved convolutional neural network as a detection model for Ponzi schemes in smart contracts"; contribution list: "the spatial pyramid pooling method is introduced to improve the convolutional neural network" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML

row_justification: Code Will Speak is trained and tested on 3,773 Ethereum contracts, 132 of them Ponzi contracts whose labels come from Chen et al.'s manually confirmed address list, split 80 % for training and 20 % for testing (precision 0.97 and recall 0.97 with 2-gram TF-IDF and bytecode features, Table II); a Ponzi contract's payout mechanics are a protocol-mechanism property (B.1 scams), and a set of one scam class needs no breakdown → PM (row by evaluation, one-class set).
column_justification: Presented as a classification model based on an improved CatBoost algorithm (abstract) → ML; SMOTE-Tomek rebalances the training set, and a CatBoost classifier over bytecode similarity to known Ponzi contracts, bytecode length, and TF-IDF weights of 2-gram opcodes issues the verdict at deployment time; "NLP" names the TF-IDF weighting, and no language model runs.
type_evidence: title: "Code will speak: Early detection of Ponzi smart contracts on Ethereum" (no type); abstract: "we borrow ideas from text feature extraction from Natural Language Processing (NLP) to build a classification model based on an improved CatBoost algorithm"; contribution list: "we propose a novel method to extract the code features of smart contracts", "we leverage TFIDF", "the bytecode similarity is introduced as a feature of the model" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML
