row_justification: Hara et al. train and test XGBoost classifiers by five-fold cross-validation on contracts from the first 6,500,000 Ethereum blocks (151,935 unique), with 295 honeypots whose source is on Etherscan as positives, labeled from the HoneyBadger repository of Torres et al., who identified honeypots by inspecting the contracts (PR-AUC 0.900 with the bytecode features added against 0.763 without them, and 0.878 for the model without post-theft features; 40 of the 295 honeypots missed); a honeypot's trap mechanics are a protocol-mechanism property (B.1 scams), all eight honeypot techniques of the labeling source are trap mechanics, and a set of one scam class needs no breakdown → PM (row by evaluation, one-class set).
column_justification: Presented as a machine-learning model (title, abstract, contribution list) → ML; TF-IDF weights and averaged word2vec embeddings of the 140 EVM opcodes, with source-code length and compiler version (and, for the first model, transaction and fund-flow features), feed an XGBoost classifier that issues the honeypot verdict at a 0.5 threshold; word2vec is a two-layer CBOW embedding, not a generative model.
type_evidence: title: "Machine-learning approach using Solidity bytecode for smart-contract honeypot detection in the Ethereum"; abstract: "we propose a machine-learning model that can detect such honeypots with high performance and prevent theft before it occurs"; contribution list: "We propose a smart contract honeypot detection models using solidity bytecode as feature with machine learning" → one type named (B.2 step 3) → ML

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2411.07498 (2024-11) in the same year
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 4,597 Etherscan-verified contracts deployed March 14 to 24, 2024 (Section 6.6, RQ5), in which the authors confirmed 15 new Ponzi contracts and verified every negative by hand; the benchmark of 139 Ponzi and 1,312 non-Ponzi contracts (Section 6.1, the main evaluation) and a near-balanced set of 340 Ponzi and 300 non-Ponzi contracts (Section 6.5) are smaller. Each set holds one class, Ponzi contracts, whose payout mechanics are PM (B.1 scams), so no breakdown is needed and the choice of set does not change the row; the three honeypots among the false positives are not cases.
column_justification: Presented as "the first LLM-driven approach for detecting Ponzi smart contracts" → LLM; static taint analysis from msg.sender and msg.value over Slither's intermediate representation and function-level code slicing build the prompt (Rule-based secondary), and a two-stage zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt, a contract analysis and then a check against a Ponzi definition, issues the verdict. The model requests nothing, and its second-stage output is terminal (method text only), so the flag is no.
type_evidence: title: "Semantic Sleuth: Identifying Ponzi contracts via large language models"; abstract, proposal sentence: "we introduce PonziSleuth, the first LLM-driven approach for detecting Ponzi smart contracts, which requires no labeled training data"; contribution 2: "enhancing LLMs with static taint analysis and automated code slicing" → LLM, the type named as driving (B.2 steps 3 and 4), Rule-based secondary

row_justification: The paper evaluates two sets and reports every result per set (Table IV; the abstract sums them to 60 vulnerabilities in 44 projects): 36 price-oracle-manipulation vulnerabilities in 30 attacked projects and 24 in 14 Code4rena projects (Table II; unit: vulnerability). The larger, the DeFiHacks set, governs; its attacked projects are taken from GPTScan's DeFiHack set (three unrelated projects excluded) and from the SoK's oracle-manipulation, liquidity, and slippage categories, and the Code4rena bugs from judged contest reports, each newly curated one "manually checked to ensure it was a POM bug" (§IV-A). Both sets are one class, which needs no breakdown; price oracle manipulation violates price-mechanism invariants (on-chain-manipulable oracles, price consistency) → PM.
column_justification: Presented as "LLM-driven" (title, abstract) → LLM, no secondary type. Three models run in a fixed chain, a Knowledge Synthesizer and a Prompt Generator (Claude 3 Haiku) building a chain-of-thought prompt from knowledge excerpted from papers, with no input from the target (Fig. 3), and an Auditor (GPT-4o-mini) receiving that prompt and the contract and returning its findings as JSON (Figs. 4 and 5). No model calls a tool (Foundry is future work), and the Auditor's output is the verdict → flag no on the method text; the only repository linked lists papers, and the Table VI ablation removes the knowledge and prompt modules, not a tool step.
type_evidence: title: "AiRacleX: Automated detection of price oracle manipulations via LLM-driven knowledge mining and prompt generation"; abstract: "we propose AiRacleX, a novel LLM-driven framework that enables pre-deployment detection of price oracle manipulation vulnerabilities by leveraging the complementary strengths of multiple large language models (LLMs)"; contribution 1: "A Novel and Transferable Multi-LLM Framework"; one type named in all three places, no agent word → B.2 step 3 → LLM

row_justification: MF2LLM is evaluated on XBlock's Ponzi set with conflicting labels removed, 6,468 contracts, 299 of them Ponzi, in three random splits that share a test set of 1,941 contracts with 90 Ponzi (Table IV) and in a temporal split; one class, and a Ponzi contract's payout mechanics are a protocol-mechanism property (B.1 scams) → PM.
column_justification: Presented as a fusion framework with large language models (title, abstract) whose LLM fuses the views (first contribution) → LLM, ML secondary (two trained graph encoders); for each contract one prompt carries the two encoders' embeddings of its opcode trace graph, statistics of that graph and of its opcode blocks, and a compressed opcode sequence, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B answers True or False (Algorithm 1, Eq. 18); no tool is called and the model stage is terminal, so the flag is no (released code, whose notebook builds the prompt and its True or False target).
type_evidence: title: "MF2LLM: A multiview multimodal fusion framework with large language models for Ponzi scheme detection on Ethereum"; abstract: "this article proposes a novel multiview multimodal fusion framework with large language models (LLMs) for Ponzi scheme detection on Ethereum"; first contribution: "leverages LLMs to fuse multiview, multimodal information" → the LLM is named as fusing the views of the trained graph encoders (B.2 step 4) → LLM (ML secondary)

row_justification: OctopusGuard is evaluated on a labeled test split of 301 BSC tokens (223 scam, 78 healthy), drawn at random together with a 900-token training split from 1,201 labeled tokens (898 scam, 303 healthy), which come from the 1,495 tokens curated out of 14,671 crawled from Dexscreener (§6.1); a token is labeled scam when at least two of three sources agree (security-firm flags, community risk platforms, and the authors' on-chain analysis, such as liquidity removal or honeypot mechanics). The scam types it reports among malicious tokens are multi-label shares that fit the 898 scam tokens, about six types per token (price manipulation 97.88 %, centralized privileged address control 87.31 %, honeypot 86.08 %, allowance bypass 31.29 %, malicious dynamic fees 22.05 %, rug pull 16.26 %; §3.2), and each is a scam mechanism at the protocol-mechanism level (allowance bypass appears only as hidden logic, a privileged arbitrary transfer); all classes sit at one level, so no per-type count is needed → PM (B.1 scams).
column_justification: A fine-tuned multimodal LLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with LoRA, §6.1) issues the verdict → LLM; the CLIP encoder that embeds K-line charts serves retrieval, which the LLM type includes. Flag no on the released code (github.com/SeamewZ/OctopusGuard, the repository §1 gives, read at commit f3c0a45, 1 February 2026, the last commit; the code is unchanged since ff58dae, 16 January 2026, the later commits changing only the README and a logo), which the method text matches: the model "performs reasoning via a predefined structured CoT process" (§5.4). In the pipeline the README names for the Qwen results (Multimodal.unified_analysis, src/mutimodal_qwen_lib.py), each run embeds the token's K-line chart with CLIP and takes the labels of up to three similar charts from a FAISS store built before the run (data_processing/klines_rag_db/run_build_vector_db.py), computes the transaction features with fixed pandas functions over the token's transfer list, downloaded before the run (extract_transaction_features, src/table_tools.py), and then calls the model in a fixed order (chart with the retrieved labels, transaction features, contract code, final synthesis), with no tool interface and no output parsed to start a further call. The "tool-augmented data" of the structured CoT (§5.2, Steps 1 and 2) is thus fetched by fixed steps before the model reasons, and the query of §5.4 ("OctopusGuard actively queries the K-line knowledge base") is the framework's lookup: the framework fixes the schedule, the lookup is in a pre-built store, and the final call is terminal (B.2 flag rules). The Qwen pipeline asks the contract-code question once (Step 5), and the Llama pipeline of the backbone comparison chains Steps 3 to 5 as three fixed calls (src/mutimodal_llama.py); neither touches the flag.
type_evidence: title: "OctopusGuard: K-line enhanced token scam detector powered by multimodal LLMs"; abstract: "we present OctopusGuard, a unified multimodal detector for token scams", whose second and third contributions are "a novel, structured tool-augmented data chain-of-thought" and "a multimodal fine-tuning pipeline that jointly trains on structured CoT"; contribution list (§1): "This design enables the LLM to learn cross-modal correlations" → one type named, in the title and the contribution list (B.2 step 3) → LLM; "tool-augmented" sets neither the column nor the flag

row_justification: RugKeeper's largest labeled set is its real-time set of 1,000 tokens sampled at random from BNB Chain contract creations in May 2025, 638 of them rug pulls that experts validated (§3.1.1, §3.4); their root causes (Fig. 2, in the rug-pull categories of the SoK by Sun et al., funds manipulation 29.8 %, token generation 25.5 %, combination 18.5 %, transaction limitation 16.8 %, external call 8.3 %, fee manipulation 0.8 %, and destroy token 0.3 %) are all privileged control over balances, minting, transfers, or fees, breaches of holder-balance integrity → PM (B.1 scams). The historical set, 512 tokens (400 rug pulls backed by on-chain evidence and reports, 112 benign tokens from the TokenScout dataset; Table 1, 93.55 % accuracy and 95.92 % F1), is one class at the same level.
column_justification: Presented as a multi-agent framework of LLM agents (Qwen2.5 Instruct models of 7B, 14B, and 32B parameters, §3.1.2) → Agentic. Flag yes on the method text alone (⊙). RugKeeper "adopts question-driven task planning to interact with the blockchain and build token contexts" (p. 13738, §1). Within a run on one contract address, "Each subtask agent is responsible not only for executing the tasks assigned by the Planner, but also for proactively generating new sub-questions when missing information is detected during task execution. The Planner then expands the corresponding nodes in the task tree and assigns new subtask agents to address these questions" (p. 13738, §2.2); the subtask agents include "on-chain information acquisition agents", whose "real-time values" the state analysis agent relies on (p. 13738); a Tx Agent that "identifies information gaps requiring Token Report data ... notifies the Leader Agent, which coordinates with the Planner to retrieve additional information and supplement the missing information" (p. 13739, §2.2); and Algorithm 1 (p. 13739) adds a generated question to the task tree and assigns it to a sub-agent "if missing information". An agent thus decides what to acquire, the Planner has it fetched from the chain, and the answer returns to the agents before the Detector Agents reason, which meets both tests of the flag (a request routed through another agent or a planner counts as the model's). The paper names no tool, chain interface, or API, does not say which agent answers a generated question, releases no code or prompts, and reports no trace; its ablation removes the whole token context (Table 2, p. 13740), not the acquisition step, so the evidence basis is the method text only.
type_evidence: title: "RugKeeper: A multi-agent LLM framework for rug pull token detection"; abstract: "This paper presents RugKeeper, a multi-agent framework leveraging large language models for rug pull detection"; contribution list (§1): "We propose RugKeeper, a novel multi-agent framework for rug pull detection that represents, to our knowledge, the first application of multi-agent systems to this problem domain" → "multi-agent" in all three places, one type named (B.2 step 3) → Agentic

row_justification: A1 is evaluated on 36 DeFi incidents on Ethereum and BSC from April 2021 to April 2025, 27 from VERITE and nine further exploits, labeled by verified exploit execution and incident documentation. Table 9 gives one primary vulnerability category per incident (tokenomics and pool accounting 13, access control nine, logic and invariant seven, arithmetic and calculation three, oracle and mispricing two, predictable randomness one, and signature one), and Table 11 lists each incident's category with a one-line rationale. Tallied from that list, 24 incidents are protocol-mechanism (13 reserve and accounting manipulations through skim, sync, reflection, and fee-on-transfer mechanics, six logic flaws over mechanism state such as the k-value error, a repeatable claim, and token-sale mispricing, three calculation errors in mechanism formulas such as Uranium's fee scaling, and two mispricing cases) and 12 are execution-semantics (nine missing access checks on mint, burn, approval, ownership, swap, and configuration functions, a reentrant refund, block-parameter randomness, and a faulty signature check) → PM, ES secondary; the tally of the paper's own list counts as its breakdown.
column_justification: In each of up to five turns the model decides which of five tools to call (source fetch, constructor parameters, on-chain state reads, code sanitizing, and concrete execution on a forked chain; revenue normalization runs in the harness), the controller returns their outputs before the model writes its Strategy contract, and the harness executes that contract and returns traces, revert reasons, and profit to the next turn (Algorithm 1, Appendix A) → Agentic, Rule-based secondary (the execution harness and profitability oracle). The sgETH trace (Fig. 2) shows the model requesting the source at block 18041975 and revising its exploit after an AccessControl revert and a missing liquidity path → flag yes on trace or log.
type_evidence: title: "AI agent smart contract exploit generation"; abstract: "we present A1, an agentic system that transforms any LLM into an end-to-end exploit generator"; contribution list (System Design): "the first end-to-end agentic exploit generation system that operationalizes LLMs as autonomous smart contract security agents" → Agentic (step 3, with "agent" and "agentic" in all three places; the LLMs named are the agents' own models)

first_release: cited version, 2020; preprint arXiv:2004.08563 (2020-04) in the same year
row_justification: Its largest labeled set is the hand-checked sample of the contracts it flags among 4,112 Etherscan contracts, 50 per vulnerability type or all where fewer (Table 2); the true positives (43 of 50 for timestamp dependency, 40 of 50 for block number dependency and for integer underflow, all 17 for dangerous delegatecall, nine of 15 for freezing ether, and all sampled for the other types) fall under its eight oracles (gasless send, exception disorder, reentrancy, timestamp dependency, block number dependency, dangerous delegatecall, integer overflow and underflow, and freezing ether), each a contract-agnostic property statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES.
column_justification: Bugs are flagged by fixed hand-written oracles adopted from prior work while an AFL-style fuzzer with a multi-objective adaptive strategy only drives input generation.
type_evidence: title: "sFuzz: An efficient adaptive fuzzer for Solidity smart contracts"; abstract: "In this work, we present an adaptive fuzzer for smart contracts on the Ethereum platform called sFuzz"; no contribution list → a fuzzer whose eight oracles are adopted from ContractFuzzer and Oyente, one type named → Rule-based (B.2 steps 2 and 3); "adaptive" names a hand-designed multi-objective seed selection, not a learned policy

row_justification: ReGuard's evaluation is Table 1, five modified Etherscan contracts (TokenSender, UGToken, E4Token, the DAO, and RoT) in which it finds seven reentrancy bugs (two in UGToken, one in E4Token, three in the DAO, and one in RoT), and the paper reports no false positive or negative for it (Table 1 marks one false positive and two false negatives for Oyente on the same contracts); every case is reentrancy, a property statable from EVM call semantics, one class at the execution-semantics level that needs no breakdown → ES (row by evaluation).
column_justification: Presented as a fuzzing-based analyzer → Rule-based; the contract is translated to C++, an AFL or LibFuzzer engine turns coverage-guided random bytes into transaction sequences, and a hand-written five-state reentrancy automaton over the runtime trace (Figure 5) issues the verdict when a reentrant call transfers ether again; no model is trained or prompted.
type_evidence: title: "ReGuard: Finding reentrancy bugs in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "We presented ReGuard, an fuzzing-based analyzer to automatically detect reentrancy bugs in Ethereum smart contracts"; contribution list: none (a demo paper), and its solution paragraph: "ReGuard extends well-designed fuzzing engine ... by generating random transactions" and feeds the traces "into a reentrancy automata" → fuzzing against a hand-written oracle, one type (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: teEther's largest labeled set is the validation of its exploits on private test networks, 1,769 (exploit, account) combinations, an account being a deployed address of an exploitable contract, of which 1,564 succeed (88.41 %; Section 5.2, Table 2; 1,301 through CALL, 255 through SELFDESTRUCT, seven through DELEGATECALL, and one through CALLCODE), for the 855 exploits it generates for 815 of 38,757 unique contracts (Section 5.1, Table 1). In every case an attacker transfers Ether from the contract by reaching a critical instruction with attacker-controlled arguments, a property statable from EVM semantics alone → ES.
column_justification: Hand-written conditions on critical instructions (CALL, CALLCODE, DELEGATECALL, and SELFDESTRUCT reached with attacker-controlled arguments) are checked by symbolic execution of paths found by A* search over the recovered control flow graph, and Z3 solves the path constraints into exploit transactions; no learned or generative model → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "teEther: Gnawing at Ethereum to automatically exploit smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "We develop a generic definition of vulnerable contracts and use this to build teEther, a tool that allows creating an exploit for a contract given only its binary bytecode" (no type); contribution list, first two items: "We provide a generic definition of vulnerable contracts, based on low-level EVM instructions" and "We develop a tool TEETHER that provides end-to-end exploit generation from a contract's bytecode only", handling hash values "symbolically" → only symbolic analysis named, the Rule-based type, and the method is symbolic execution with constraint solving against a hand-written definition (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: 148 known vulnerabilities in 128 contracts across ten oracles (assertion failure, integer overflow, reentrancy, TOD, block dependency, unhandled exception, unsafe delegatecall, leaking/locking ether, unprotected selfdestruct).
column_justification: Ten hand-written bug oracles over execution traces decide; evolutionary fuzzing and constraint solving only generate inputs.
type_evidence: title: "ConFuzzius: A data dependency-aware hybrid fuzzer for smart contracts"

row_justification: The governing set is the manually labeled ground truth of 750 contracts sampled from the 6,581 that all five static tools analyzed (Table III), with 26 reentrancy and 110 transaction-order-dependence contracts; both are state-inconsistency hazards (two orderings of the same transactions reach different states, limited to calls that send Ether), contract-agnostic and statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES. The scan of 89,853 Etherscan contracts yields 47 zero-days from 195 manually analyzed reports that only SAILFISH raised.
column_justification: Hazardous-access queries over a storage dependency graph, followed by a value-summary analysis and symbolic evaluation (Rosette with SMT solvers), decide; no learned or generative model is used → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "SAILFISH: Vetting smart contract state-inconsistency bugs in seconds" (no type); abstract: "This paper presents SAILFISH, a scalable system for automatically finding state-inconsistency bugs in smart contracts" (no type); contributions, second and third bullets: "hazardous access queries over a unified, compact graph representation" and "a novel value-summary analysis that efficiently computes global constraints over storage variables" → no type named, B.2 step 3, static and symbolic analysis → Rule-based.

row_justification: The governing set is the 579 contracts manually labeled by two annotators (Kappa 0.71), with 111 defects in Table 4 (TSD 5, DuEI 6, SBE 5, RE 12, NC 13, GC 6, UEC 22, and BID 42); all eight defects (transaction state dependency, DoS under external influence, strict balance equality, reentrancy, nested call, greedy contract, unchecked external calls, and block info dependency) are statable from bytecode and EVM semantics → ES. The scan of 165,621 contracts (25,815 with a defect at impact levels one to three) is not verified and does not govern.
column_justification: Symbolic execution of EVM bytecode builds the control-flow graph and stack events, and eight hand-written rules over them and three features (Money Call, Loop Block, and Payable Function) decide; it is compared against Oyente, Mythril, and Securify → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "DefectChecker: Automated smart contract defect detection by analyzing EVM bytecode" (no type); abstract: "we propose DefectChecker, a symbolic execution-based approach and tool to detect eight contract defects that can cause unwanted behaviors of smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain platform" → one type named (symbolic execution, Rule-based), B.2 step 3 → Rule-based.

row_justification: VeriSmart's largest labeled set is its CVE benchmark of 60 contracts (Table II), drawn at random from 487 CVE reports of arithmetic overflows and labeled by those reports, of which the paper finds two wrong (#13 and #31), leaving 58 vulnerable contracts; per query, 490 of its 492 alarms are confirmed true and the other 484 of its 976 arithmetic queries are inspected and found safe. Every case is an integer overflow, underflow, or division by zero, statable from the code and EVM arithmetic → ES; the 25 ZEUS contracts (172 arithmetic operations) and the access-control assertion study on the same 60 contracts (55 proved safe) are ES as well.
column_justification: CEGIS-style inference of transaction and loop invariants from fixed templates; presented as a verifier → Rule-based
type_evidence: title: "VERISMART: A highly precise safety verifier for Ethereum smart contracts"; abstract: "We present VERISMART, a highly precise verifier for ensuring arithmetic safety of Ethereum smart contracts"; contributions: "We present a new verification algorithm for smart contracts" and "We provide VERISMART, a practical implementation of our algorithm"; one type named, verification → Rule-based (B.2 steps 2 and 3)

first_release: cited version, 2022; preprint arXiv:2208.07119 (2022-08) in the same year
row_justification: The governing set is the 76 reported attack transactions of six known attacks on four bridges, all detected, plus seven unreported suspicious ones (Table 4, unit transactions), with inconsistent event parsing 56 (THORChain's three attacks with 6, 41, and 6, and pNetwork with 3), unrestricted deposit emitting 16 (Qubit Bridge), and unauthorized unlocking 4 (Anyswap); each violates the bridge's deposit-to-unlock invariant that properties RD, CP, and AU state (Section 2.2) → PM.
column_justification: Hand-written security properties over paired cross-chain transaction patterns decide.
type_evidence: title: "Xscope: Hunting for cross-chain bridge attacks" (no type); abstract: "Based on those patterns, we design Xscope, an automatic tool to find security violations in cross-chain bridges and detect real-world attacks"; contribution 2: "We introduce a set of security properties and patterns that capture sufficient conditions to characterize cross-chain bridge bugs"; no type is named, and the analyzer checks hand-written properties with the Z3 solver → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2503.01944 (2025-03) in the same year
row_justification: FlashGuard is evaluated on 20 real-world non-price flash-loan attacks (2020 to 2024, five chains, Table 4), all detected. Tallied from the root causes in its Table 7, 17 violate protocol-mechanism invariants (an approval not revoked after a canceled campaign at Hedgey, Sec. 3.1; improper liquidation checks at Euler; collateral valuation, validation, or logic at Warp, Cheese Bank, bZx, and Midas; LP-USDC conversion at Platypus; slippage control at JIMBO; and exchange-rate, liquidity-index, supply, pool, wrapper, migration, lending, and deflationary-token logic at the other nine), and three are execution-semantics flaws (reentrancy at Akropolis and Origin, input validation at xToken) → PM, ES secondary. Six synthetic tests in three execution-semantics classes (improper access control, unchecked return values, and uninitialized storage pointers) and 614,629 transactions examined on five chains (Table 6) add no other level.
column_justification: Detection is a hand-written mempool signature rule flashLoan ∧ approve ∧ (transfer ∨ withdrawal) over known flash-loan providers' function selectors with a benign-address exclusion list; no learning or LLM.
type_evidence: title: "Protecting DeFi platforms against non-price flash loan attacks" names no type; abstract: "we present FlashGuard, a runtime detection and mitigation method for non-price flash loan attacks" names none; contribution 2: "Heuristic-Based Detection", an algorithm that "monitors the mempool for non-price flash loan attack signatures" → a hand-written signature rule → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: The governing set is the ground-truth vulnerabilities in 18,496 Etherscan contracts (Section 6.4, Figure 10), the union of the true vulnerabilities all systems report, with ILF's detectors reporting only true positives and the baselines' false positives removed by manual inspection. By the types of ILF's six detectors (Table 3) they are Leaking 302, Suicidal 28, Locking 64, Block Dependency 799, Unhandled Exception 90, and Controlled Delegatecall 18 (1,301 in all), each a property statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES, no secondary.
column_justification: Presented as a fuzzer learned from symbolic execution by imitation learning ("Learning to fuzz", title) → ML; hand-written vulnerability oracles decide what is reported (Rule-based secondary).
type_evidence: title: "Learning to fuzz from symbolic execution"; abstract: "we propose to learn an effective and fast fuzzer from symbolic execution, by phrasing the learning task in the framework of imitation learning"

row_justification: Peculiar is evaluated on reentrancy alone, on dataset-wild, 47,398 .sol files with about 203,716 contracts from the SmartBugs Wild dataset, which two of the authors labeled by hand (Section IV; the abstract gives 40,932 files, which the paper does not explain), at 91.80 % precision and 92.40 % recall (Table I), and on dataset-vul, a subset of 1,197 vulnerable and 471 non-vulnerable contracts (Table II). One class, so no breakdown is needed, and reentrancy is statable from EVM call semantics → ES.
column_justification: GraphCodeBERT, a pretrained code encoder, is fine-tuned with a linear classifier over the crucial data flow graph (built from a tree-sitter AST around each call.value line) and outputs a label, not text → ML (B.2 step 2, an encoder is ML).
type_evidence: title: "Peculiar: Smart contract vulnerability detection based on crucial data flow graph and pre-training techniques" (pre-training); abstract: "we propose a novel approach, Peculiar, which uses Pre-training technique for detection of smart contract vulnerabilities"; contribution list, second item: "We implement our approach as Peculiar and apply it on the smart contract vulnerability detection task" (no type) → one type named, and the pretrained model is GraphCodeBERT, an encoder, so ML (B.2 step 2 boundary, step 3)

row_justification: The largest labeled set is Table 1's vulnerable transaction sequences on 443 CVE contracts, each confirmed by the concrete validator and counted in validated sequences, with 1,982 integer overflows and underflows, 203 divisions by zero, 77 assertion violations, and 654 ERC-20 standard violations, so 2,262 of 2,916 are execution-semantics properties → ES. The ERC-20 violations break transfer and transferFrom semantics that the authors' harness rules encode from the standard (Appendix C), recorded as the DM secondary (scope shared); the 242 labeled CVE reports of Table 2 and the 104 leaking and suicidal contracts of Table 3 are ES.
column_justification: Presented as language-model-guided symbolic execution, where the language model is a statistical model of vulnerable transaction sequences and not an LLM → ML; fixed bug oracles decide what is reported (Rule-based secondary).
type_evidence: title: "SmarTest: Effectively hunting vulnerable transaction sequences in smart contracts through language model-guided symbolic execution"; abstract: "combining symbolic execution with a language model for vulnerable transaction sequences"; contribution list, item 1: "We present a new technique for effectively finding vulnerable transaction sequences in smart contracts" (no type); the language model is an n-gram model learned from vulnerable transaction sequences, not a large generative model (B.2 step 2, ML), and the title names it as guiding symbolic execution (Rule-based) → step 4 → ML, Rule-based secondary

row_justification: Evaluated on 514,880 functions from 42,910 contracts labelled for reentrancy (701 functions), timestamp dependence (3,368), integer overflow/underflow (3,503) and delegatecall (149), all VM/language-level properties.
column_justification: A dual-modality teacher graph network over source and bytecode transfers to a bytecode-only student via mutual-learning losses; the vulnerability label is a learned classification.
type_evidence: title: "Cross-modality mutual learning for enhancing smart contract vulnerability detection on bytecode"

first_release: cited version, 2024; preprint arXiv:2404.17839 (2024-04) in the same year
row_justification: Clear's governing set is the dataset of Qian et al. it adopts (Section 4.1), about 40K real-world contracts labeled by vulnerability type, unit contracts; its positives are the 4,290 contracts "identified to contain vulnerabilities": reentrancy 680, timestamp dependency 2,242, and integer overflow or underflow 1,368, all execution-semantics classes → ES.
column_justification: A Transformer encoder (six layers, eight heads, no pretrained weights named), trained in a contrastive stage with masked-language-model augmentation and correlation labels and then fine-tuned, classifies each contract's vulnerability → ML (F1 gain of 9.73% to 39.99% over deep-learning baselines).
type_evidence: title: "Improving smart contract security with contrastive learning-based vulnerability detection"

row_justification: xFuzz's largest labeled evaluation set is its non-cross-contract run on Dataset2 (7,391 Etherscan contracts; Section 6.2.2, Table 7), 209 vulnerabilities found, unit vulnerabilities, with per-type precision and recall: reentrancy 149, delegatecall 35, and tx-origin 25 (Table 7 lists 156 reentrancy reports at 95.5% precision). The cross-contract run on the same contracts finds 18, all confirmed by the industry partner's security experts (Table 6: reentrancy 13, delegatecall three, and tx-origin two). Reentrancy, delegatecall misuse, and tx.origin authorization are execution-semantics properties → ES; the per-type counts mean no ‡ is due.
column_justification: Presented as machine-learning-guided cross-contract fuzzing (title) → ML; a learned path filter prunes benign paths, and hand-written bug oracles decide what is reported (Rule-based secondary).
type_evidence: title: "xFuzz: Machine learning guided cross-contract fuzzing"

row_justification: The governing set is 1,880 contracts from SmartBugs Wild and DAppSCAN, labeled by manual annotation as normal (837) or defective (1,043) for one class, atomicity violation (Table 1; unit: contract); a set of one class needs no breakdown. The paper defines the class by the principle that "transactions must be fully successful or completely fail" (§1), a property of the VM's execution semantics, and names four forms in its related work (reentrancy, check-effect-interaction races, improper exception handling, and cross-domain non-atomicity across contracts or chains; §2) without counting any of them, and Table 1 records only Normal and Defective → ES.
column_justification: A GCN classifies each contract's bytecode control-flow graph, its node features an adaptively weighted fusion of Node2Vec structural and Word2Vec opcode embeddings (Algorithm 1) → ML; the CFG builder only disassembles the bytecode and partitions basic blocks, applying no detection rule, so no secondary type.
type_evidence: title: "AtomGraph: Tackling atomicity violation in smart contracts using multimodal GCNs"; abstract: "we introduce AtomGraph, an automated framework designed for detecting atomicity violations. This framework leverages Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) to accurately identify atomicity violations through multimodal feature learning and fusion"; contributions: "propose AtomGraph for automated detection" and "a novel adaptive weighting fusion mechanism", no further type; one type named (graph convolutional networks, ML) → B.2 step 3 → ML

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2503.10041 (2025-03) in the same year
row_justification: NumScout's largest labeled set is 95 contracts sampled at random from its 6,617 and labeled by two authors (Table III); its positive cases (TP plus FN) are Div In Path 8, Operator Order Issue 10, Minor Amount Retention 20 (a division remainder left locked in the contract), Exchange Problem 4 (rounding in token-amount calculations during exchanges), and Precision Loss Trend 4, all integer-division and rounding defects statable from the code and EVM arithmetic → ES, 46 of 46; the full run flags 1,774 of the 6,617 contracts at 89.7% precision.
column_justification: Pre-defined detection patterns in bytecode symbolic execution decide; the LLM only prunes functions unrelated to numeric operations beforehand and never sees analysis results
type_evidence: title: "NumScout: Unveiling numerical defects in smart contracts using LLM-pruning symbolic execution" (LLM and symbolic execution named); abstract: "We also propose NumScout, a symbolic execution-based tool designed to detect these five defects", which uses "a large language model (LLM) to prune functions which are unrelated to numerical operations"; contributions: "We develop NumScout, the first tool designed for the defined numerical defects" (no type word) → the abstract presents the symbolic-execution tool, and the LLM only prunes its input and is not named as driving it (B.2 steps 4 and 7) → Rule-based, LLM secondary

first_release: cited version, 2023; preprint arXiv:2310.01152 (2023-10) in the same year
row_justification: GPTLens is run on 13 Etherscan contracts, each with one CVE-reported vulnerability (Section IV-A), unit contracts; Table I lists only the CVE identifiers, labels and descriptions come from the CVE database, and the paper names the labeled flaw of only two cases in passing (CVE-2018-19830, a constructor typo, Section IV-C; CVE-2018-10666, missing access control on setOwner, Section II-C), which does not cover most of the set → glossary line 4 (CVEs with no class) → ES ‡.
column_justification: The title and contribution 1 name LLM-powered detection, and contribution 2 casts the LLM as "auditor and critic agents"; the types stand in different places → LLM by B.2 step 6, Agentic secondary. The same LLM proposes candidate vulnerabilities as auditor and scores them as critic, and a fixed weighted sum ranks them; the released scripts run auditor, critic, and ranking in a fixed order with plain chat calls and no tool (flag no, released code).
type_evidence: title: "Large language model-powered smart contract vulnerability detection: New perspectives"; abstract: "we propose an adversarial framework dubbed GPTLens", in which "the LLM plays dual roles, i.e., AUDITOR and CRITIC, respectively"; contribution 1: "a systematic analysis of the advantages (opportunities) and challenges of LLM-powered smart contract vulnerability detection techniques"; contribution 2: "the LLM takes on the roles of the auditor and critic agents respectively"; contribution 3: "GPTLens is simple, effective and purely LLM-driven" → types named in different places, none presented as driving the other → B.2 step 6, the contribution list names LLM first → LLM; Agentic secondary (contribution 2 names agents)

subgroup: an agent's comments feed a trained classifier
row_justification: Agent4Vul is evaluated on the public dataset of Qian et al. (cross-modality mutual learning, WWW 2023), 40,000 real-world contracts labeled for four vulnerability classes, split at random into 80 % for training and 20 % for testing and run five times (§4.1); the paper states 4,290 vulnerable contracts with per-class counts of delegatecall 136, integer overflow and underflow 1,368, reentrancy 680, and timestamp dependency 2,242, which sum to 4,426 (the three classes other than delegatecall sum to 4,290, and the paper does not say whether a contract carries more than one class); every class is statable from the code and VM semantics → ES.
column_justification: Presented as "multimodal LLM agents" that power the framework → Agentic (ML secondary). The Commentator agent (GLM-4 or Qwen, zero-shot; §4.1, §4.4, §5.2) writes vulnerability-oriented comments; the Vectorizer agent runs embedding models (Voyage-lite-02-instruct or GritLM-7B), an encoder and so ML under B.2; a fixed compiler and BinaryCFGExtractor step (§3.3) feeds a graph attention network, and a LightGBM or fully connected classifier over the fused features issues the verdict (§3.4; Algorithm 1, p. 5). Flag no on the method text, since the framework fixes the schedule, the tools' output never returns to the Commentator, and its comments start no tool call (B.2 flag rules); no code is released.
type_evidence: title: "Agent4Vul: Multimodal LLM agents for smart contract vulnerability detection"; abstract: "we propose Agent4Vul, a novel framework utilizing multimodal LLM agents to enhance smart contract vulnerability detection", then "we develop a multimodal learning architecture"; contribution list (§1): "A robust multimodal LLM agent-based detection framework" and "Dual agents guided vulnerability representation" → the step 2 boundary, applied first (step 3), reads the Vectorizer, an embedding model, as ML and leaves the Commentator as an LLM agent; of the types named, the paper presents the agents as what powers the framework ("powered by LLM-based agents", §1) → Agentic (B.2 step 4)

row_justification: Improper access control (a transfer, state write, low-level call, or selfdestruct reached before any msg.sender check) on the largest labeled set, 5,000 recent verified Etherscan contracts, where two researchers checked each report (91 true and 11 false positives, Table III); also 15 CVE contracts (14 found, Table II) and 83 repositories sampled from DAppSCAN (40 true and six false positives, Table IV). One class, so no per-class counts are needed; a generic missing caller check → ES.
column_justification: The contribution list presents TRACE as "integrating LLMs with traditional program analysis techniques", the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary). GPT-4o locates sensitive functions and completes non-compilable snippets, and a rule-based check of msg.sender conditions over the call graph and each function's CFG decides; on the 5,000 on-chain contracts, all compilable, both LLM steps are skipped. The pipeline compiles each completed contract and, on failure, returns the errors to the LLM for revision on the pipeline's schedule, and the LLM calls no tool → flag no.
type_evidence: title: "Trace: Securing smart contract repository against access control vulnerability" (no type word); abstract: "This paper presents TRACE, a tool designed to secure non-compilable smart contract repositories against access control vulnerabilities" (no type word); contribution list, second item: "By integrating LLMs with traditional program analysis techniques, we developed TRACE" → two types presented equally → B.2 step 5 → LLM

subgroup: agents converse or debate, no tool
row_justification: The largest labeled set is the 1,408 high- and medium-risk findings (499 high, 909 medium) of the Code4rena set (102 projects, 6,454 contracts), 1,104 of them "complex logic vulnerabilities" with no class and 304 specific ones with no per-class counts, so no breakdown covers most of the set → ES by the glossary (line 2), ‡. The smaller labeled sets, 110 contracts (10 in each of 10 common classes, plus 10 secure) and 13 CVEs, do not govern, and the 11 new findings of Table 4 were only submitted for verification. The 13 CVEs are PropertyGPT's, among them an airdrop that lets the owner mint beyond the total supply (CVE-2018-18425), which breaks holder-balance integrity and gives the PM secondary, as for SmartAuditFlow.
column_justification: Presented as LLM-powered multi-agent systems with "a multi-agent conversational architecture" (TSE title, abstract) → Agentic. The released code fixes each run. The targeted-analysis configuration runs a contract analysis, then 41 detector prompts in a fixed order with one turn each, then a bug summary, and the broad-analysis configuration runs the analysis, up to three review and summary cycles, and the summary. No agent is given a tool or function call, and the one command the code runs, at the fixed summary phase, is called by the framework, so the role-playing agents converse over the source and emit findings without acquiring evidence (flag no, released code). The method text's "actively interacts with external data sources as needed" names no source or tool, and the code, the stronger evidence, decides.
type_evidence: TSE title: "... via LLM-powered multi-agent systems"; abstract: "a multi-agent conversational architecture"

row_justification: The largest labeled set is the Code4rena set, 784 high- and medium-severity findings in 243 of 6,454 contracts from 72 projects (Section 4.2.1), reported without a class breakdown → glossary line 2 (contest findings) → ES ‡. The 143 SmartBugs-curated contracts (DASP classes, no per-class counts), the 185 high- or medium-severity findings of the Sherlock set, and the 13 CVEs of Table 4, PropertyGPT's benchmark (four access control, three overflow, four logic error, one delegatecall, and one bad randomness), are smaller. Among the logic-error CVEs, an airdrop that lets the owner mint beyond the total supply (CVE-2018-18425) breaks holder-balance integrity and gives the PM secondary.
column_justification: Presented as a plan-execute workflow of LLM calls, with no agent named in the title, the abstract, or the contribution list → LLM, with the static analyzers it names as the Rule-based secondary. The released code runs five fixed stages (initial analysis, audit plan, task extraction, one model call per planned task, and report formatting); static-analysis output supplied with the contract (Slither, in the paper) is pasted into the first prompt, the model's plan only chooses audit tasks inside the fixed pipeline, and the paper's retrieval sits at a fixed calibration step over a curated knowledge base, so no tool result the model requested re-enters it within the run (flag no, released code).
type_evidence: title: "SmartAuditFlow: A dynamic plan-execute framework for advanced smart contract security analysis" (no type); abstract: "we propose SmartAuditFlow, a dynamic Plan-Execute framework that customizes audit strategies based on the unique characteristics of each smart contract" (no type); contribution list, item 1: "intermediate findings from LLM analysis", and item 3: "integrating inputs from traditional static analysis tools" and RAG "to provide LLMs with" security information; no agent named, and the static tools serve as inputs to the model → step 4 → LLM, Rule-based secondary

subgroup: agents reason over analysis output placed in the prompt
row_justification: ACTaint's largest labeled set is the 624 SmartBugs-Wild contracts that AChecker flagged, in which two annotators, with a third resolving disagreements, found 481 access-control vulnerabilities (Table II, 425 detected and 56 missed; counted in vulnerabilities); its 15 CVE contracts, evaluated per function, and the 99 vulnerabilities in 93 ACFix contracts are of the same class. The class, "insufficient enforcement of permissions," is checked at critical-variable writes, selfdestruct, low-level and delegate calls, tx.origin checks, Ether transfers, and assembly, and a missing or spoofable check on the caller is a generic missing access check (B.1 Missing checks) → ES; one class, so no breakdown is needed.
column_justification: Presented as "an LLM-based multi-agent system" (abstract) → Agentic (Rule-based secondary). The released code runs Slither once, builds critical-variable dependency graphs, and passes them in the prompt to a sink agent and then, when it reports sinks, a taint agent, one model call each with no tool interface, so no agent invokes a tool during a run (flag no, released code).
type_evidence: title: "ACTaint: Agent-based taint analysis for access control vulnerabilities in smart contracts"; abstract: "we propose an LLM-based multi-agent system, named ACTaint"; contribution list, item 1: "We propose a novel LLM-based multi-agent approach to detect access control vulnerabilities in smart contracts"; agents are named in all three places, and the title presents the taint analysis as agent-based → step 4 → Agentic, Rule-based secondary

subgroup: analyzers called by a fixed rule on the model's output
row_justification: The governing set is 400 contracts (Table II; unit: contract), 350 SolidiFI bug-injected positives, 50 in each of seven classes (reentrancy, integer overflow or underflow, timestamp dependency, TOD, unchecked send, tx.origin, and unhandled exceptions), labeled from the SolidiFI directory taxonomy and BugLog files, and 50 OpenZeppelin negatives, which do not count. Every class is statable from the code and EVM semantics → ES, 350 of 350, no secondary.
column_justification: Presented as an agent framework that calls tools (title) → Agentic, Rule-based secondary (Slither, Mythril). Algorithm 1 fixes the schedule, in which a first Qwen3-Coder-Flash pass that finds the contract safe ends the run, Slither otherwise runs, and Mythril "is triggered deterministically" when the preliminary type is reentrancy, integer overflow or underflow, unchecked send, or tx.origin, or when Slither reports a high- or medium-impact issue (§III-D); the results return once to a refinement call whose output is the verdict → flag no (a fixed rule calls the tools on the model's output). Table III ablates the acquisition step (RAG-only against the full system; "The present ablation isolates the combined contribution of tool feedback", §V), and Algorithm 1 gives the schedule of the step it removes. The prototype's released code (github.com/sz-xiaohuolong/SmartContract-Audit-Agent, matched to the paper by its title, modes, metric, and benchmark), read at the version the paper describes (commit 2b816f4, 19 April 2026; README 354374e), calls Slither on every contract and Mythril by the same rule and gives the model no tool → flag no, evidence basis released code. Its versions of January to March 2026 handed both analyzers to the model as callable tools, which would code yes; the flag codes the system the paper describes (B.2). Two differences from Algorithm 1 do not touch the flag: the code has no early exit after a first pass that finds the contract safe, and it infers candidate types from the source when the model gives none.
type_evidence: title: "VeriRAG-Agent: A retrieval-augmented agent framework with dynamic tool calling for smart contract auditing"; abstract: "This paper proposes VeriRAG-Agent, a framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation, dynamic tool calling, and corrective re-reasoning"; contribution 1: "a closed feedback loop coupling retrieval, LLM hypothesis generation, and Slither/Mythril verification"; the title names an agent framework that calls the analyzers, the agent driving them → B.2 step 4 → Agentic (Rule-based secondary)

row_justification: SymGPT finds 5,783 ERC rule violations in 4,000 contracts (3,400 ERC-20, 500 ERC-721, and 100 ERC-1155; Section 5.1.1), each reviewed by at least two authors, with 122 false positives (Table 5). Its rules come from the standards' texts (132 in its study, in privilege-check, functionality, API, and logging categories, Table 1), so each violation is a deviation from the standard as the named description (shared).
column_justification: The LLM extracts rules from the three ERC documents and translates the natural-language ones into a DSL once, before any contract is analyzed (of the 138 rules it extracts, the standards' 132 and six spurious ones, 42 are interfaces that need no translation; of the other 96 it translates 69 and fails on 27, the 24 return-value rules, for which no DSL is defined, and three underspecified ones; Section 5.1.2); constraint synthesis and symbolic execution on Slither and Z3 issue the reports for each contract. The released code (v1.0.0, commit 4d4cd6b) audits contracts in its default mode from the shipped GPT-generated rules and makes no per-contract LLM call, so the model stage is offline and the flag is no (evidence basis released code).
type_evidence: abstract: "a tool that combines LLMs with symbolic execution", the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary)

row_justification: The governing set is the labeled dataset of 375 adversarial contracts (142 on Ethereum, 233 on BSC) from DeFi attacks of April 2020 to July 2024, with benign contracts as negatives (Section 4.1.1); its only breakdown, untrusted or unsafe calls 13.3 %, access-control mistakes 14.4 %, and coding mistakes 72.3 % ("following prior research", the SoK of Zhou et al.), gives root-cause categories, not levels, so the attacker-contract rule applies → PM ‡ (B.1). The live Ethereum deployment (Section 6.5, 26 confirmed attack contracts) lists reentrancy and access-control-flaw root causes among its cases (Table 2), recorded as the ES secondary.
column_justification: Contribution 4 presents "an ML-based system"; an XGBoost classifier over deployment and implementation features and a transformer trained from scratch on PSCFT tokens (pruned semantic-control-flow tokens of the lifted bytecode), combined by a KNN meta classifier, issue the verdict → ML; no pretrained language model is used.
type_evidence: title: "LookAhead: Preventing DeFi attacks via unveiling adversarial contracts" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we propose Lookahead, a new framework for detecting DeFi attacks via unveiling adversarial contracts" (no type); contribution 4: "We build and evaluate an ML-based system consisting of two open-weights classifiers and one meta classifier model" → ML (B.2 step 3, one type named)

row_justification: 115 DeFi protocol incidents, one per protocol, each labeled by its earliest attack transaction (Section V-A; "over 22 million transactions" in the abstract; 109 detected, 94.8% TPR, Section V-C); the paper describes them as exploits against "a diverse set of vulnerabilities" with no per-type counts, Table IV (Appendix D) lists the protocols by name without their attack types, and the price-manipulation attacks counted in the DeFiRanger comparison (six in DeFiRanger's set and 23 others, the remaining 86 being 74.8% of the set; Section V-D) cover a quarter of it → glossary line 3 ("DeFi incidents") → PM ‡; the threat model (Section II) names improper access control, reentrancy, and undefined behaviors among its targets, and the RevestFinance attack (Section V-C) is a reentrancy → ES secondary.
column_justification: The paper says it uses the term "model" not in the machine learning sense (Introduction); its two components are an Interaction Model that flags any fingerprint of critical incoming calls not seen before and an invariant engine inspired by Daikon that mines four fixed invariant classes, under a fixed alarm rule; no learned decision function → Rule-based; GPT-4.1 only pre-filters, before monitoring, the variable pairs the invariant engine compares (Section IV-D) → LLM secondary (B.2 step 7).
type_evidence: title: "HOUSTON: Real-time anomaly detection of attacks against Ethereum DeFi protocols"; abstract: "we propose a novel approach for real-time, generic, explainable identification of attacks against DeFi protocols"; contributions: "We introduce models to capture the normal behavior of DeFi applications", with "model" used "not in the machine learning sense" (Introduction); no type is named → method (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: Hand-written Datalog rules run over more than 81,000 cross-chain transactions of the Nomad and Ronin bridges, and every flagged case is explained by its origin (Tables 3 and 4, Section 5; unit transactions). The positives break the bridge's lock-before-release, with 382 Nomad attack withdrawals on Ethereum that have no counterpart on Moonbeam, cross-referenced with PeckShield (Section 5.2.5), 37 transfers accepted before cross-chain finality, five on Nomad and 32 on Ronin (Section 5.2.1), and seven reverted withdrawal attempts with forged token inputs (Section 5.1.3) → PM. The two Ronin hack transactions (Section 5.2.5) belong to an incident at the trust boundary (validator keys stolen; Supplementary Appendix B.1), recorded as the out secondary; phishing transfers, user transfers to the bridge, and withdrawals never completed are not attacks on the mechanism and are not counted.
column_justification: Hand-written Datalog rules over decoded cross-chain events and transactions from three chains
type_evidence: title: "XChainWatcher: Identifying anomalies in cross-chain bridges" (no type); abstract: "We propose XChainWatcher (Cross-Chain Watcher), a modular and extensible logic-driven anomaly detector for cross-chain bridges"; contribution 1: "The first open-source framework for performing anomaly detection in cross-chain bridges"; no type is named, and the method is hand-written cross-chain rules run in Soufflé, "a high-performance Datalog-inspired engine" → Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: VRust's largest labeled set is the 240 reports its eight checkers raise on 12 Solana projects (Table 4), 25 of them true positives after manual verification, among them the Wormhole missing key check and the 12 previously unknown vulnerabilities reported to developers (three of them critical vulnerabilities in the Solana Program Library, confirmed by its developers). By checker, integer overflow and underflow 12, cross-program invocation four, missing owner check two, missing signer check two, account (type) confusion two, missing key check one, numerical precision one, and bump seed one, each statable from the code and the Solana runtime's semantics (arithmetic, deserialization type safety, and generic owner, signer, key, and program-id checks on input accounts) → ES.
column_justification: Eight checkers apply hand-written state-transition rules in a whole-program fixed-point data-flow analysis over Rust MIR (with HIR layouts for type confusion and name heuristics for signer and bump-seed accounts), and the reports are confirmed by hand; nothing is learned or generated → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "VRust: Automated vulnerability detection for Solana smart contracts" (no type named); abstract: "A key technical novelty is a set of static analysis rules for validating untrustful input accounts", checked "by translating source code into Rust MIR-based inference rules"; contribution list: "whole program static data flow analysis on Rust MIR-based inference rules" → Rule-based (step 3, one type named)

first_release: cited version, 2023; preprint arXiv:2309.03006 (2023-09) in the same year
row_justification: FuzzDelSol's largest labeled set is the 16 reports analyzed in depth from its run on 6,049 Solana mainnet programs (Section 6.2, Table 3; 14 exploitable bugs and two false alarms), each marked with its oracle class; by our tally of Table 3 the 14 are three missing signer checks, five arbitrary CPIs, five integer bugs, and one lamports theft, each statable from the program and the Solana runtime semantics → ES. The run's 92 potential vulnerabilities in 52 programs (30 missing signer checks, 12 arbitrary CPIs, 30 integer bugs, and 20 lamports-theft reports without any of the other classes) are unconfirmed, so not a labeled set; the Neodyme workshop programs and the emulated Wormhole missing key check (Section 6.1, Table 1) are also at the execution-semantics level.
column_justification: Hand-written bug oracles (missing signer, owner, and key checks, arbitrary CPI, integer bugs, and lamports theft; Section 5.3.3) inside a binary-only coverage-guided fuzzer built on LibAFL issue the verdict; no learned or generative model → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Fuzz on the beach: Fuzzing Solana smart contracts" (fuzzing); abstract: "propose FuzzDelSol, the first binary-only coverage-guided fuzzing architecture for Solana smart contracts"; contribution list, first two items: "We present the first fuzzing architecture" and "We design and implement new bug oracles" → fuzzing with hand-written oracles, one type named, Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: ZepScope's largest labeled set is the manual check of 300 warnings sampled from its run on 35,882 contracts (100 per chain, 31 false positives, so 269 confirmed; Section 6.2, Table 2), which gives no per-category counts; the warnings flag functions "potentially containing insecure OpenZeppelin code" (Section 6.2), vulnerabilities with no class → glossary line 4 → ES ‡. The 51-bug benchmark (Section 6.1, Table 1; 25 access control, five arithmetic overflow, one front running, and 20 caused by insecure OpenZeppelin checks with no class) also gives ES, 30 of its 31 classified cases; its front-running bug is the PM secondary, as are the timestamp or state checks among the mined facts (Section 4.6), whose conditions refer to mechanism state.
column_justification: Check facts are mined from the OpenZeppelin library code by static analysis (a Slither call graph and inter-procedural alias analysis) and matched against contracts by edit-distance similarity over check elements and majority voting, and CHECKER issues each warning; error messages are compared through Word2Vec embeddings and Word Mover's Distance (Section 5.3.1), an ML component recorded as secondary; no generative model → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Using my functions should follow my checks: Understanding and detecting insecure OpenZeppelin code in smart contracts" (no type); abstract: "we propose a novel tool named ZepScope that comprises two components: MINER and CHECKER" (no type); no contribution list → no type named, so the method decides (B.2 step 3), mined check facts matched by static analysis in the framework of Slither → Rule-based

row_justification: AChecker's largest labeled set is the sample of about 60 of its 624 SmartBugs-wild reports that two researchers inspected independently (53 true positives, 88.3 % precision; Section IV, Tables IV and V); every case is an access-control vulnerability, one class, so no breakdown is needed, and a missing or violated check whose condition refers only to the caller is generic → ES (B.1, missing checks). Its other labeled sets are smaller and of the same class: 15 CVE contracts (recall 80 %, Table III), 20 SmartBugs-wild contracts classified by a third-party expert (Table VI), and the ten inspected of 21 flagged popular contracts (nine true positives, Table VII).
column_justification: Static data-flow analysis infers access-control checks and their state variables, taint analysis tracks user input to them, and symbolic execution filters intended behavior; all hand-written, with no learned or generative model → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "AChecker: Statically detecting smart contract access control vulnerabilities" (static analysis); abstract: AChecker, "an approach for detecting access control vulnerabilities", that "infers access control implemented in smart contracts via static dataflow analysis"; contribution list, first and second items: "a novel static data-flow-analysis-based technique" and "a novel symbolic execution-based approach" → one type named, Rule-based (B.2 step 3)

row_justification: ReX generates exploits for 56 SmartBugs-Curated contracts (Table 10: reentrancy 10, access control 10, arithmetic 10, low-level calls six, bad randomness five, DoS five, time manipulation four, and other six), the larger labeled set; the 50 classified contracts are at the execution-semantics level → ES. Table 1 scores 114 attempts per model on the same benchmark in eight classes, front running (transaction-order dependence) four among them, all execution-semantics. The 38 real incidents of Web3-AEG (Table 11) fall in the same classes plus four cross-contract cases, which carry no property class.
column_justification: The abstract presents ReX as linking "LLM-based exploit synthesis to the Foundry stack" → LLM, Rule-based secondary (each PoC is judged by forge test against predefined class-level safety invariants). The framework, not the model, runs forge build and forge test and returns compile and test errors for regeneration on a fixed schedule → flag no (feedback the model does not request).
type_evidence: title: "Prompt to pwn: Automated exploit generation for smart contracts" (no type word); abstract: "We study that gap with ReX, an execution-grounded framework that links LLM-based exploit synthesis to the Foundry stack"; contribution list: "the first systematic empirical study of LLM-based automated exploit generation (AEG) for smart contracts" and "We implement the REX framework to evaluate LLM-based smart-contract AEG" → one type named → LLM

first_release: cited version, 2026; preprint arXiv:2609.14098 (2026-09) in the same year
row_justification: A stress-test benchmark of 13 purpose-built contracts with documented ground truth (nine deception vectors and four controls, Sections 3.2 and 3.3) scoring 22 single-shot LLMs; 11 contracts carry a privileged drain, "a function or sequence of functions that allows the attacker to extract all deposited funds" (Section 3.1), a breach of holder-balance integrity (B.1 scams), and two controls (C2 and C4) are benign. A benchmark takes row n/a (B.1) and is shown at the protocol-mechanism level, where its tasks fall.
column_justification: A benchmark is shown in the column of the detectors it scores (B.3); the systems it scores are LLMs given hex-encoded runtime bytecode in a single shot, "without tools or follow-up turns" (Section 3.1), so the model stage is terminal → LLM, flag no.
type_evidence: title: "The Deception Delta: Adversarial evaluation of LLM-based smart contract bytecode forensics"; abstract: "We evaluate 22 frontier models on 13 purpose-built contracts (9 deception vectors, 4 controls) across six prompt strategies"; contributions, first bullet: "Adversarial contract stress-test benchmark" → benchmark (B.3) scoring LLMs, one type named → LLM (B.2 step 3).

row_justification: SA-BGL detects money laundering among Bitcoin transactions, a system without smart contracts → non-DeFi (B.3), row n/a, not counted. Its largest labeled set is WalletExplorer, 317,987 transactions from March 2014 to May 2021, 62,217 of them labeled as laundering through the BitLaunder and BitcoinFog services and 255,770 as normal (F1 0.9025, Table III); Elliptic++ adds 4,545 illicit and 42,019 licit labeled transactions among 203,769. Laundering transactions carry no level of their own, so the work is shown in the PM row, as illicit-account classifiers are (Supplementary Appendix B.1).
column_justification: The title presents semantic augmentation with LLMs as the contribution beyond graph structure → LLM, ML secondary (B.2 step 4; read as a combination of graph learning and an LLM, the tie-break gives the same). For each transaction the framework computes nine behavioral factors with z-scores and p-values against baselines built beforehand from verified normal transactions, fills a fixed prompt template, and calls LLaMA-3-70B once at temperature 0; BERT encodes the generated text, and a dual-tower cross-attention fusion with the bipartite graph embeddings feeds the classifier that issues the verdict. The model calls no tool and the framework fixes the schedule → flag no, on the method text only (no code is released).
type_evidence: title: "Beyond graph structure: Semantic augmentation with LLMs for Bitcoin money laundering detection under economic networks"; abstract: "we propose a semantic-augmented bipartite graph learning framework for Bitcoin money laundering detection, which leverages large language models (LLMs) to enrich node semantics beyond structural information"; contribution list: "We propose a bipartite graph learning method with LLM-driven semantic augmentation for Bitcoin money laundering detection, named SA-BGL" → two types named, graph learning and an LLM; the title presents the LLM augmentation as the contribution beyond graph learning (B.2 step 4) → LLM, ML secondary

subgroup: an LLM paired with a trained classifier
row_justification: CodeXplain is evaluated on the iAudit set of Ma et al., 3,544 samples the paper counts as contracts (1,734 vulnerable, 1,810 non-vulnerable), whose positives are "curated from 263 reputable audit reports" (Section 4.1) and carry binary labels with no per-case class breakdown → glossary line 2 (audit findings) → ES ‡; line 4 also matches, and the first matching line applies. Its 14 named types (reentrancy, timestamp dependency, integer overflow, unchecked send, and ten more) are all execution-semantics properties, so no secondary row.
column_justification: Presented as combining LLM-generated code explanations with supervised learning (abstract, contribution list), the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM, ML secondary; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 writes one explanation for each of nine fixed prompts per contract, and a CodeT5-encoder fusion classifier trained on the labels issues the verdict; the framework fixes the schedule and no tool is called, so the flag is no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "... Training on LLM explanations to detect smart contract vulnerabilities"; abstract: "we propose CodeXplain, a novel SCVD approach that leverages the deep insights into code from LLM and the supervised learning capabilities of deep learning models"; contribution list: "a hybrid SCVD framework, CodeXplain, that combines the strengths of LLM-generated code explanations with the supervised learning ability" → the two equally (B.2 step 5) → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (ML secondary)

first_release: cited version, 2026; preprint arXiv:2604.04211 (2026-04) in the same year
row_justification: LOCARD's labeled sets are 1,200 THORChain cross-chain swap records for single-transfer tracing (Thor25HF-Mini, Table I, with ground truth from THORChain's official swap records; ordinary swaps, not attacks) and a subset of Thor25 traces annotated as linked to one exploiter address of the Bybit hack (size not stated), on which a five-transaction group-tracing case study is run (Section VII-C). The swaps are benign and the Bybit theft, a signing compromise at the trust boundary, is recorded as the out secondary, so no case counts at a level; the tracer takes the row of the incident it traces by the glossary (B.1, post-incident tracer), from the stated target "laundering sub-flows from the Bybit hack" → line 3 (hacks) → PM ‡.
column_justification: Presented as an agentic framework (title and abstract) → Agentic, Rule-based secondary (validation and heuristic scoring run as code); the Strategic Core, its Orchestrator, "determines the next strategic action, such as issuing additional retrieval tasks", and in the released workflow it routes to the Worker, which invokes blockchain tools in a thought-action-observation loop and returns their results to it → flag yes (released code).
type_evidence: title: "LOCARD: An agentic framework for blockchain forensics"; abstract: "we introduce LOCARD, the first agentic framework for blockchain forensics"; contributions: "We present LOCARD, the first ABF framework" (ABF, Agentic Blockchain Forensics) → Agentic (B.2 step 3, one type named)

row_justification: No labeled set; the paper labels 161,329 Uniswap and 470,712 PancakeSwap pools as one-day Simple Rug Pulls by its own rule (a pool whose events fall within one day, whose lower-value token is paired there only, and that has one Mint and one Burn of at least 99 % of the minted LP tokens; Def. 3.1, after Cernera et al.), with 145,654 and 238,280 scammer addresses, and reports no manual confirmation or correctness for them → stated target 'Rug Pulls' → glossary line 3 → PM ‡; liquidity-removal rugs are PM under the scam rule.
column_justification: No B.2 type is named in the title, the abstract, or the contribution bullets, so the method decides (step 3); rug pulls are identified by a hand-written definition (Def. 3.1), scam stars by StarDetector, chains by a search for maximal chains, and major flows by MajorFlowDetector (proved correct in Theorem 4.6), clusters by direct ETH and BNB transfers and shared scam pools, and contract similarity by an AST-Jaccard score; no model is learned → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: 'Serial scammers and attack of the clones: How scammers coordinate multiple rug pulls on decentralized exchanges' (no type); abstract, first sentence (the abstract has no proposal sentence): 'We explored the ubiquitous phenomenon of serial scammers' (no type); contribution bullets: 'We constructed two one-day Simple Rug-Pull datasets', 'We formally defined and identified typical scam patterns', 'We formalized the concept of scam clusters', and 'We proposed a cluster-aware scam profit formula' (no type) → step 3, the method decides.

subgroup: scam and rug-pull tokens by market behavior
row_justification: 500 rug-pull vs 500 benign tokens → PM
column_justification: Temporal GNN
type_evidence: proposal: "a temporal graph neural network-based solution"

row_justification: The one labeled case set is the RQ4 case study, the Nomad Bridge exploit (one incident), which an upgrade-aware Foundry invariant fuzzer detects with an oracle built from the proof-verification category (a message must not be processed unless it has been proven under a trusted root); the check refers to the bridge's own proof state → PM. The 727 unique invariants mined from 20,000 reverted transactions (12,222 reverted by an invariant, 6,958 clustered into 19 categories, Table V) are generated properties and reverts the paper does not label as attacks or bugs, so they do not govern; generic guards among the mined categories (access control, address sanity, and low-level input validation) are recorded as the ES secondary.
column_justification: The abstract's proposal sentence ("embeds these invariants using our BERT-based fine-tuned model, and clusters them by semantic intent") and contribution 1 ("RAVENBERT: A BERT-based embedding model") name a fine-tuned encoder and clustering (DBSCAN in the best configuration), ML by the B.2 step 2 boundary; no generative model is used, and two authors name the clusters by manual review; the case-study oracle is hand-written (Rule-based secondary); a study, not a detector.
type_evidence: title: no type; abstract, proposal sentence: "embeds these invariants using our BERT-based fine-tuned model, and clusters them by semantic intent"; contribution 1: "RAVENBERT: A BERT-based embedding model finetuned on a set of revert-inducing transaction invariants" → ML (B.2 step 3, one type named)

first_release: cited version, 2025; preprint arXiv:2509.23679 (2025-09) in the same year
row_justification: Table V gives per-type counts for the two labeled sets. The larger, D_m, holds 58 subcontract-misuse traces annotated by domain experts in 15 DApps from 16 real attacks; 31 are variable conflicts, in which reused subcontracts compute a critical variable such as a token's value inconsistently (Fig. 1a, LP tokens valued low in swap and high in swapUnderlying), a price-consistency failure (PM), and 27 lack a security check, which the paper defines as an omitted security check or incorrect access control (ES where the condition is generic; a check on mechanism state would be PM and only add to the majority) → PM, ES secondary. D_b, 56 contracts from a prior library-misuse study and mostly access-control incompleteness (ES), is smaller.
column_justification: Satellite matches method-level bytecode features to find reused subcontract code and checks SMV indicators grouped by type, a rule-based static analysis that issues the verdict; a transfer-learning model only recovers inherited methods as its input (ML secondary) → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Satellite: Detecting and analyzing smart contract vulnerabilities caused by subcontract misuse" names no type; abstract: "we propose Satellite, a new bytecode-level static analysis framework for subcontract misuse vulnerability (SMV) detection in smart contracts" and "Satellite utilizes a transfer learning method to recover the inherited methods"; contributions: "We propose Satellite, the first bytecode-level static analysis framework for detecting" SMVs; the static analysis framework is presented as the contribution and transfer learning only recovers its input (B.2 steps 4 and 7) → Rule-based, ML secondary

row_justification: Evaluated on SmartBugs-curated (143 contracts, 182 tagged vulnerabilities by DASP class), on a Code4rena set (784 high- and medium-severity findings in 243 of 6,454 contracts from 72 projects, with no class breakdown), and on the 13 CVEs selected after PropertyGPT, with 25 newly disclosed ones (Section V-B). The largest labeled set, the Code4rena findings, has no breakdown → glossary line 2 (audit or contest findings) → ES ‡. Among the 13 CVEs, an airdrop that lets the owner mint beyond the total supply (CVE-2018-18425) breaks holder-balance integrity and gives the PM secondary, as for SmartAuditFlow.
column_justification: Presented as a framework for lightweight models distilled from large teacher models (abstract). The students are pretrained generative models (LLaMA-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama, Gemma-2, and Mistral-Nemo variants) fine-tuned with SFT and QLoRA → LLM. The teacher models serve only in offline distillation and are not involved at inference (Section III-A); at detection the student reads the contract, outputs findings with a rationale, and calls no tool, so the model stage is terminal and the flag is no (method text).
type_evidence: title: "HKT-SmartAudit: Distilling lightweight models for smart contract auditing" (no type word); abstract: "we introduce HKT-SmartAudit, a framework for developing lightweight models optimized for smart contract auditing", distilled from "large teacher models" into "compact student models" (no type word); contribution list, first item: "Hybrid Knowledge Transfer Framework: We introduce HKT-SmartAudit, a novel framework that transfers knowledge from both advanced large language models and external domain-specific sources" (no type word) → B.2 step 3, the method: the students are fine-tuned generative models (LLaMA-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama, Gemma-2, and Mistral-Nemo variants) → LLM

first_release: cited version, 2026; arXiv:2604.26094 (2026-04) posted after it
row_justification: No evaluation set gives an attack type per case. The largest labeled set by positive cases is the real-world scan of about three million DEX transactions from January 2021 to December 2024, whose detections include 682 publicly disclosed incidents, identified by exploiter tags, and 56 previously undisclosed attacks validated by hand, against 79 false positives; the zero-shot set of 726 attack incidents from Phalcon and DeFiHackLab (Table 3 lists projects only), the balanced benchmark of 534 DeFiHackLab attack traces and 534 benign traces (Table 1), and the mixed set of 13,300 transactions (Table 2, no malicious count) give no type either → glossary line 3 ("attack incidents") → PM ‡. In the zero-shot set the paper names missed incidents of private key leakage, and Table 3 lists Bybit, a signing compromise; these are at the trust boundary, recorded as out secondary. It also names unverified call input attacks, in which a single external call drains the assets, recorded as ES secondary.
column_justification: The abstracted logic path of one confirmed attack is the template, and a weighted set-similarity score, with its weight and threshold tuned by grid search, flags later transactions that reach the threshold → Rule-based. CodeBERT clustering (ML) and GPT-4.1 validation (LLM) label function signatures offline, as input to that match, and are recorded as secondary types (B.2 step 7).
type_evidence: title: "GenDetect: Generalizing reactive detection for resilience against imitative DeFi attack cascade" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we develop a reactive detection framework, GenDetect, which achieves strong benchmark performance" (no type); contributions: "reactive detection generalization system" and "semantic extraction and logic matching framework" (no type) → B.2 step 3, the method (set-similarity matching against an attack template decides) → Rule-based; the abstract's goal sentence: "rapidly abstracted into an actionable and generalizable detection rule"

first_release: cited version, 2026; preprint arXiv:2604.13611 (2026-04) in the same year
