The paper treats these inconsistencies as faults of the code ("incorrect implementations or missing critical security checks in smart contracts will lead to fund theft", §1), not of the text, so it is not adjacent as DocCon is (B.3).
column_justification: Presented as built on pre-trained models (title, abstract, contribution list) → ML, no secondary type (Fig. 3): a fine-tuned BERT classifier keeps the comments that state a permission (§3.2); the contract's AST, parsed with python-solidity-parser, yields the commented function, the functions it calls, and its modifiers (§3.3, §4); and CodeT5, fine-tuned on the task, embeds each comment-code sequence, from which a BiLSTM predicts consistent or inconsistent (§3.4). BERT is an encoder, CodeT5 is used only to embed and generates no text, and the BiLSTM issues the verdict (B.2 boundary; the "pre-trained language model" of the contribution list is not a large generative model, as for SmarTest); the AST extraction applies no detection rule. Baselines: SmartCoCo on the 125-pair comparison set (38 of the 41 inconsistencies at precision 90.5 %, against 39 at 97.5 %; recall 92.7 % against 95.1 %, Table 2), and the learned CCI detectors of Corazza et al. (F1 85.0 %), Deep-JIT (34.8 %), and Rabbi et al. (73.5 %), with the framework itself on CodeBERT embeddings at 86.8 %, against 91.4 % (Table 4).
type_evidence: title: "Towards detecting comment-code inconsistency in smart contract via pre-training techniques" (pre-training, no generative model named); abstract, proposal sentence: "In this work, we employ pre-training techniques to detect CCIs on permission in smart contracts"; contribution list (§1): "We propose a new framework for detecting permission CCIs in smart contracts and define the detection as a two-stage classification issue" and "the pre-trained language model can provide remarkable performance improvement in CCI detection"; method (abstract, Fig. 3): "we utilize BERT to classify permission comments", CodeT5 adopted "to embed comment-code pairs", and "we make use of BiLSTM to predict inconsistencies" → one type named, learned models (B.2 step 3) → ML; BERT is an encoder and CodeT5 only embeds, producing no text (B.2 boundary)

row_justification: Two labeled sets, each one class (§4.2, §4.6). The larger is the 835 detections sampled "strategically ... based on their underlying oracles" from the 16,581 POMAs that POMABuster flags (Table 2) in 434,387,877 ERC-20 transfer logs of the 758 Ethereum tokens with a market capitalization of at least US$1M, January 2021 to May 2023 (unit: POMA, a manipulating trade with its linked arbitrage, which the paper also counts as a transaction). Each was checked on Uniswap prices read from an archive node and counted a true positive when the manipulating transaction moved the DEX's spot price by 2 % or more and the arbitrage exploited the move; all 835 were (worst-case false positive rate 0.95 % at 99 % confidence, against 28.58 % for the reimplemented DeFiRanger, 64 false positives among 294 sampled). The other, the paper's ground truth for false negatives, is 27 attacks: the nine Code4rena applications that Web3Bugs classes as price oracle manipulation (S1), each proof of concept run on a local test chain as written and split into two transactions in one block and in consecutive blocks, checked by an external auditor (§4.2, Appendix C); POMABuster detects all 27, DeFiRanger(o) 7. Every case is a price oracle manipulation, a trade that moves the price of a DEX "that the victim smart contract uses as its price oracle" followed by an arbitrage at the moved price (§2.2), a breach of price consistency at an on-chain-manipulable oracle (B.1) → PM; one class needs no breakdown, as for DeFiRanger. The sampled set's check confirms the price move and the arbitrage, not a victim's use of the price (the paper calls the revenue "operator profit" because arbitragers "may be bonafide third parties", §4.7), while the Code4rena victims are the audited applications; either set gives PM. The "6.5X" gain over prior work (abstract, §4.5) does not follow from Table 2, 16,581 against DeFiRanger(o)'s 5,371 (3.1 times). Deployment point: POMABuster reads the transfer logs of mined transactions (Google BigQuery, §4.1) and "performs offline detection of POMAs" (§5.2); the contribution list's detection "based on the blockchain's transactions at runtime" (§1) is detection on committed blocks, at 0.042 seconds per block (Appendix F), still a reading of transactions already on chain; and the online detection over pending transactions that §5.2 sketches is a goal whose resources the paper only estimates, with pending transactions POMABuster "cannot be run in real-time" until it is parallelized (Appendix F), a use left to future work → post-hoc.
column_justification: Presented as first-principle rules adapted from the SEC's definitions of wash sales and market domination (abstract, contribution list) → Rule-based, no secondary type. Algorithm 1 rebuilds trades from pairs of ERC-20 transfer logs (Definition 1); Algorithm 2 marks a trade as a price oracle manipulation when its amount, or a wash sale's summed amount, reaches a fraction σ of the token's total supply (Definitions 3 and 5); Definition 6 marks an arbitrage as a chain of trades with no loss in any token and a positive total gain; and Definition 7 reports an attack when such an arbitrage trades a manipulated token, within n blocks (§3.3, §3.4, §3.6). σ = 0.01 % and n = 2 are thresholds set on a seven-month subset of the logs, σ as the largest value whose candidates include every transaction DeFiRanger(o) flags (§4.3); nothing is learned. The one baseline is DeFiRanger, reimplemented because its authors released neither code nor data (§4.1). POMABuster's source code and datasets are released (§4.1, footnote 1).
type_evidence: title: "POMABuster: Detecting price oracle manipulation attacks in decentralized finance" (no type); abstract: "We first devise first-principle rules for detecting POMAs based on traditional stock market manipulation attacks" and, the proposal sentence, "We then propose POMABuster, which leverages these rules to detect POMAs spanning both single and multiple transactions"; contribution list (§1): "Propose first-principle definitions of POMAs based on the SEC's identification of suspicious trading patterns in traditional stock markets" and "we develop POMABuster, a POMA detection engine to efficiently identify potential POMAs ... POMABuster requires no prior knowledge of attack patterns, as it is based on first-principle definitions" → one type named, rules (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based

row_justification: The largest labeled set is the known-vulnerability set, 30,137 contracts from the Messy-Q Ethereum dataset kept where Oyente and Slither agreed and then inspected by hand for false positives (§5.1.1, §5.3.1; unit: contract), split 80:20 for training and testing (Table 4). Table 7 counts its vulnerable contracts per type, reentrancy 73, timestamp dependency 179, delegatecall 58, and transaction-ordering dependency 45, against 30,137 it lists as normal, and Table 5 scores each type (ASCD's F1 0.95, 0.94, 0.96, and 0.87, the mean of five seeds; the best baseline's 0.93, 0.90, 0.93, and 0.89, DefectChecker leading on transaction ordering). All four types are statable from the code and EVM semantics (delegatecall misuse; transaction-order dependence as a property of code, B.1 Ordering) → ES by evaluation; with per-type counts the ‡ falls. The abstract's "accuracy of 77% in detecting unknown vulnerabilities" is measured on a second, smaller set drawn from SmartBugs curated (136 contracts labeled by hand, §5.1.2): DeepSVDD flags as anomalous 135 of the 175 labeled vulnerabilities of six types withheld from training (access control 11 of 14, arithmetic 11/13, denial of service 5/5, short address 0/1, unchecked calls 37/45, gas-related issues 71/97; Table 6). That set holds only vulnerable cases ("it is not possible to directly provide an F1-value", §5.3.2), so the 77 % is a detection rate that counts no false alarm and no identification of the type; Table 6's F1 of 87.0 % adds an unstated number of clean contracts and treats them as the positive class. The six withheld types are execution-semantics properties as well (access control as a generic authorization check, Table 1), so no secondary row is recorded.
column_justification: Presented as an anomaly-detection model (abstract, contribution list) → ML, no secondary type. An LSTM over the runtime bytecode's opcode sequence and a GIN over the control-flow graph, its edges weighted by jump type, are pre-trained on normal contracts and contracts of the four known types and concatenated into a 512-dimensional feature; DeepSVDD, trained on normal contracts with an autoencoder as its feature map, flags a contract whose distance from the hypersphere's center exceeds δ = 52, chosen by grid search for the best validation F1, which the paper calls "an upper-bound benchmark" (§5.3.1); four binary two-layer networks then assign the known types, and a flagged contract that none of them claims is reported as carrying an unknown vulnerability (§4, §4.3, §4.4). No model generates text; Oyente and Slither only label the data (§5.1.1), and the CFG extractor partitions basic blocks and applies no detection rule.
type_evidence: title: "Anomaly detection services for blockchain smart contracts with unknown vulnerabilities" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "This article proposes a new Anomalous Smart Contract Detector, named ASCD, to effectively detect known and unknown vulnerabilities in smart contracts" (no type), then "detecting them with an anomaly detection technique named DeepSVDD" and "By joining LSTM and GIN, the semantic and control flow features are fused"; contribution list (§1.2): "We propose a new vulnerability detection model, ASCD, to detect both known and unknown vulnerabilities in smart contracts ... effectively detected using the single-category anomaly detection model DeepSVDD" and "a new method for feature extraction of smart contracts, which fuses the semantics and heterogeneous control flow features of a smart contract" → one type named, learned models (B.2 step 3) → ML

row_justification: STING is evaluated on 62 of 86 historical Ethereum mainnet attacks drawn from public incident lists (CertiK, DefiLlama, Rekt, DeFiHackLabs, Paradigm), those of 2021 and 2022 and some major earlier ones; 24 are left out of scope by root cause (17 private-key compromises or rug pulls, four off-chain component compromises, three without a fund loss on mainnet; Section 5.1, Table 3), unit attacks. Its semantic synthesis counterattacks 54 of the 62 (87.1 %), against 12 for a generalized front-runner; the eight failures are five cross-block attacks and three bridge or cryptography vulnerabilities whose signatures or proofs are tied to the attacker's wallet. Table 4 lists the attacks without a type, and the paper classifies none by the property it violated → glossary line 3 ("real-world recent exploits", attacks on DeFi protocols) → PM ‡; no evaluated case is placed at another level, so there is no secondary row. Its deliverable is a counterattack contract, an executable exploit of the victim contract that front-runs the attacking transaction and moves the funds at risk, and the paper measures its success → offensive (B.3); its input is an attacking transaction already identified ("We also assume that there is an identified attacking tx"), so post-incident also applies, and offensive takes precedence. The paper gives the set as 62 (abstract, Section 5), 63 (Table 4 caption), and 64 (conclusion).
column_justification: Attack information is identified on an archive node by Datalog-style inference rules over execution predicates (malicious entities by contract age, fund flows, and data dependencies; Section 4.1); the counterattack contract is synthesized by forced execution that rewrites control flow and call targets at JUMP and CALL, with fine-grained taint analysis as a further layer, in single-transaction replay, syntactic, and semantic syntheses run in parallel (Section 4.2), and validated by execution (Section 4.3). No model is learned (machine learning appears only as future work) → Rule-based.
type_evidence: title: "Your exploit is mine: Instantly synthesizing counterattack smart contract" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "In this paper, we present STING, a novel run-time defense mechanism against smart contract exploits" (no type), and "The key idea is to instantly synthesize counterattack smart contracts from attacking transactions"; contributions: "We propose a runtime counterattack defense to protect the assets of victim smart contract" and "We develop a series of novel techniques to precisely identify attacking txs and effectively synthesize exploit contracts in a timely manner" (no type) → no type named → B.2 step 3, the method (inference rules, forced execution, and taint analysis; nothing learned) → Rule-based

row_justification: Benchmark, row n/a. SC-Bench holds 5,377 Ethereum contracts with 15,975 violations of ERC rules (Table II: 5,211 ERC-20, 110 ERC-721, and 26 ERC-1155 contracts; Section III-B gives 5,241 ERC-20), each labeled with the rule broken and the function: 139 real violations, found by manual inspection of 30 ERC-20 contracts submitted for audit, and 15,836 injected by rule-specific edits to the contract's AST that compile (Section III); injection covers 85 of the 132 rules of the three standards (the introduction says 88). Every task is a violation of a rule the ERC standards state (such as a required event, a return value, or a throw condition), a property that exists because the standard defines it (B.1 description test, shared) → shown in the description-mismatch row. GPT-4, the one detector scored, finds 0.9 % of the violations without the oracle and 22.9 % with it (Section IV).
column_justification: A benchmark is shown in the column of the detectors it scores (B.3); it scores GPT-4 alone, given the ERC's official document with all its rules ("The first presents an ERC's official document with all rules to GPT") or, in the oracle setting, the violated rule and the code site with "a simple True-or-False question", at temperature zero; the model calls no tool and its answer ends the run → LLM, flag no (method text only; the release holds the dataset, results, and injection scripts).
type_evidence: title: "SC-Bench: A large-scale dataset for smart contract auditing" (no type); abstract: "We present SC-Bench, the first dataset for automated smart-contract auditing research" (no type), scored with GPT-4 ("without the oracle, GPT-4 can only detect 0.9% violations"); no contribution list → a dataset that scores one LLM → benchmark (B.3), one type named → LLM (B.2 step 3)

subgroup: agents advise analyzers that the orchestrator schedules
row_justification: The governing set is SoliAudit, 348 contracts "with labeled ground-truth vulnerabilities" (48 single-contract deployments and 300 cross-contract systems; §IV-B2), against which detections are compared "focusing on vulnerability types detectable by both tools" (§IV-A3): 409 vulnerabilities (unit: vulnerability; Table II), of which UniFuzz detects 394 (accuracy 96.33 %, as CrossFuzz). Table II counts them by type: assertion failure 139, integer overflow 126, block dependency 59, transaction order dependency 39, integer underflow 29, leaking ether 6, reentrancy 6, arbitrary memory access 2, locking ether 1, unprotected selfdestruct 1, and unsafe delegatecall 1. Each is statable from the code and EVM semantics (an assertion the code makes, arithmetic, dependence on block state, transaction-order dependence as a property of code by B.1 Ordering, ether leaked or locked as by ILF's oracles, a write to an arbitrary storage location, a generic missing owner check, and delegatecall misuse) → ES, 409 of 409, no ‡. The Etherscan set (503 production contracts) is labeled only where experts confirmed the tools' flags (44 of UniFuzz's 60; Table III, §IV-A3), a smaller set whose seven types, unchecked return value among them, are also ES, and the target types the paper names (reentrancy and state corruption, §III-A; integer overflow and underflow and access control, §IV-B2) are ES, so no secondary row is recorded. The abstract reports only coverage; Tables II and III report vulnerabilities found against a labeled set and confirmed by experts, so the work enters (B.3 scope); the coverage comparisons (RQ1, RQ2; Fig. 2, Table I) score no case.
column_justification: Presented as a framework that integrates "multi-layer static and semantic analysis, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) leveraging audit-driven knowledge, and orchestrated multi-agent collaboration" (abstract), "a unified, semantic, agent-driven fuzzing framework" (§I), whose agents carry its LLM work: Fig. 1 names the LLM semantic layer ("The Semantic Layer employs LLM to interpret code intent beyond syntax", §III-A) the "Semantic Analysis Agent" and places the "Input Generation Agent" in the RAG-based parameter generation, where parameters "are generated using a language model" (§III-B2), Gemini-1.5-flash (§IV-B1) → Agentic (B.2 steps 2, 4, and 5), with LLM (the title's "LLMs") and Rule-based secondary (Slither, the dataflow graph, and the evolutionary fuzzing loop, whose Feedback Agent applies "standard genetic operations" and whose executed test cases yield the vulnerability report, §III-C, Fig. 1; B.2 step 7). §III-C describes the first agent, as the "Code Analysis Agent", only as extracting "optimal sequences and critical paths from multi-layer analysis results". Flag no on the method text: the framework sets the schedule. Algorithm 1 runs Slither and the dataflow analysis before the one semantic-analysis call; the Input Generation Agent draws its strategy by fixed weights (optimal sequence 0.25, critical path 0.25, mutation 0.20, combined 0.20, random 0.10; Algorithm 3) and applies RAG parameters to every sequence (Algorithm 3, line 15), which Algorithm 2 requests from the RAG server with retries and a fallback "to boundary values when RAG services are unavailable" (§III-B2); retrieval is a top-k cosine lookup in a FAISS index of audit-report chunks built before the run (§III-B1); and in Fig. 1 the loop's mutation and crossover send "Query RAG" and receive "Get Params". Successful sequences "are stored for future retrieval, creating a self-improving feedback loop" (§III-B2), so results return to later prompts on the framework's schedule, not at a model's request; no model decides whether, which, or when a tool runs (B.2 flag rules). The paper speaks of "an open-source implementation provided for community adoption" (§I) but names no repository and reports no trace or ablation of a tool step, so the evidence is the method text only.
type_evidence: title: "UniFuzz: A unified fuzzing framework for smart contract vulnerability detection with LLMs and audit reports"; abstract: "We introduce UniFuzz, a unified framework that integrates multi-layer static and semantic analysis, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) leveraging audit-driven knowledge, and orchestrated multi-agent collaboration", then "UniFuzz employs Large Language Models (LLMs) for deep semantic analysis and targeted test input generation, guided by insights from real-world audit reports and coordinated through specialized agents"; no enumerated contribution list, §I: "We introduce UniFuzz, a unified, semantic, agent-driven fuzzing framework that integrates multi-layer analysis, RAG-enhanced audit knowledge, and collaborative multi-agent coordination for comprehensive vulnerability detection across both single and cross-contract scenarios" → agents named in the proposal sentence and §I, LLM-driven by Fig. 1 (the "Semantic Analysis Agent" is the LLM semantic layer, and the "Input Generation Agent" serves the RAG-based parameter generation), so the B.2 step 2 boundary does not set them aside; §I names them as driving the fuzzing (step 4), and the proposal sentence presents them as integrated with static and semantic analysis and RAG (step 5, the newest type) → Agentic, with LLM (title) and Rule-based (fuzzing, static analysis) secondary

row_justification: The governing set is the verification of 30 contracts retrieved from Etherscan, 8 ERC-20, 18 ERC-721, and 4 ERC-1155, chosen from 50 after proxies were removed ("Verification Results"; unit: contracts, counted per violated property in Figs. 15–17). The compliance check finds 9 non-compliant contracts (Fig. 15): two ERC-20 contracts without the Approval event, six ERC-1155 contracts without balanceOf and the URI and TransferSingle events (six, although the set is said to hold four ERC-1155 contracts), and one ERC-721 contract with none of the required functions or events. Model checking finds 7 ERC-20 contracts in violation of the properties of Table 8 (Fig. 16: P1, transfer's balance check, 4; P3, transferFrom fires Transfer, 2; P4, transferFrom throws unless the sender is authorized, 7; P5, approve fires Approval, 2) and 10 ERC-721 contracts in 65 violations of the 18 properties of Table 9 (Fig. 17, its bars summed: P18, ownerOf throws for the zero address, 7; P4, P10, and P15, 5 each). Each property transcribes a requirement the standard states (Tables 8 and 9 print the requirement beside its CTL formula: throw conditions, required events, and the functions and events of the interface), so every case is a property that exists because EIP-20, EIP-721, or EIP-1155 defines it (B.1 description test; shared) → DM, and a set whose cases all sit at one level needs no breakdown; the authorization checks the standards require are coded as their transfer semantics, as for SymGPT's privilege-check rules and TokenCat's Type-II. The paper reports its outputs correct ("our tool generates accurate outputs for all verified properties", under "False positives and false negatives"), so the set is labeled by detections whose correctness it reports; read as unconfirmed, the set would be unlabeled and the stated target ("compliance with established standards", the ERCs named) would give glossary line 1 → DM ‡, the same row. The evaluation of four LLMs by BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, cosine similarity, and G-Eval (Fig. 14) scores property generation, not violations, so it is not a set of cases (B.1); the user-defined functional templates and the gas-related execution properties are not evaluated and name no attack class, so no secondary row is recorded.
column_justification: nuXmv issues the verdict, a property satisfied or violated with a counterexample: each contract is modeled as a hierarchical extended finite state machine with inheritance and transaction-execution refinements (Algorithms 3–9), abstracted into BIP and translated to SMV by BIP-to-NuSMV, and checked against CTL properties; a static module compares the function and event selectors of the compiled bytecode (PUSH4 and PUSH32) with those of the ERC interface (Algorithm 2). Mistral, chosen over Gemma 7B, Llama 2, and Llama 3 (Fig. 14), extracts each function's and event's requirements from the annotations of the ERC interface (Algorithm 1) and fills the CTL templates of Table 6 with them, and the user validates the generated properties before verification (Fig. 13); the model sees no verification result. It translates the standard's requirements into the properties the model checker decides on, the role SymGPT's model plays, but SmartGuard presents a model checking-based tool whose LLM writes that input, where SymGPT presents the two types as combined and PropertyGPT presents the LLM as driving verification (B.2 step 6) → Rule-based, LLM secondary; as a rule-based entry it carries no flag.
type_evidence: title: "SmartGuard: Verifying safety and compliance of Ethereum smart contracts" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we introduce SmartGuard, a model checking-based tool for Ethereum smart contracts" (model checking), then "we abstract contract models into Behavioral Interaction Priority (BIP) and utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) for formalizing properties into Computation Tree Logic (CTL) formulas"; contribution list (five bullets): first "We model Smart Contracts as Hierarchical Extended Finite State Machines (H-EFSMs)", then the BIP abstraction, "For standard-related properties, we use LLMs to automatically generate CTL properties from natural language requirements extracted from ERC interfaces", "We conduct verifications of smart contract models using model checking against specified properties", and "a static verification approach to ensure that the ERC-based contracts comply with the relevant Ethereum standards" → model checking named in the proposal sentence and the LLM in another sentence and in the third bullet, neither presented as driving the other nor as combined with it (steps 4 and 5 do not decide) → step 6: the contribution list puts the formal modeling for model checking first, the LLM third, where it extracts the standard's requirements and writes them as the properties the model checker decides on → Rule-based (LLM secondary)

subgroup: business-logic invariants inferred without a description
row_justification: The largest labeled set is Dataset 1's overall-detection evaluation (§5.3, Table 6): 253 true positives, with 8 false positives (precision 96.9 %), among RcAudit's reports on 132 DeFiHackLabs projects (1,082 contracts) associated with logic-flaw incidents (Table 1), each report first assessed by three LLMs, disagreements adjudicated by hand, and the labels verified by two authors (unit: vulnerability). The recall evaluation on the same 132 incidents, each report matched against the documented exploit root cause (74 rediscovered, 56.1 %, against SmartInv 34, GPTScan 9, PromFuzz 3, and ItyFuzz 3; Table 5), is smaller. Neither set is broken down by the property violated or confined to a stated list of types → glossary line 3 (logic-flaw incidents, exploits on DeFi protocols, from DeFiHackLabs) → PM ‡, as for PropertyGPT and ItyFuzz; DeFiHackLabs is an incident record, not an audit or contest corpus. Its "intent" is not stated intent: an LLM distills function- and contract-level business intent from the code, call graph, and read and write sets, "optionally augmented with developer documentation" (§4.1.2, Fig. 4), and the Arbiter validates findings against this "inferred business intent" (§4.3), and no evaluated project is said to supply documentation, so the decision path reads no named description (reads_description = no; B.1 Description read); no evaluated finding is tied to a statement in a named description, and a stated target of logic or intent vulnerabilities with no named description is not DM (B.1 description test), so no DM secondary is recorded. The cases the paper describes are mechanism invariants (PM): OTSeaStaking's claim resets the withdrawal flag and permits a second withdrawal (§3.1), AzukiDAO processes a claim without checking its claimed marker, a check over mechanism state (§5.2; B.1 missing checks), and TokenRewards resets a user's debt while payouts are paused (§5.4). Dataset 3's 22 previously unknown vulnerabilities in 13 audit and bounty projects from Code4rena, Cantina, and Sherlock (8 high- and 11 medium-severity, confirmed by the project teams and audit platforms) carry no breakdown ("Most issues violate invariants in staking, liquidity, or reward distribution logic", §5.4), so the glossary's line for audit and contest findings places them at ES, the secondary row, as SynerFuzz's untyped exploit set gives its secondary; Dataset 2 (18 audited high-TVL projects) holds no positive case. Fuzzing runs in a local instrumented EVM emulator, seeded by a replay of the target's historical transactions that bootstraps seeds and constants and holds no post-exploit information (§4.2.1, §5.3), so the detector is static.
column_justification: No agent is named in the title, the abstract, or the contribution list (B.2 step 2), and the paper presents its LLM reasoning as the method that runtime contexts ground → LLM, Rule-based secondary: the fuzzer, ItyFuzz's engine with an instrumented EVM emulator, the candidate-invariant filter that flags violating contexts, and Slither and Aderyn for storage layouts (§4.1.1, §4.2, §5). GPT-5 distills function- and contract-level business intent (§4.1.2, Fig. 4); DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus scores the functions for each sampled state and synthesizes transactions for the function and base state the scheduler draws (§4.2, Figs. 5 and 6); Claude Haiku 3.5, the Runtime Logic Auditor, reasons over each violating context the filter retains, and GPT-5, the Evidence-Based Arbiter, validates, deduplicates, and re-scores the hypotheses against the inferred intent (§4.3, Fig. 7). Flag no on the method text: the framework, not the model, sets the schedule. The model's scores enter a two-stage sampling the designers wrote (Algorithm 2, Eqs. 1–3) and its transactions join the seeds and are executed, a mapping from the model's output to execution that is part of the schedule (B.2, VeriRAG-Agent); the scoring and synthesis calls run asynchronously in background processes, on the first state of each group and on later states with probability 0.01 (§4.2.1, §5), so the states a model sees are drawn by the framework, not requested by the model, and no call receives the result of the transaction it proposed; the Auditor and the Arbiter call no tool and request no new run or context, reasoning over what the filter hands them. The model thus chooses inputs inside a schedule the framework sets. Table 2 ablates the model's guidance of the fuzzer (intent-aware scheduling, LLM-synthesized transactions), not a step at which a model requests evidence and reasons over it, and the archived implementation (Zenodo, the paper's refs. [17] and [18]) was not read, so the evidence basis is the method text.
type_evidence: title: "Evidence-grounded logic vulnerability detection for smart contracts via runtime context reasoning" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we present RcAudit, a system for detecting smart-contract logic vulnerabilities via runtime-context–enhanced LLM reasoning" (LLM), then "applies a state- and intent-aware fuzzing strategy to generate logic-critical runtime contexts, and performs LLM reasoning over selected contexts"; contribution 1: "We present RcAudit, which integrates runtime execution evidence with LLM reasoning for logic vulnerability auditing"; contribution 2: "We design a framework that integrates contract fuzzing with a reasoning mechanism that evaluates the contract from two distinct perspectives" → the LLM reasoning is presented as the detection method, which the fuzzing's runtime contexts enhance (B.2 step 4); read as combined, the tie-break of step 5 also gives the newer type → LLM (Rule-based secondary); no "agent" in any of the three places (step 2)

row_justification: The governing set is D_label, the 180 token contracts with source code that the authors labeled while building the taxonomy, at least 20 for each behavior (§VI); Fig. 19 gives its 234 labeled behaviors by type (FRBScan's 231 true positives and 3 false negatives, all three analysis failures, accuracy 98.7 %; unit: behavior in a contract): FRB1 rebasing balances 20, FRB2 supply deflation on transfer 20, FRB3 supply inflation on transfer 21, FRB4 fees charged on transfer 69, FRB5 front-running 24, FRB6 rewards allocated to holders 20, FRB7 freezing a holder's tokens 20, FRB8 pausing transfers 20, and FRB9 reentrant transfers 20. FRB2, FRB4, and FRB6 credit the recipient of a transfer with less than the call's _value, FRB3 credits the parties with more, and FRB1 and FRB6 change holders' balances outside any transfer, against EIP-20's "Transfers _value amount of tokens to address _to" and the Transfer event it requires; the paper names FRB1–FRB4 as inconsistencies TokenScope detects ("Tokenscope is capable of identifying FRB1-4, where these inconsistencies are typically manifested", §VI.1), and the first of the B.1 token rules places such cases at DM, shared, as it places TokenScope's fees charged inside a standard method → 150 of 234. FRB7 and FRB8 are an owner's privilege to freeze a holder's tokens or halt every transfer (B.1 scams, holder-balance integrity, as for Pied-Piper) and FRB5 sells the token's own holdings on an exchange ahead of a holder's swap (front-running a victim's trade, B.1 ordering), PM, 64; FRB9's callbacks to the sender and recipient after the balance update open a reentrancy (ES), 20 → DM by majority, PM and ES secondary. The paper's scope ("behaviors of Ethereum ERC20 token contracts that deviate from the ERC20 standard", §IV) is not taken as given: EIP-20 states no freeze, pause, front-running, or callback rule, so those cases are not DM. If FRB4's fee, which goes to the token's owners, were read as a privilege to tax balances rather than as a transfer amount that differs from the call, the row would be PM (133 of 234). The 100 contracts sampled from the 804,844 of D_wild (no false positive or negative) and the Ramifi case are smaller sets. The title, the research questions (RQ1–RQ3), and three of the four contributions present the study of these behaviors, their threats, and their prevalence (65.8 % of 804,844 tokens carry at least one), and the tool is developed "to enable a large-scale study" (abstract, §IX) → study (B.3), as for Trace2Inv, shown and not counted.
column_justification: Gigahorse builds the control-flow graph of the bytecode and its basic facts (Fig. 11), and hand-written Datalog rules run on Soufflé infer, in turn, reachability and dependency, function parameters, token operations, function-level behaviors, and the nine behaviors (Figs. 12–17), with token-behavior heuristics such as the over-approximation of total-supply operations (§V); nothing is learned → Rule-based, no secondary type. The rules encode the standard transfer (a NORMALTRANSFER subtracts the amount from the sender and adds it to the receiver) and recognize ERC-20 tokens by the standard's functions, so the decision reads EIP-20 as rules its authors encoded from it.
type_evidence: title: "Unveiling financially risky behaviors in Ethereum ERC20 token contracts" (no type); abstract, proposal sentence: "we conduct the first systematic study that uncovers these behaviors and their concrete threats to DeFi applications" (no type), then "we develop FRBScan, a novel tool that automatically identifies financially risky behaviors in ERC20 token contracts by combining Datalog analysis with token behavior inference heuristics"; contribution 3 of four: "We develop a novel tool, FRBScan, which accurately, efficiently, and automatically identifies financially risky behaviors in token contracts by combining Datalog analysis with precise heuristics" → Datalog analysis with heuristics, one type (B.2 step 3) → Rule-based; the other three contributions (analyzing FRBs and their threats, the taxonomy, the large-scale study) present the measurement (B.3, study)

subgroup: an LLM paired with a trained classifier
row_justification: DeepDesc's largest labeled set is its machine-auditable set (§4.1.1, Table 3): 1,093 vulnerable contracts from the collection of Qian et al. (cross-modality mutual learning, WWW 2023), with per-type counts (delegatecall 196, integer overflow 275, timestamp dependency 349, reentrancy 273; unit: contract), each type scored as a binary task against 500 non-vulnerable functions drawn from the Top200 contracts (§4.1.3, Table 7). All four types are execution-semantics properties, statable from the code and EVM semantics, so the set needs no breakdown → ES (B.1, Which cases count), as for Smart-LLaMA-DPO and Agent4Vul. The machine-unauditable set that the paper calls its core objective (§4.1.2, §4.3; Table 4: 210 vulnerable functions from Web3Bugs and DefiHacks, 138 price oracle manipulation, 34 atomicity violations, and 38 inconsistent state updates) is smaller, so it does not govern (B.1, Governing set); price oracle manipulation, the majority of it, is PM (on-chain-manipulable oracles) → PM secondary. No evaluated property is stated in a named description: the descriptions are the model's own, and the retrieved Code4rena reports are third-party texts (B.1), so there is no DM secondary.
column_justification: Presented as integrating RAG-enhanced LLMs with deep learning (abstract, contribution 1), the two equally → tie-break, the newer type → LLM, ML secondary; GPT-3.5-turbo writes one description of each code sample from a fixed few-shot prompt that holds the code and the formatted Code4rena report nearest to it, retrieved from a FAISS index of 1,201 reports built before the run (k = 1; §3.1–3.2), and a classifier over the BERT embeddings of code and description, fused by MLB pooling and trained on the labels, issues the verdict (§3.3); the framework fixes the schedule, the model calls no tool, and a lookup in a store built before the run does not count (B.2), so the flag is no (method text only).
type_evidence: title: "DeepDesc: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with large language models for smart contract vulnerability detection" (LLM); abstract, proposal sentence: "integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs) and deep learning"; contribution 1: "combines the code understanding capabilities of RAG-integrated LLMs with ... deep learning" → the two equally (B.2 step 5) → tie-break, the newer type → LLM (ML secondary); the classifier's encoder is BERT, ML by the B.2 boundary
